agent.what: Each agent is one fresh session of the model named here, with no memory of the other sessions, given the evidence files and the instructions and allowed to read nothing else.

meta.what: Thirty independent AI agents, each given the same evidence pack and the same instructions, each walked from the raw partner-reported tuna figure to its own estimate of Kiribati's true tuna exports (FOB value of fish that Kiribati-resident operators sold to non-residents) in six signed layers. This file holds the aggregates across agents, their principles and their notes; no agent did arithmetic that is published.
notes: Spread across agents (10th to 90th percentile, min, max) is disagreement given identical evidence. It is not a standard error and not a confidence interval; shared blind spots do not appear in it.
own_lo_mean and own_hi_mean are the averages of the 80% ranges the agents themselves gave for each layer and for the end value; they are wider than the spread across agents.
The official figures were in the evidence pack as evidence of what the compiler recorded; they were not the target. Each agent's note on how it used them is in official_use.
Residence and ownership are conditions in the agents' reasoning, never findings about any vessel or company. No names appear in the pack or in this file.
meta.themes_note: Themes were written by one summariser pass over the principles (tracker/agents/themes_prompt.md); counts were recomputed by tracker/build_themes.py from the members it listed.

layers.label: Freight and insurance (CIF to FOB)
layers.description: Importers value goods at their own border, including freight and insurance. Exports are valued at the exporter's border. The layer removes the difference.

layers.label: Catch of vessels run by non-resident operators
layers.description: Fish caught by a Kiribati-flagged vessel whose operator is resident elsewhere is not a Kiribati export: the sale is between two non-residents. The layer removes it. Access fees such operators pay are income, not goods, and are not part of the bridge.

layers.label: Resident catch coded to another origin
layers.short:
Resident catch
coded to
another origin
layers.description: Fish caught by Kiribati-resident operators that importers did not code as Kiribati-origin, for example from vessels under another flag or coded to the country of landing or processing. The layer adds it.

layers.label: Resident sales by routes the partner series does not capture
layers.short:
Resident sales
by routes
not recorded
layers.description: Fish sold by residents to non-residents at sea, to partners that do not report, landed in third countries, or under product codes outside the tuna series. The layer adds it.

layers.label: Treatment: processing, merchanting, re-exports
layers.description: Goods sent for processing without a change of ownership, merchanting, fish consumed at home and re-exports change what counts as a good. The layer adds or removes accordingly.

layers.label: Other adjustments named by the agent
layers.description: Anything else the agent judged material, named in its rationale; zero when nothing.

start.label: Partner-reported tuna, sum of monthly returns (CIF)

rationales.text: Importers record CIF (P4). Sea-to-port freight and insurance, including about 38 days to Thai ports, are removed at 5% of the raw total (range 2-9%). Applied first, so L2 onward is on an FOB basis. Rate is a prior, not observed.

Kiribati-flagged catch run from abroad is not a Kiribati export (P2, P3). Resident-operated share of FOB mirror taken as 18% (80% range 8-41%), from 7,415 resident-pattern hours and 43 of 116 register vessels with address hints (02, P5). Rest removed.

The mirror follows the flag (P3). Allows for 2.4% (0.8-7%) of the 234.9 USD m of Nauru- and Tuvalu-flagged imports (03) being run by Kiribati residents, as the three registers form one fleet family (02). No file shows operators of those flags; range is wide and bounded below by zero.

Resident sales by routes the partner series misses (P6): buyers outside the importers listed, fresh air-freighted fish, products outside the codes. Taken as 11% (4-30%) of the resident catch identified in L2 and L3. No direct data (01, 02).

Small deduction (P7): resident fish sent abroad for processing with no change of ownership, or resold as merchanting, is not a gross goods export. Central 3% of resident flow, range from +3% to -10%. Not observable in the pack, so kept small (05).

Timing (P7): importers record fish about 38 days after hand-over. Moving the monthly series back by that lag lowers the year by 1.88 on the whole mirror (01); scaled to the resident share of fish. Lag comes from 2018-2021 chain data (02).

Remove freight, insurance and carrier handling to reach FOB at the vessel: about 8.5% on the Thai route (70.84 of 81.77) and 6% on other routes. No freight data in the pack; rates are model knowledge. P3.

Keep Kiribati-flag fish only where the operator is resident (P1, P2). Resident-address hours of 7,415 point to a small minority, so about 8% of the FOB mirror is kept and 92% removed. Hours lack a denominator: range keeps 3% to 22%. P4.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels flagged elsewhere, importers code that fish to the other flag (P2). The pack has no residence data for other registers; taken as 15% of resident fish already in the mirror, range from zero. Weakest layer.

Adds (a) annual-only reporters' extra 3.71 CIF, scaled to resident share and FOB, and (b) 25% of resident fish sold by routes outside the partner series: other buyers, fresh or other HS codes, and about a third of at-sea chains not reaching Thailand. P5.

If resident fish goes to affiliated plants abroad under retained title, or moves under a lease, it is not a goods export on arrival (BPM6 10.17(f), Table 5.1). Taken as 5% of retained resident fish, negative, with a positive tail. P7.

Timing: ownership passes at the at-sea sale, the mirror records arrival about 42 days later. Fewer arrivals in early 2024 than early 2023 imply a small downward cut-off adjustment on the resident share. P7.

Importers record CIF (P2, file 05). Remove freight and insurance at 5.5% of the Thai value (70.84) and 7.5% of the rest (10.93); longer routes to the Americas sit at the high end. Applied to the whole mirror.

If the operator is not resident, the sale is between non-residents (P1, P3). Resident share of the FOB mirror taken as 12.0% (7,415 resident-pattern hours, file 02); the rest, 67.80, is removed. Band 5%-25%.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels on other registers, importers code that catch to the other flag (P1, P4). Take 4% of Nauru and Tuvalu coded imports at FOB plus 0.1% of five other flag states (file 03). Weakly evidenced; wide band.

Resident sales missed by the partner series (P5): 12% of the resident base for carriers, destinations and products outside the series; resident share of annual-only partner returns (3.71); 35% of annualised customs tuna (0.00, file 06).

No evidence sizes processing without change of ownership, merchanting, sales between residents or fish kept in the economy (P6). Centre set at zero with a symmetric band; a negative tail is possible if exported fish was bought from non-residents.

Timing: importers record arrival about six weeks after the at-sea sale, so the mirror year and sale year differ slightly (P8, file 02). With roughly flat flows the net effect is set to zero with a narrow band.

Importers record CIF; exports are FOB. Removing sea freight and insurance for frozen tuna carried by reefer from the catch area to Thai and other ports, taken at 5.5% of CIF (range 3 to 8.5%). Same rate in all years.

Origin follows the catching vessel's flag, so fish from Kiribati-flagged vessels run by non-resident operators is in the mirror but is not a Kiribati export. Resident-run share taken as 15% of Thai-coded and 40% of other flows (18% overall); the rest removed.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels under other flags, importers code that fish to the flag state. Small allowance: Nauru and Tuvalu registers hold most register-fleet encounters, but the pack gives no sign of Kiribati residence for them.

Resident share of fish coded Kiribati by partners reporting annually only (3.71 USD m CIF outside monthly sums), plus a small allowance for non-listed processors and fresh or chilled lines. Home customs shows no tuna exports in 2023, so it adds nothing.

Small deduction for resident-run fish delivered for processing where ownership does not pass until after processing, and for any merchanting. No direct evidence; the range includes zero. Local-use fish is outside the mirror.

Timing: imports are recorded about six weeks after the sale at sea (median lag 38 to 42 days). Moving the mirror back by that lag on the resident portion lowers 2023 slightly, as early-2024 imports are below early-2023 imports.
Importers value CIF. Freight, insurance and trader margin taken as 7.5% of the raw mirror (range 5-11%) to reach FOB at the point ownership passes.

Resident-run share of the FOB mirror set at 18% (range 9-36%). The other 82% is Kiribati-flag fish run by operators not resident in Kiribati; sales between non-residents are not Kiribati exports. Share rests on register hints and hours.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels under other flags, importers code that fish to those flags. Assumed about 1% of Nauru and Tuvalu coded value plus a little elsewhere, FOB. No operator data, so wide range.
Resident sales at sea to carriers for non-reporting markets, fresh fish and other codes: 30% uplift on resident in-mirror fish (4.08), plus resident share of annual-only reports (3.71 CIF, 0.62).
Small net deduction for resident fish retained or toll-processed without change of ownership, partly offset by merchanting margins. Nothing in the pack sizes it, so near zero with a wide range.
Timing: ownership passes about 38 days before the importer records arrival. Early-2024 flow is below early-2023 flow; the whole-mirror shift of -1.6 is applied to the resident share.
Importers value CIF. I take 7% off Thai-bound fish (70.84, carrier freight over weeks) and 2.5% off other destinations (10.93, mostly direct landing). Ranges 4-10% and 1-5%.

After FOB the mirror is 76.54. If operators are resident in Kiribati for about 12.00 of it (roughly 16%, range 6-35%), the rest is a sale between non-residents. Resident-pattern hours are low and weakly tied to the mirror.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels on other flags, importers code that fish to those flags. The Nauru and Tuvalu series rose strongly, but the pack has no operator residence for them, so I add a small amount with a wide range.

Resident fish missed by the monthly series: annual-only partners (3.71 more in annual totals, resident part about 0.55), non-reporting buyers (Thai share 87% vs 67.5% in the carrier chain), and chilled or other products. Mostly judgement.
Small allowance for resident fish held on consignment or processed without change of ownership, which is not yet a goods export. No pack evidence on size; the range includes zero.
Timing: ownership changes at sale at sea, the import is logged about 6 weeks later. Early-year imports (Jan to mid-Feb) fall from 10.64 to 9.45 in the next year, scaled to the resident part.
Importers value CIF; the at-sea sale is FOB. Carrier freight and insurance on frozen tuna hauled for weeks assumed 5.5% of CIF (range 3-9%), same rate each year. P2, P4; files 01, 05.

Removes Kiribati-flagged catch run by non-residents. Resident-run share of the FOB mirror set at 17% (about 10-29%) from 7.4k register-address hours. Thai-bound carrier trade is 87% of the mirror and mostly foreign-run. P2, P3, P4; files 02, 01.
Adds fish run by Kiribati residents under other flags, coded to those flags. 1.5% of Nauru plus Tuvalu imports (234.9 USD m), as FOB; range 0.5-4.5%. Evidence thin, kept small. P6; files 03, 02.

Adds the resident-run share of partner gaps: annual-only reporters (3.71 USD m, observed) and unlisted buyers (6% of raw, inferred), as FOB, plus 1.0 USD m fresh or chilled tuna outside the HS codes. P5; files 06, 01.
Deducts 10% (range 0-20%) of the resident-run total for catch owned by non-residents under charter or processing arrangements, and merchanting margins, which are not gross goods exports. P7; file 05.

Timing: sale at sea precedes the importer's record by a median 42 days, so each mirror year holds late sales of the prior year. January-February arrival shift (-1.16 USD m CIF) scaled to resident-run FOB. P4; files 01, 02.

Importers value CIF. Thai-bound fish is 87 percent of the 2023 mirror and moves by carrier over a long route, so about 8 percent is removed for Thai-bound fish and 4 percent for other partners, 7.5 percent blended. Sale point is at sea or ex-vessel. P4, P1; files 01, 05.

Mirror codes by flag, not operator residence. Resident-pattern hours are 7,415, a small and weakly mirror-linked base. About 19 percent of the FOB mirror is treated as resident-operated (range 7 to 40); the rest is sales between non-residents. P2, P3, P5; files 02, 03, 05.

Resident operators may run vessels flagged elsewhere, and importers code by flag. Other-flag imports are large (Nauru and Tuvalu alone 235) but no link to Kiribati residents is observed, so a fraction of a percent of them is added, with a range from zero. P2, P3; files 03, 05.

Adds the resident share of annual-only partner returns (gross gap 3.71) plus 15 percent of resident-operated catch sold via non-reporting destinations, third-country landings or codes outside the mirror. Coefficient is a judgment. P6; files 01, 06.

If the resident operator is paid for fishing and the catch belongs to a non-resident owner, the transaction is a service, not a goods sale. Taken as 10 percent of resident catch (range 0 to 25). Customs showed no tuna exports. P7, P8; files 05, 06.

Ownership changes about 38 days before Thai arrival, so the year's exports are arrivals shifted by that lag. Early-year Thai arrivals were lower in 2024 than in 2023, trimming 2023 slightly; scaled by the resident share. P1; files 01, 02.

Importers value CIF. Remove about 6% freight and insurance on Thai-coded fish (70.84) and 8% on other partners (10.93); long reefer chain (P3). Range is 3-10% of the mirror; the pack holds no freight data.

Remove fish of Kiribati-flag vessels whose operator is not resident in Kiribati. Resident-operated part set near 31% of the FOB mirror (35% of Thai-coded, 6% of other partners' landings), anchored on 7,415 resident-address hours and a mirror that does not follow those hours (P1, P2, P4).

Fish of resident operators coded to another flag or to a landing or processing country. No operator data for other registers, and Nauru and Tuvalu flows are large, so a small positive is allowed. Low resident-address hours this year give little reason for more (P2, P5).

Annual-only reporters add 3.71 to the monthly mirror (annual 85.48 versus 81.77), taken at 25% resident; plus resident fresh or chilled and other-code lines, and sales at sea to destinations that do not report. Customs tuna near zero (P5, P8).
Small deduction for resident fish sent for processing abroad without change of ownership, and resales that are merchanting rather than own catch (P6). No evidence on scale; the range spans zero.

Timing: ownership changes at sea; importers record arrival about 38 days later. January to mid-February imports were lower in 2024 than in 2023, so shifting the window trims the resident part slightly (P7). Flows are lumpy.

Importers record CIF; exports are FOB. Freight and insurance taken as 4% of Thai-coded value (long reefer haul; Thai share 87%) and 3% of other partners' value. Smaller if a resident operator carries its own fish (P4, P1).

Removes fish from Kiribati-flag vessels whose operators are not resident: a sale between non-residents is not a Kiribati export. Resident share taken as 14% of the FOB mirror, given low resident-pattern hours (7.4k) and few address hints. If the operator is resident, it stays.

Adds fish of Kiribati-resident operators carried under other flags and coded to other origins, taken as a quarter of resident Kiribati-flag fish. Nauru and Tuvalu are coded at 181 and 54 USD m. No hours exist for other flags, so the range is wide.

Adds resident fish outside the seven importers' monthly series: about a fifth of resident fish for other buyers, third-country landings and other HS lines, plus the resident share of annual-only reporters (3.71 gap to Comtrade totals). Sales at sea delivered to a reporter are already in the mirror.

Small deduction (3.5% of resident fish) for fish not sold to a non-resident in the year: processing without change of ownership and fish kept in the economy. Merchanting and re-exports taken as negligible. Larger if resident operators use toll-processing contracts.

Calendar timing: fish sold at sea reaches the importer about 42 days later. Thai-coded January-February arrivals fall from 10.22 (2023) to 8.61 (2024), so 2023 sales sit slightly below 2023 arrivals. Applied to the resident part only.

Importers value at CIF, Kiribati exports are FOB (P4). Freight and insurance taken at 7% of the Thai-bound part (87% of the mirror) and 6% of the rest; about 6.9% overall. Range 4-11% Thai, 3-15% other (fresh air freight).

Mirror follows flag, not residence (P2, P3). Resident-pattern hours (7,415) are a small part of Kiribati-flag effort and most flagged fish comes from chartered or foreign-run vessels (P5). Residents assumed 13% of FOB mirror value (range 3-28%); the rest removed.

Resident operators may also run vessels under other flags, including the neighbouring registers, or have fish coded to a landing or processing country (P3, P5). Sized at 18% of resident fish already in the mirror. Not directly observed, so the range is wide.

Resident fish missed by the monthly series: annual-only reporters (annual minus monthly gap 3.71, resident share about 0.45) plus a 30% uplift for sales at sea, third-country landings and non-reporting buyers; a third of at-sea transfers did not reach Thailand (P6).

If a resident unit manages catch for a non-resident owner, or fish is processed abroad without change of ownership, there is no Kiribati sale (P8, P1). Taken as 8% of resident fish in L2-L4. No contract data; range 1-20%.

Cut-off timing: at-sea sales reach the importer's record about 38 days later (P8). Thai arrivals in January to mid-February 2024 were below those of 2023, so 2023 sales were slightly below 2023 arrivals for the resident share.

Importers value imports CIF. Removing about 3.5 percent of Thai-bound fish and 5 percent of other buyers' fish gives value at the point of sale. Range 1 to 7 percent of the mirror. Uses the Thai and non-Thai split.

Flag does not decide residence. If the operator is not resident in Kiribati (charterers, foreign-run partners), the sale is between non-residents. Resident share taken as 22 percent of FOB value (range 8 to 42), anchored on register-address hours and low official tuna returns.

If Kiribati-resident operators also run vessels flagged elsewhere, importers code that fish to other origins. No direct evidence; sized at about 17 percent of the resident core with a wide range. Nauru and Tuvalu series show flag switching is common.

Resident sales at sea to carriers bound for non-reporting buyers, third-country landings, fresh product and unlisted species sit outside the seven-reporter, listed-code mirror. About a third of at-sea transfers are not followed by a Thai call. Sized at about 18 percent of the resident core.

If some resident-owned fish is consigned for processing without change of ownership it is not a goods export; resident merchanting adds only a net margin. Not directly sized; small net negative with a wide range.

Timing. Sale at sea precedes the importer's record by about six weeks, so 2023 sales equal the mirror shifted back. Net effect is early-2024 minus early-2023 Thai flows, applied to the resident Thai-bound share.
Importers value at CIF. Freight and insurance after the sale point come out: about 6% on Thai-bound fish, 7% on others, wide for carrier margins and trader terms. Applied to the whole mirror.

Kiribati flag does not make the operator resident. About 20% of flag-coded fish is taken as run by Kiribati-resident operators (resident-address hours 7,415; hints on 43 of 116 vessels). The other 80% is a sale between non-residents. Share very uncertain.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels under other flags, importers code the fish to those flags (Nauru plus Tuvalu series 235). A small share, about 1.3%, is assumed. No direct evidence; wide range.

Resident sales the series cannot see: annual-only reporters (3.71 gap, resident share), non-reporting ports and non-HS fresh fish (15% of resident fish), and a thin 2023 non-Thai series (13% of mirror against 24-34% in 2017-22).

Net small. Fish sent for processing without change of ownership is not a goods export (negative); resident merchanting margins on fish bought from non-resident-run vessels add a little (positive). Nothing in the pack sizes either.

Timing. Importers record on arrival, about 38 days after the at-sea sale; true exports follow the sale date. Shifting monthly Thai arrivals back 1.25 months lowers 2023 slightly, applied to the resident share only.
Freight and insurance in CIF values: 6.0% of Thai-coded 70.84 and 2.5% of other partners' 10.93. The carrier leg to Thailand drives most of it. Contract terms and rates are uncertain.

Keeps only the resident-operated part of the FOB mirror: 14% (6-30%), 10.81 of 77.25. The rest is Kiribati-flag fish run by non-resident operators, so sales between non-residents. Share inferred from register address hours (7,415).

Fish of Kiribati-resident operators on vessels flagged elsewhere: 1% of Nauru/Tuvalu-coded fish (234.9 CIF) plus 0.1% of other Pacific flags, converted to FOB. No vessel-level evidence; bounded by pool size.
One-third of resident-run mirror catch (3.60) for sales at sea or landings no partner coded to Kiribati, plus 0.51 for annual-only reporters (gap 3.71 at 14% resident share, FOB).
No evidence of processing without change of ownership or merchanting by residents; centred on zero. Toll processing would raise the export to the final sale value; local use would lower it.
Timing: ownership passes at sale, about 38 days before the Thai import date. Monthly Thai data give -1.10 on all Thai-coded fish at 60% weight; resident share 14% and FOB applied.

CIF to FOB: freight and insurance of about 6.5% on Thai-bound carrier fish (70.84) and 3% on other partners (10.93). Rates are from model knowledge, ranges 4.5-9% and 1.5-4.5%. Handling margins may sit inside the range.

Removes Kiribati-flag fish whose operator is probably not resident (charter, foreign-run, flag of convenience). Inferred resident share of the FOB mirror 28% (80% range 11-46%). Resident-address hours 7,415 are a hint only; no fleet total is given.

Adds fish of Kiribati-resident operators on vessels of other flags that importers code elsewhere. Nauru and Tuvalu series show vessels change register, but there is no address data for them. Set small, floor at zero, wide upper range.

Two parts. About 1.01 for partners reporting annually only (annual total 3.71 above the monthly sum, converted to FOB and resident share). About 3.00 for sales to non-reporting partners, fresh or chilled fish outside the listed HS codes, and third-country landings.

Small allowance for resident catch sent for processing without change of ownership or kept at home, partly offset by possible net merchanting margins. Evidence cannot size it, so the centre is near zero with a wide two-sided range.

Timing of ownership change (named). Ownership changes at sea about 42 days before the importer records the fish. With arrivals falling between January-February 2023 and 2024, sales in the calendar year are lower than arrivals. Scaled by chain share 68%, FOB factor and resident share.
CIF to FOB (P3). About 5% off Thai-bound 70.84 and 8% off other 10.93, 5.4% overall; the 87% Thai share keeps the blend low. Range reflects 3-7% on Thai-bound and 5-12% on other fish.

Charged on the FOB mirror, 77.36. Kiribati-flag fish counts only if the operator is resident (P1, P2). Resident-pattern hours of 7.4k, with a flat mirror, suggest about 11% resident-operated (range 4-25%), so 89% is removed (P4).

Added if Kiribati-resident operators run vessels under other flags that importers code to that flag (P2). Assumed 1% of Nauru and Tuvalu coded imports (234.9) and 0.1% of other Pacific flags (738.8), at FOB. No address data for these flags; wide range.

Resident fish the partner series does not hold: sales at sea or landings with no reporting importer, other HS lines, annual-only reporters (gap 3.7). Set near 30% of recorded resident catch (P5). Only 2-4 monthly reporters in much of 2023 argues for a wide range.

Small and two-sided (P7): fish kept in the economy or processed without change of ownership removes; merchanting margins and double-recorded re-exports reshape. Centre at minus 3% of resident exports; the range allows a small positive.

Timing (P8): the mirror counts arrival month, ownership changes at sale at sea about six weeks earlier. Shifting the series back lowers 2023 by 1.8%; applied to the at-sea share of resident exports, about 1.3% of them.
Remove carrier freight and insurance: 5% of Thai-recorded value (long carrier haul, 87% of 2023 mirror) and 3.5% of other partners (shorter hauls). Ranges 3-7.5% and 2-5.5%.

Remove fish from Kiribati-flagged vessels whose operator is not resident. Resident-operated share of FOB mirror set at 17% (range 6-40%): register-address hours of 7,415 are small against the mirror and most flagged effort runs under charter or foreign ownership.

Add catch of Kiribati-resident operators carried under other flags or coded to landing or processing country. Sized at under 2% of Nauru- and Tuvalu-coded imports plus a small allowance elsewhere. No operator data for those flags, so the range is wide.

Add resident-operated sales the monthly series cannot see: annual-only reporters (gap 3.71, resident share only, 0.61) plus 20% of the resident part for non-reporting buyers, third-country landings and fresh or chilled lines outside the HS codes.

Small net treatment effect: resident fish processed abroad without change of ownership is removed; merchanting margins on fish bought from non-residents are added. No data, so set near zero with a wide range.

Timing: imports are dated at arrival, sales at change of ownership. A 38-day median lag moves about 1.25 months of flow across each year end; from January-February arrivals, net effect on the resident part is a small reduction.
Importers value CIF. Carrier freight and insurance taken as about 6.5% of Thai-coded 70.84 and 6% of other partners' 10.93. Ownership changes at the vessel, before freight. Range 4-9%.

If the operator is not resident, the sale is between non-residents. Resident-pattern hours (7,415) imply about 7% of Kiribati-flag output is resident-operated (range 3-14%), so 93% of the FOB mirror (76.51) is removed.

Resident operators may run vessels flagged elsewhere, coded to those flags. Nauru and Tuvalu flagged imports (234.9 CIF) are 2.7 times the Kiribati series; about 1.1% of them is assumed resident-operated. Very uncertain.

Resident fish sold by routes the series misses: fresh or chilled fish outside the HS codes, non-reporting destinations, and annual-only partners (annual total 3.7 above monthly sum). Taken as 22% of resident-operated fish plus a resident share of that gap.

No material treatment adjustment: direct sales to non-residents are a change of ownership, and processing without ownership change, merchanting and re-export are not evidenced. Range leans up for processing-contract cases.

Timing: partner records lag the sale by about six weeks (median 42 days), but true exports are by sale date. Thai-coded early-year imports fall slightly from 2023 to 2024, so a small negative on the resident share.

Importers record CIF; strip freight, insurance and brokerage. About 8.5% of value for Thai-bound fish (87% of the 2023 mirror) and about 6% for other buyers, 8.2% overall. Margin is assumed, not observed.

If the operator is not resident in Kiribati, the sale is between non-residents. Resident share of Kiribati-flag fish set near 19% (7-38%): resident-address hours were 7,415 and only 43 of 116 register vessels carry an address hint. The rest is removed.

Add fish caught by Kiribati-resident operators on vessels of other flags, coded to those flags. Taken as 2% (0-7%) of the FOB Nauru- and Tuvalu-coded series. The pack has no residence data for those flags, so the range is wide.

Resident share of the extra 3.71 that annual-only reporters add (Comtrade annual less monthly sum, only 2-5 monthly reporters for much of 2023), plus 15% of the resident base for at-sea sales to carriers bound for unreported buyers and other codes.

Remove about 10% of resident-operated flows where the catch may be owned by a non-resident (contract fishing or toll processing), so only the fee is a service, not a good. Upper end allows a small merchanting margin.
Timing: sales at sea precede import recording by about 38 days, so the calendar-year shift is early-2024 imports less early-2023 imports, scaled to the resident share. No other item identified.

Importers value CIF; exports are FOB where ownership changes (P4). Freight and insurance on frozen tuna, 87% of the mirror going to Thailand and the rest on shorter hops, taken at 5.4% of the mirror, range 3% to 8%.

Removes 72% of the FOB mirror as Kiribati-flag fish run by operators not resident in Kiribati; a sale between non-residents is not a Kiribati export (P1, P2). Resident share 28%, range 12% to 43%, from 7,415 address-pattern hours and low mirror value per such hour (P6).

If Kiribati-resident operators run ships under Nauru, Tuvalu or other flags, importers code that fish elsewhere (P3, P7). Taken as about 2% of Nauru- and Tuvalu-coded imports (235 million USD CIF), converted to FOB. No operator data, so the range is wide.

Resident sales the monthly series misses (P5): annual-only reporters' extra 3.7 million, scaled by resident share (1.0); 12% of resident-run mirror fish sold by routes with no partner record (2.6); fresh chilled fish outside the tuna codes (1.5).

Some resident-run fish may be consigned for processing abroad without change of ownership, and the same fish can be recorded by two importers after landing in one and re-export to another (P1). Taken as about 3.5% of resident-run fish.
Timing: importers record arrival, a median 38-42 days after the at-sea sale (P5). Moving Thai arrivals back to sale dates lowers 2023 by 1.6 million, about 2.3%; applied to the resident share.
Importers value CIF. Freight and insurance taken as 6% of Thai-recorded value (70.84) and 3.5% of other partners (10.93), since other partners often receive direct landings. P3; files 01, 06.

If the operator is not resident, the sale is between non-residents. Resident-operated share taken as 14% of the FOB mirror (10.80); the remaining 86% is removed. Anchored on 7,415 resident-pattern hours and 43 of 116 vessels with usable addresses. P1, P2, P4; file 02.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels flagged to other Pacific states, importers code that fish elsewhere. No register data for those flags; taken as 1% of the FOB value of Nauru- and Tuvalu-coded imports. P2, P5; file 03.

Three parts: partners reporting annually only (3.71 CIF, resident share) 0.49; resident fish reaching buyers or codes outside the series, 15% of resident fish in the mirror, 1.62; fresh or chilled tuna outside the HS codes, 0.80. P5; files 01, 06.

No evidence of toll processing or merchanting by residents; Kiribati has no tuna processing of scale, and fish kept for local use is neither exported nor in the mirror. Zero, with a range for unknown joint-venture contracts. P8; model knowledge.

Timing: importers record fish one to two months after the sale at sea (median 38 days), so the calendar-year mirror differs from sales in the year. Estimated from Thai monthly values (-1.83), applied to the resident share at half weight. P6; files 01, 02.

Thai-bound fish (70.84) at about 6% freight and insurance, other partners (10.93) at about 3%. Importers record CIF; an export is valued at the point of sale (P3, P2). Contract terms are unobserved, hence the range.

Resident-operated share of the FOB mirror taken as 22% (range 10-45%), so 78% is removed as sales between non-residents. Basis: small register-address hours that do not track the mirror (P1, P4). Largest single source of uncertainty.

Catch of resident operators on vessels flagged elsewhere is coded to other flags (P2, P6). No address data for other registers; set near 10% of the resident mirror part, with a range from almost nothing to several USD m.

Resident share of annual-only partner records (+0.8; annual total 85.48 vs monthly 81.77), missing non-Thai destinations given few 2023 monthly reporters (+1.5), and chilled fish outside the HS codes (+1.0) (P5).

About 3% of resident fish may move within a group, go for toll processing without change of ownership, or stay in the economy, so is not a goods export (P8). Merchanting by resident traders could offset. Thin evidence.

Timing: sales at sea precede import records by a median 38 days, so early-year arrivals belong to the prior year. Applying the resident share to the Thai flow shift gives a small negative (P5). Other timing effects not sized.
Remove freight and insurance: about 6.5% of the 70.84 Thai-recorded value and 5% of the 10.93 other-partner value, importers valuing CIF.

FOB mirror 76.62. Resident-operated share set near 11% (low resident-pattern hours, 7,415, and few register address hints), so about 89% is catch of vessels with non-resident operators, a sale between non-residents.
Resident operators with vessels flagged elsewhere would be coded to other origins. No direct data; set at about 30% of the resident-coded amount, range from zero.
Annual-only partners add 3.71 CIF (observed), scaled to the resident share; plus about 25% of resident-coded fish for omitted destinations, fresh tuna codes and sales at sea not coded to Kiribati.
About 5% of the resident total removed for fish kept locally, processing without change of ownership and merchanting, which are not ordinary goods exports.
Timing: sales at sea precede the import record by about 6 weeks (median 38-42 days). Resident activity rose in 2023, so sale-year exports exceed import-year records slightly.
Importers value CIF. Freight and insurance taken as 5% of the CIF mirror (range 2.8-7.2%) for frozen carrier shipments, 87% of which go to Thailand (P3, P4).

Flag does not fix residence (P2). About one-third of Kiribati-flag value judged resident-operated (80% range 15-53%), so two-thirds of the FOB mirror is sold between non-residents. Based on 43 of 116 vessels with address hints and 7,415 resident-pattern hours (P5).

Resident operators may run vessels flagged in Nauru or Tuvalu, whose catch importers code to those states (P3). Taken as about 1.8% of the FOB Nauru and Tuvalu mirror (USD 235m CIF). No residence data exist for those flags.

Thai share of 87% against 68-75% implied by carrier chains, and only 2-4 reporting partners a month, suggest some non-Thai sales were not coded to Kiribati; resident share applied. Small allowance for fresh and other forms outside the HS set (P6).

Small net effect: fish a resident operator sends for processing before any sale is not a goods export, and merchanting counts margin only. Taken as about 2% of resident-operated catch, sign uncertain (P7).

Timing of ownership change. Sales at sea precede the importer's record by about six weeks, so early-2023 arrivals belong to 2022 sales and early-2024 arrivals to 2023 sales. January 2024 arrivals were lower; resident share applied (P7).

Importers record CIF (P4). Freight, insurance and any trader margin before first sale taken as 6 percent of the mirror. Range 3.5 to 10 percent because most 2023 fish (87 percent) went to Thailand on carriers over five to six weeks.

The mirror follows the flag, not the operator (P2, P3). Resident-pattern hours of 7.4k, about two to three vessel-equivalents, suggest a minority resident share. Set at 24 percent of FOB mirror (10 to 45); the other 76 percent is removed.

If operators resident in Kiribati run vessels on the Nauru or Tuvalu registers, importers code that fish to those flags (P3, P6). Those flags carry 235 USD m; a 2 percent resident-operated share gives 4.7. No direct evidence of the share, so the range is wide.

Annual-only reporters add 3.71 CIF to the monthly sum; at FOB and resident share that is 0.8. Add about 2.4 for fresh or chilled fish outside the HS set, non-reporting partners and third-country landings (P6). At-sea sales mostly already reach Thai records.

Goods for processing without change of ownership and merchanting are not gross goods exports (P1). No evidence of material resident tolling or trading of this fish; local landings are not in the mirror. Zero, with a small upside for processed-product sales.

Cut-off timing: ownership changes at sale, importers record about 38 days later (P8). The Thai monthly series gives a small net shift for the resident share. Includes a small allowance for fish counted by two importers after onward shipment.

Importers value imports CIF (05). Carriage and insurance come off at about 8% for carrier cargo to Thailand (Thai share 87% of the mirror, 01) and 5% for other routes, 7.6% overall. Rates are model knowledge. P3, P8.

Coded by flag (P1; 05), but Kiribati-flag vessels run from abroad sell between non-residents (P2). Resident-run share set at 12.0% of the FOB mirror, scaled from 7,415 resident-address hours (02), with almost no tuna in customs returns (06). Hours are not value. P4, P7.

Fish caught by Kiribati-resident operators on vessels under other flags is coded to those flags, so the mirror misses it (P1, P5; 03, 05). No direct evidence; set at 18% of resident-run Kiribati-flag catch, wide range. Inferred.

Adds the annual-versus-monthly partner gap (85.48 vs 81.77; 01, 06) at FOB and resident share (0.41), plus 16% of resident catch for sales at sea bound for ports that do not report, third-country landings, and fresh or other products outside the HS codes. P5.

Small deduction for merchanting margins and for fish processed abroad without change of ownership, neither a full goods export (P6; 05). Set at 4% of resident-run catch; direction fairly clear, size not. Inferred.

Sale at sea precedes arrival by a median 42 days (P6; 02), so 2023 sales map to arrivals from mid-February 2023 to mid-February 2024. Net shift in Thai arrivals is -1.23 CIF (01); applied at FOB and resident share. Contract terms could change the sign.

Importers value CIF. Bulk reefer freight and insurance over a median 38-42 day voyage to Thailand is taken as 6% of the mirror (range 3-10%) and removed, giving FOB at the point of sale. No freight rates are in the pack.

The flag-coded mirror holds all Kiribati-flag catch. Register-address hours (7.4k) point to a resident minority. About 12% of the FOB mirror (range 4-28%) is taken as resident-operated; the rest, fish sold between non-residents, is removed.

If a Kiribati-resident operator runs vessels under other flags (locally based foreign-flag vessels, reflagging among Kiribati, Nauru, Tuvalu), importers code that fish elsewhere. Sized at a quarter to a third of resident Kiribati-flag fish, with a long upper tail.

Resident fish reaching buyers outside the monthly series: annual-only reporters, non-reporting partners, fresh or other HS lines. The 2023 Thai share (87%) exceeds later years (70%), so non-Thai flows look partly uncaptured; only the resident fraction is added.

Small net removal: resident-operated fish sent to affiliated plants abroad for processing without change of ownership is not a goods export, and merchanting is recorded net. No processing data exist, so the range spans removal and a small addition.
Timing. The mirror counts arrival; ownership passes about 40 days earlier. Replacing this year's January-February arrivals with next year's, applied to the resident share, gives a small reduction.

Importers value imports CIF (P3). Thailand takes 70.84 of 81.77; remove about 7.5% of CIF for long-haul reefer freight and insurance, and about 4% on the non-Thai part (landings, shorter hauls). Rates are model knowledge: ranges 4-11% and 1-8%.

If the operator is not resident in Kiribati, a sale between non-residents is not a Kiribati export (P1). Resident-address hours are small (7,415) and the flag-coded mirror does not follow them (P4), so about 12% of the FOB mirror is treated as resident-run; the rest is removed.

Resident operators may run vessels flagged elsewhere (Nauru and Tuvalu registers move with Kiribati in the fish-transfer chain) or land fish coded to a processing country (P5). No direct count; set near 28% of the resident-run amount in the mirror, with a wide range.

Resident sales at sea to carriers, landings in third countries, fresh or chilled fish under other HS codes, and partners reporting annually only (gap 3.71, resident share only) are outside the monthly series (P5). Not measured; sized near one third of the resident mirror amount.

Goods sent for processing without change of ownership are not goods exports, and merchanting is recorded net (P6). Nothing shows either is large for resident operators; a small net removal, with a range that includes a small addition.

Timing: ownership changes at sea about 42 days before the importer records arrival (P6). With resident flows up from 2022 hours, calendar-year sales slightly exceed arrivals. Small net of possible double counting where one lot passes two importers.

P1: importers record CIF (files 00, 05). Frozen tuna carried to Thailand bears about 7% freight and insurance, direct landings about 5%. Blend by the 87% Thai share (file 06) gives 7.2% of the raw mirror. Sized from model knowledge; plausible range 4-10%.

P2, P3, P8: flag does not set residence. Resident share of the FOB mirror set at 20% (range 8-40%) from resident-pattern hours of 7.4k (file 02) and the 87% Thai carrier-route share (file 06). The other 80% is a sale between non-residents and is removed.

P4: if a Kiribati-resident operator runs vessels under another flag, importers code the fish to that flag (files 03, 05). No direct count exists, so about 1.7% of the FOB Nauru and Tuvalu series (file 03) is added; the range runs down to near zero.

P4, P5: adds resident fish the series misses: destinations outside the seven reporters (about 15% of resident mirror), annual-only partners (Comtrade annual 85.48 less monthly 81.77, file 06) and fresh or other-species products outside the HS codes (about 1.0).
P7: the pack cannot size tolling, merchanting or re-export effects and the question counts fish residents caught, so the layer is centred on zero with a symmetric range rather than a guessed value.

P6, P8: timing. Importers record at arrival, about 40 days after sale (file 02). Thai-route arrivals in early 2024 were below early 2023 (file 01), so fewer 2023 sales fall in the next year than 2022 sales fell into 2023. Applied to the resident share, FOB.

Importers record CIF. Remove freight and insurance: about 7% of Thai-bound value (87% of the 2023 mirror, carried by reefer to Thailand) and 3% of other partners' value (mostly direct landings). Thai and non-Thai split from file 06.

Share of Kiribati-flag fish run by Kiribati-resident operators set at 30% (80% range 12-58%); the other 70% is a sale between non-residents. Flag does not decide residence, and the address hint covers 7,415 fishing hours, only a proxy.

If Kiribati-resident operators also run vessels under other flags (Nauru and Tuvalu carry large coded volumes), that catch is outside the Kiribati-origin series. Set at 10% of the resident-operated amount, range 0-35%; nothing in the pack sizes it directly.

Adds resident fish the monthly seven-reporter series misses: partners reporting annually only (annual total 3.71 higher, taken at FOB and resident share), non-reporting hubs (15% of resident fish; 2023 reporter coverage thin) and fresh tuna under other codes (1%).

No tuna passed customs in the 7 months reported, so no local-processing adjustment. Processing without change of ownership and net merchanting could move this either way; they are not sized, so the range is wide around zero.

Sales at sea precede Thai customs records by about 38 days, so calendar-2023 sales match arrivals from early February 2023 to early February 2024. Early-2024 arrivals were below early-2023 in January (6.07 against 8.98) and above in February (8.45 against 4.15); net effect scaled to Thai-bound resident fish.

start.label: Partner-reported tuna, sum of monthly returns (CIF)

rationales.text: Importers record CIF (P4). Sea-to-port freight and insurance, including about 38 days to Thai ports, are removed at 5% of the raw total (range 2-9%). Applied first, so L2 onward is on an FOB basis. Rate is a prior, not observed.

Kiribati-flagged catch run from abroad is not a Kiribati export (P2, P3). Resident-operated share of FOB mirror taken as 19% (80% range 8-44%), from 8,496 resident-pattern hours and 43 of 116 register vessels with address hints (02, P5). Rest removed.

The mirror follows the flag (P3). Allows for 2.4% (0.8-7%) of the 228.8 USD m of Nauru- and Tuvalu-flagged imports (03) being run by Kiribati residents, as the three registers form one fleet family (02). No file shows operators of those flags; range is wide and bounded below by zero.

Resident sales by routes the partner series misses (P6): buyers outside the importers listed, fresh air-freighted fish, products outside the codes. Taken as 11% (4-30%) of the resident catch identified in L2 and L3. No direct data (01, 02).

Small deduction (P7): resident fish sent abroad for processing with no change of ownership, or resold as merchanting, is not a gross goods export. Central 3% of resident flow, range from +3% to -10%. Not observable in the pack, so kept small (05).

Timing (P7): importers record fish about 38 days after hand-over. Moving the monthly series back by that lag lowers the year by 1.55 on the whole mirror (01); scaled to the resident share of fish. Lag comes from 2018-2021 chain data (02).

Remove freight, insurance and carrier handling to reach FOB at the vessel: about 8.5% on the Thai route (68.75 of 97.57) and 6% on other routes, whose share is larger this year. No freight data in the pack. P3.

Keep Kiribati-flag fish only where the operator is resident (P1, P2). Resident-address hours of 8,496, close to 2023, point to a small minority: about 8% of the FOB mirror kept, 92% removed. Range keeps 3% to 22%. P4.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels flagged elsewhere, importers code that fish to the other flag (P2). No residence data for other registers in the pack; taken as 15% of resident fish in the mirror, range from zero.

Adds (a) annual-only reporters' extra 7.05 CIF, scaled to resident share and FOB, and (b) 25% of resident fish sold by routes outside the partner series: other buyers, fresh or other HS codes, at-sea chains not reaching Thailand. P5.

If resident fish goes to affiliated plants abroad under retained title, or moves under a lease, it is not a goods export on arrival (BPM6 10.17(f), Table 5.1). Taken as 5% of retained resident fish, negative, with a positive tail. P7.

Timing: ownership passes at the at-sea sale, the mirror records arrival about 42 days later. Fewer arrivals in early 2025 than early 2024 imply a small downward cut-off adjustment on the resident share. P7.

Importers record CIF (P2, file 05). Remove freight and insurance at 5.5% of the Thai value (68.75) and 7.5% of the rest (28.82); longer routes to the Americas sit at the high end. Applied to the whole mirror.

If the operator is not resident, the sale is between non-residents (P1, P3). Resident share of the FOB mirror taken as 11.8% (8,496 resident-pattern hours, file 02); the rest, 80.82, is removed. Band 5%-25%.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels on other registers, importers code that catch to the other flag (P1, P4). Take 4% of Nauru and Tuvalu coded imports at FOB plus 0.1% of five other flag states (file 03). Weakly evidenced; wide band.

Resident sales missed by the partner series (P5): 12% of the resident base for carriers, destinations and products outside the series; resident share of annual-only partner returns (7.05); 35% of annualised customs tuna (0.70, file 06).

No evidence sizes processing without change of ownership, merchanting, sales between residents or fish kept in the economy (P6). Centre set at zero with a symmetric band; a negative tail is possible if exported fish was bought from non-residents.

Timing: importers record arrival about six weeks after the at-sea sale, so the mirror year and sale year differ slightly (P8, file 02). With roughly flat flows the net effect is set to zero with a narrow band.

Importers record CIF; exports are FOB. Removing sea freight and insurance at 5.5% of CIF (range 3 to 8.5%), the same rate as other years. A larger non-Thai share may carry slightly different freight, within the range.

Origin follows the flag, so fish from Kiribati-flagged vessels run by non-resident operators is not a Kiribati export. Resident-run share 15% of Thai-coded and 40% of other flows (22% overall, up because non-Thai flows rose to 28.8); the rest removed.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels under other flags, importers code that fish to the flag state. Same small allowance as 2023; resident-pattern hours rose only 15% and the pack shows no resident link for other registers.

Resident share of fish coded Kiribati by annual-only partners (7.05 USD m CIF outside monthly sums), plus a small allowance for non-listed processors and fresh or chilled lines. Customs tuna exports of 0.59 show only a little local landing.
Small deduction for resident-run fish delivered for processing where ownership does not pass until after processing, and for any merchanting. No direct evidence; the range includes zero.

Timing: imports follow sales at sea by about six weeks. Early-2025 imports are below early-2024 imports, so calendar-year sales in 2024 sit slightly below calendar-year imports for the resident portion.
Importers value CIF. Freight, insurance and trader margin taken as 7.5% of the raw mirror (range 5-11%) to reach FOB at the point ownership passes.

Resident-run share of the FOB mirror set at 17% (range 8.5-34%). Resident hours rose 15% while the mirror rose 19%, so share is flat. The rest is Kiribati-flag fish run by operators not resident in Kiribati.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels under other flags, importers code that fish to those flags. Assumed about 1% of Nauru and Tuvalu coded value plus a little elsewhere, FOB. No operator data, so wide range.
Resident sales at sea to carriers for non-reporting markets, fresh fish and other codes: 30% uplift on resident in-mirror fish (4.60), plus resident share of annual-only reports (7.05 CIF, 1.11).
Small net deduction for resident fish retained or toll-processed without change of ownership, partly offset by merchanting margins. Nothing in the pack sizes it, so near zero with a wide range.
Timing: ownership passes about 38 days before the importer records arrival. Early-2025 flow is below early-2024 flow; the whole-mirror shift of -1.8 is applied to the resident share.
Importers value CIF. I take 7% off Thai-bound fish (68.75) and 2.5% off other destinations (28.82, larger share this year, mostly direct landing). Ranges 4-10% and 1-5%.

After FOB the mirror is 92.04. If operators are resident in Kiribati for about 14.00 of it (roughly 15%, range 6-33%), the rest is a sale between non-residents. Resident-pattern hours rose only modestly (7,415 to 8,496).

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels on other flags, importers code that fish to those flags. No operator residence data for those flags, so a small central value with a wide range, slightly above 2023 as resident hours rose.

Resident fish missed by the monthly series: annual-only partners (7.05 more in annual totals, resident part about 1.0), non-covered buyers, chilled or other products. The 2024 Thai share (70%) is close to the carrier chain's 67.5%, so little route gap.
Small allowance for resident fish on consignment or processed without change of ownership. No pack evidence on size; the range includes zero.
Timing: sale at sea precedes the port record by about 6 weeks. Early-year Thai imports fall from 9.45 to 8.45 the next year, scaled to the resident part.
Importers value CIF; the at-sea sale is FOB. Carrier freight and insurance on frozen tuna hauled for weeks assumed 5.5% of CIF (range 3-9%), same rate each year. P2, P4; files 01, 05.

Removes Kiribati-flagged catch run by non-residents. Resident-run share of the FOB mirror set at 19% (about 11-33%) from 8.5k register-address hours. Thai share fell to 70% as non-Thai buyers grew. P2, P3, P4; files 02, 01.
Adds fish run by Kiribati residents under other flags, coded to those flags. 1.5% of Nauru plus Tuvalu imports (228.8 USD m), as FOB; range 0.5-4.5%. Evidence thin, kept small. P6; files 03, 02.

Adds the resident-run share of partner gaps: annual-only reporters (7.05 USD m, observed) and unlisted buyers (6% of raw, inferred), as FOB, plus 1.0 USD m fresh or chilled tuna outside the HS codes. P5; files 06, 01.
Deducts 10% (range 0-20%) of the resident-run total for catch owned by non-residents under charter or processing arrangements, and merchanting margins, which are not gross goods exports. P7; file 05.

Timing: sale at sea precedes the importer's record by a median 42 days, so each mirror year holds late sales of the prior year. January-February arrival shift (-2.18 USD m CIF) scaled to resident-run FOB. P4; files 01, 02.

Importers value CIF. Thai-bound fish is 70 percent of the 2024 mirror, so the blended deduction is lower than in 2023: about 8 percent Thai-bound and 4 percent other partners, 6.8 percent blended. Point of sale is at sea or ex-vessel. P4, P1; files 01, 05.

Resident-pattern hours are 8,496, up 15 percent while the mirror rose 19 percent, so the share is held at about 19 percent of the FOB mirror (range 7 to 40). Customs tuna stayed negligible. The rest is sales between non-residents. P2, P3, P5, P8; files 02, 03, 06.

Resident operators may run vessels flagged elsewhere and importers code by flag. Other-flag imports remain large (Nauru and Tuvalu 229) but no link to Kiribati residents is observed; slightly more than 2023 as resident hours rose. Wide range from zero. P2, P3; files 03, 05.

Adds the resident share of annual-only partner returns (gross gap 7.05, the largest of the three years) plus 15 percent of resident-operated catch sold via non-reporting destinations, third-country landings or codes outside the mirror. P6; files 01, 06.

If the resident operator is paid for fishing and the catch belongs to a non-resident owner, it is a service, not a goods sale. Taken as 10 percent of resident catch (range 0 to 25). Customs tuna of 0.59 was small. P7, P8; files 05, 06.

Ownership changes about 38 days before Thai arrival, so the year's exports are arrivals shifted by that lag. Early-year Thai arrivals in 2025 were close to those in 2024, so the shift is very small after scaling by the resident share. P1; files 01, 02.

Importers value CIF. Remove about 6% freight and insurance on Thai-coded fish (68.75) and 8% on other partners (28.82), which are larger this year (P3). Range is 3-10% of the mirror; no freight data in the pack.

Remove fish of Kiribati-flag vessels with a non-resident operator. Resident-operated part about 27% of the FOB mirror: 35% of Thai-coded, 6% of other partners' landings, mostly home-port landings (28.82). Resident-address hours of 8,496 are close to 2023 (P1, P2, P4).

Fish of resident operators coded to another flag or landing or processing country. No operator data for other registers; hours rose only modestly from 2023, so the allowance stays small but slightly above 2023 (P2, P4, P5).

Annual-only reporters add 7.05 (annual 104.62 versus 97.57), taken at 25% resident; plus resident fresh or chilled and other-code lines, and non-reporting destinations. Customs tuna 0.59 in 10 months shows a few resident landings (P5, P8).
Small deduction for resident fish processed abroad without change of ownership, and merchanting-type resales (P6). Same size as 2023 because nothing in the pack separates the years; range spans zero.
Timing: sale at sea precedes the Thai record by about 38 days. January to mid-February imports fell from 2024 to 2025, so shifting the window trims the resident part a little (P7). Flows are lumpy.

Importers record CIF; exports are FOB. Freight and insurance taken as 4% of Thai-coded value and 3% of other partners' value; non-Thai share is larger in 2024 (30%), so the blended rate is lower. Smaller if a resident operator carries its own fish.

Removes fish from Kiribati-flag vessels whose operators are not resident. Resident share kept at 14% of the FOB mirror: resident-pattern hours (8.5k) rose about as fast as the mirror, and customs tuna was only 0.59. A sale between non-residents is not an export.

Adds fish of Kiribati-resident operators carried under other flags and coded to other origins, taken as a quarter of resident Kiribati-flag fish. Nauru and Tuvalu are coded at 166 and 63 USD m. No hours exist for other flags, so the range is wide.

Adds resident fish outside the seven importers' monthly series: about a fifth of resident fish for other buyers, third-country landings and other HS lines, plus the resident share of annual-only reporters (7.05 gap to Comtrade totals, the largest of the three years).

Small deduction (3.5% of resident fish) for fish not sold to a non-resident in the year: processing without change of ownership and fish kept in the economy. Merchanting and re-exports taken as negligible.

Calendar timing: fish sold at sea reaches the importer about 42 days later. Thai-coded January-February arrivals fall from 8.61 (2024) to 7.87 (2025), so the shift is small. Applied to the resident part only.

Importers value at CIF, Kiribati exports are FOB (P4). Freight and insurance taken at 7% of the Thai-bound part (70% of the mirror) and 6% of the rest, which now includes more short-haul buyers; about 6.7% overall. Range 4-11% Thai, 3-15% other.

Mirror follows flag, not residence (P2, P3). Resident-pattern hours rose only 15% (8,496) while the mirror rose 19%, so the resident share is held at 13% of FOB mirror value (range 3-28%) under the P5 minority view; the rest removed.

Resident operators may run vessels under other flags, including the neighbouring registers, or have fish coded to a landing or processing country (P3, P5). Sized at 18% of resident fish in the mirror. Not directly observed, so the range is wide.

Resident fish missed by the monthly series: annual-only reporters (annual minus monthly gap 7.05, resident share about 0.85) plus a 30% uplift for sales at sea, third-country landings and non-reporting buyers; a third of at-sea transfers did not reach Thailand (P6).

If a resident unit manages catch for a non-resident owner, or fish is processed abroad without change of ownership, there is no Kiribati sale (P8, P1). Taken as 8% of resident fish in L2-L4. No contract data; range 1-20%.

Cut-off timing: at-sea sales reach the importer's record about 38 days later (P8). Thai arrivals in January to mid-February 2025 were below those of 2024, so 2024 sales were slightly below 2024 arrivals for the resident share.

Importers value imports CIF. Removing about 3.5 percent of Thai-bound fish and 5 percent of other buyers' fish gives value at the point of sale; the larger non-Thai share lifts the average. Range 1.3 to 7.7 percent of the mirror.

If the operator is not resident in Kiribati, the sale is between non-residents. Resident share taken as 21 percent of FOB value (range 8 to 42): resident-pattern hours rose 15 percent but the surge in non-Thai landings is more likely foreign-run. Official tuna returns remain very low.

If Kiribati-resident operators also run vessels flagged elsewhere, importers code that fish to other origins. No direct evidence; sized at about 17 percent of the resident core with a wide range. Same share as 2023.

Resident sales at sea to carriers bound for non-reporting buyers, third-country landings, fresh product and unlisted species sit outside the mirror. Sized at about 18 percent of the resident core, as in 2023; range widened with the larger core.

If some resident-owned fish is consigned for processing without change of ownership it is not a goods export; resident merchanting adds only a net margin. Not directly sized; small net negative with a wide range.
Timing. Sale at sea precedes the importer's record by about six weeks. Net effect is early-2025 minus early-2024 Thai flows (a small fall), applied to the resident Thai-bound share.

Importers value at CIF. Freight and insurance after the sale point come out: about 6% on Thai-bound fish, 7% on others (non-Thai share is larger this year), wide for carrier margins. Applied to the whole mirror.

Resident-address hours are 8,496, up 15%; resident share set at 22% of the FOB mirror. The rest is chartered or foreign-run catch sold between non-residents. Based on partial register hints, so the band is wide.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels under other flags, importers code the fish to those flags (Nauru plus Tuvalu series 229). A small share, about 1.5%, is assumed, slightly above 2023 with hours. No direct evidence.

Annual-only reporters add 7.05 beyond the monthly sums (resident share only). About 15% of resident-operated fish is assumed to move by routes the series cannot see: non-reporting ports, third-country landings, fresh fish outside the HS list.
Net small. Processing without change of ownership is not a goods export (negative); resident merchanting margins add a little (positive). Nothing in the pack sizes either, so the band straddles zero.
Timing. Importers record on arrival, about 38 days after the at-sea sale. Early-2024 and early-2025 Thai arrivals are similar, so the year shift is almost nil; applied to the resident share only.
Freight and insurance in CIF values: 6.0% of Thai-coded 68.75 and 2.5% of other partners' 28.82. A larger non-Thai share lowers the blended wedge to 5.0%.

Keeps only the resident-operated part of the FOB mirror: 13.5% (6-29%), 12.52 of 92.72. The rest is Kiribati-flag fish run by non-resident operators. Resident-pattern hours 8,496, up 15% on 2023 against mirror up 19%.

Fish of Kiribati-resident operators on vessels flagged elsewhere: 1% of Nauru/Tuvalu-coded fish (228.8 CIF) plus 0.1% of other Pacific flags, converted to FOB. No vessel-level evidence; bounded by pool size.
One-third of resident-run mirror catch (4.17) for sales at sea or landings no partner coded to Kiribati, plus 0.93 for annual-only reporters (gap 7.05 at 13.5% resident share, FOB).
No evidence of processing without change of ownership or merchanting by residents; centred on zero. Range slightly wider than 2023 as resident activity and customs tuna exports (0.59) are higher.
Timing: ownership passes at sale, about 38 days before the Thai import date. Monthly Thai data give -0.37 on all Thai-coded fish at 60% weight; resident share 13.5% and FOB applied.

CIF to FOB: freight and insurance of about 6.5% on Thai-bound carrier fish (68.75) and 3% on other partners (28.82). Rates are from model knowledge, ranges 4.5-9% and 1.5-4.5%. Handling margins may sit inside the range.

Removes Kiribati-flag fish whose operator is probably not resident (charter, foreign-run, flag of convenience). Inferred resident share of the FOB mirror 30% (80% range 11-47%). Resident-address hours 8,496 are a hint only; no fleet total is given.

Adds fish of Kiribati-resident operators on vessels of other flags that importers code elsewhere. Nauru and Tuvalu series show vessels change register, but there is no address data for them. Set small, floor at zero, wide upper range.

Two parts. About 2.00 for partners reporting annually only (annual total 7.05 above the monthly sum, converted to FOB and resident share). About 3.30 for sales to non-reporting partners, fresh or chilled fish outside the listed HS codes, and third-country landings.

Small allowance for resident catch sent for processing without change of ownership or kept at home, partly offset by possible net merchanting margins. Evidence cannot size it, so the centre is near zero with a wide two-sided range.

Timing of ownership change (named). Ownership changes at sea about 42 days before the importer records the fish. With arrivals falling between January-February 2024 and 2025, sales in the calendar year are lower than arrivals. Scaled by chain share 68%, FOB factor and resident share.
CIF to FOB (P3). About 5% off Thai-bound 68.75 and 8% off other 28.82, 5.9% overall. The non-Thai share rose to 30%, so the blended freight rate is higher than in 2023. Range 3-7% and 5-12%.

Charged on the FOB mirror, 91.82. Resident-pattern hours of 8.5k (up 15% on 2023) and a mirror that rose with more reporters point to about 12% resident-operated (range 4-27%); 88% removed because the operator is not resident (P1, P2, P4).

Same rule as 2023 (P5): 1% of Nauru and Tuvalu coded imports (228.8) and 0.1% of other Pacific flags (944.5), at FOB, for Kiribati-resident operators under other flags. No address data for these flags; wide range.

Same rule as 2023 (P5): about 30% of recorded resident catch for unmatched sales at sea, other HS lines and annual-only reporters. The annual-only gap is larger this year (7.1), scaled by the resident share. One third of at-sea sales has no Thai call (02).

Small and two-sided (P7): fish kept in the economy, processing without change of ownership, merchanting margins and re-exports. Centre at minus 3% of resident exports; the range allows a small positive.
Timing (P8): arrival month against sale at sea about six weeks earlier. Shifting the monthly series back lowers 2024 by 2.3%; applied to the at-sea share of resident exports, about 1.6% of them.

Remove freight and insurance: 5% of Thai-recorded value and 3.5% of other partners. Non-Thai share rose to 30% of the mirror (shorter hauls), so the blended rate is near 4.6%. Ranges 3-7.5% and 2-5.5%.

Remove fish from non-resident operators. Resident-operated share held near 2023 at 18% (range 6-40%): register-address hours rose 15% to 8,496 while the mirror rose 19%, so foreign-run effort still dominates the flag-coded fish.

Add resident-operated catch under other flags or coded to landing or processing country, under 2% of Nauru- and Tuvalu-coded imports (both near 2023 levels) plus a small allowance elsewhere. Same principles as 2023; wide range.

Add resident-operated sales missed by the monthly series: annual-only reporters (gap 7.05, largest of the three years; resident share only, 1.22) plus 20% of the resident part for non-reporting buyers, third-country landings and non-HS lines.
Small net treatment effect: processing without change of ownership removes, merchanting margins add. No data in the pack, so near zero, scaled to the slightly larger resident part, with a wide range.
Timing: 2023 sales arriving in January 2024 against 2022 sales arriving in January 2023, from monthly arrivals and the 38-day median lag. The net shift on the resident part is a small reduction.

Importers value CIF. Freight and insurance taken as about 6.5% of Thai-coded 68.75 and 6% of other partners' 28.82, whose mix includes longer hauls. Ownership changes at the vessel, before freight. Range 4-9%.

If the operator is not resident, the sale is between non-residents. Resident-pattern hours (8,496, up 15%) track the mirror, so about 7% is resident-operated (range 3-14%); 93% of the FOB mirror (91.37) is removed.

Resident operators may run vessels flagged elsewhere, coded to those flags. Nauru and Tuvalu flagged imports (228.8 CIF) are 2.2 times the Kiribati series; about 1.15% of them is assumed resident-operated. Very uncertain.

Resident fish sold by routes the series misses: fresh or chilled fish outside the HS codes, non-reporting destinations, and annual-only partners (annual total 7.1 above monthly sum). Taken as 22% of resident-operated fish plus a resident share of that gap.

No material treatment adjustment: direct sales to non-residents are a change of ownership, and processing without ownership change, merchanting and re-export are not evidenced. Range leans up for processing-contract cases.

Timing: partner records lag the sale by about six weeks, but true exports are by sale date. Thai-coded January-February imports are slightly lower in 2025 than 2024, so a small negative on the resident share.
Importers record CIF; strip freight, insurance and brokerage. About 8.5% for Thai-bound fish (70% of the 2024 mirror) and about 6% for other buyers, 7.8% overall. Margin is assumed, not observed.

If the operator is not resident in Kiribati, the sale is between non-residents. Resident share of Kiribati-flag fish set near 20% (7-40%): resident-address hours were 8,496, up 15% on 2023, and most register vessels carry no resident-address hint. The rest is removed.

Add fish caught by Kiribati-resident operators on vessels of other flags, coded to those flags. Taken as 2% (0-7%) of the FOB Nauru- and Tuvalu-coded series. No residence data exist for those flags, so the range is wide.

Resident share of the extra 7.05 that annual-only reporters add (Comtrade annual less monthly sum), plus 15% of the resident base for at-sea sales to carriers bound for unreported buyers and fish outside these codes. Mostly inferred.

Remove about 10% of resident-operated flows where the catch may be owned by a non-resident (contract fishing or toll processing), so only the fee is a service, not a good. Upper end allows a small merchanting margin.
Timing: sales at sea precede import recording by about 38 days, so the calendar-year shift is early-2025 imports less early-2024 imports, scaled to the resident share. No other item identified.

Importers value CIF; exports are FOB where ownership changes (P4). Freight and insurance on frozen tuna, 70% of the mirror going to Thailand and the rest on shorter hops, taken at 5.2% of the mirror, range 3% to 8%.

Removes 70% of the FOB mirror as Kiribati-flag fish run by operators not resident in Kiribati (P1, P2). Resident share 30%, range 13% to 45%, from 8,496 address-pattern hours (15% above 2023) and the mirror value per such hour (P6). Larger non-Thai landings add no residence evidence.

If Kiribati-resident operators run ships under Nauru, Tuvalu or other flags, importers code that fish elsewhere (P3, P7). Taken as about 2% of Nauru- and Tuvalu-coded imports (229 million USD CIF), converted to FOB. No operator data, so the range is wide.

Resident sales the monthly series misses (P5): annual-only reporters' extra 7.0 million, scaled by resident share (2.0); 12% of resident-run mirror fish sold by routes with no partner record (3.3); fresh chilled fish outside the tuna codes (1.5).

Some resident-run fish may be consigned for processing abroad without change of ownership, and the same fish can be recorded by two importers after landing in one and re-export to another (P1). Taken as about 3.5% of resident-run fish.
Timing: importers record arrival, a median 38-42 days after the at-sea sale (P5). Moving Thai arrivals back to sale dates lowers 2024 by 0.7 million, about 1.1%; applied to the resident share.
Importers value CIF. Freight and insurance taken as 6% of Thai-recorded value (68.75) and 3.5% of other partners (28.82); the larger non-Thai share adds a little. P3; files 01, 06.

If the operator is not resident, the sale is between non-residents. Resident-operated share taken as 14% of the FOB mirror (12.94); the remaining 86% is removed. Resident-pattern hours 8,496, close to 2023. P1, P2, P4; file 02.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels flagged to other Pacific states, importers code that fish elsewhere. No register data for those flags; taken as 1% of the FOB value of Nauru- and Tuvalu-coded imports. P2, P5; file 03.

Three parts: partners reporting annually only (7.05 CIF, resident share) 0.94; resident fish reaching buyers or codes outside the series, 15% of resident fish in the mirror, 1.94; fresh or chilled tuna outside the HS codes, 0.80. P5; files 01, 06.

No evidence of toll processing or merchanting by residents; Kiribati has no tuna processing of scale, and fish kept for local use is neither exported nor in the mirror. Zero, with a range for unknown joint-venture contracts. P8; model knowledge.

Timing: importers record fish one to two months after the sale at sea, so the calendar-year mirror differs from sales in the year. Thai monthly values give -0.61 for 2024, applied to the resident share at half weight. P6; files 01, 02.
Thai-bound fish (68.75) at about 6% freight and insurance, other partners (28.82) at about 3%. Importers record CIF; an export is valued at the point of sale (P3, P2). Contract terms are unobserved.

Resident share held at 22% (range 10-45%): address hours of 8.5k are only slightly above 2023 (7.4k) while the mirror rose 19% (P4). 78% of the FOB mirror is removed as sales between non-residents (P1).
Catch of resident operators on vessels flagged elsewhere is coded to other flags (P2, P6). No address data for other registers; about 10% of the resident mirror part, with a wide range.

Resident share of annual-only partner records (+1.5; annual total 104.62 vs monthly 97.57), plus chilled fish outside the HS codes and non-reporting destinations (+1.5). Non-Thai share looks normal, so little else missing (P5).
About 3% of resident fish may move within a group, go for toll processing without change of ownership, or stay in the economy (P8). Merchanting by resident traders could offset. Thin evidence.
Timing: early-2024 Thai arrivals were sold at sea in 2023, early-2025 arrivals in 2024; the two nearly cancel, so the resident share of the net shift is close to zero (P5).
Remove freight and insurance: about 6.5% of the 68.75 Thai-recorded value and 5% of the 28.82 other-partner value, importers valuing CIF.

FOB mirror 91.66. Resident-operated share set near 12% (resident-pattern hours 8,496, only modestly above 2023), so about 88% is catch of vessels with non-resident operators, a sale between non-residents.
Resident operators with vessels flagged elsewhere would be coded to other origins. No direct data; set at about 30% of the resident-coded amount, range from zero.
Annual-only partners add 7.05 CIF (observed), scaled to the resident share; plus about 25% of resident-coded fish for omitted destinations, fresh tuna codes and sales at sea not coded to Kiribati.
About 5% of the resident total removed for fish kept locally, processing without change of ownership and merchanting, which are not ordinary goods exports.
Timing: sales at sea precede the import record by about 6 weeks. Resident hours changed little in 2024, so the year-assignment effect is close to zero.
Importers value CIF. Freight and insurance taken as 5% of the CIF mirror (range 2.8-7.2%). Non-Thai buyers rose to 30% of value and may include costlier air or small-lot freight (P3, P4).

Flag does not fix residence (P2). Judged 36% of Kiribati-flag value resident-operated (80% range 17-57%): resident-pattern hours rose to 8,496 from 7,415 while the mirror rose 19%. The rest is sold between non-residents (P5).

As 2023: resident operators running Nauru- or Tuvalu-flagged vessels would be coded to those states (P3). About 1.8% of the FOB Nauru and Tuvalu mirror (USD 229m CIF). No residence data for those flags.

Thai share fell to 70.5%, close to the 68% carrier-chain share, and reporting partners rose to 5-11 a month, so little looks missed. Small allowance for non-reporting destinations and for forms outside the HS set; resident share applied (P6).
Same logic as 2023: processing before sale and merchanting margin net to a small amount, taken as about 2% of resident-operated catch, sign uncertain (P7).
Timing of ownership change. January 2025 arrivals matched January 2024, so the six-week lead between sale at sea and import record has little net effect on the year; resident share applied (P7).

Importers record CIF (P4). Freight, insurance and any trader margin taken as 6 percent of the mirror, range 3.5 to 10 percent. Non-Thai buyers (30 percent of 2024) are on shorter legs, which pulls the share slightly down, offset by wider spread.

Resident-pattern hours of 8.5k, close to 2023 (P5). Share set at 22 percent of FOB mirror (9 to 42); the non-Thai flows, 30 percent of the 2024 mirror, are assumed mostly foreign-run fleets selling to home markets (P2, P3). The other 78 percent is removed.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels on Nauru or Tuvalu registers, importers code that fish to those flags (P3, P6). Those flags carry 229 USD m; a 2 percent resident-operated share gives 4.6. Same wide range as 2023, no direct evidence of the share.

Annual-only reporters add 7.05 CIF to the monthly sum; at FOB and resident share that is about 1.5. Add about 2.4 for fresh or chilled fish outside the HS set, non-reporting partners and third-country landings (P6). Range wider as the reporter count rose in 2024.

Goods for processing without change of ownership and merchanting are not gross goods exports (P1). No evidence of material resident tolling or trading of this fish. Zero, with a small upside for processed-product sales.

Cut-off timing: importers record about 38 days after the sale at sea (P8). Early-January arrivals fell from 2024 to 2025 in the Thai series, giving a small negative shift for the resident share, plus a small allowance for fish counted by two importers.

Importers value imports CIF (05). Carriage and insurance come off at about 8% for carrier cargo to Thailand (Thai share 70% of the mirror, 01) and 5% for other routes, 7.1% overall. Rates are model knowledge. P3, P8.

Coded by flag (P1; 05), but Kiribati-flag vessels run from abroad sell between non-residents (P2). Resident-run share set at 11.5% of the FOB mirror, scaled from 8,496 resident-address hours (02), with almost no tuna in customs returns (06). Hours are not value. P4, P7.

Fish caught by Kiribati-resident operators on vessels under other flags is coded to those flags, so the mirror misses it (P1, P5; 03, 05). No direct evidence; set at 18% of resident-run Kiribati-flag catch, wide range. Inferred.

Adds the annual-versus-monthly partner gap (104.62 vs 97.57; 01, 06) at FOB and resident share (0.75), plus 16% of resident catch for sales at sea bound for ports that do not report, third-country landings, and fresh or other products outside the HS codes. P5.

Small deduction for merchanting margins and for fish processed abroad without change of ownership, neither a full goods export (P6; 05). Set at 4% of resident-run catch; direction fairly clear, size not. Inferred.

Sale at sea precedes arrival by a median 42 days (P6; 02), so 2024 sales map to arrivals from mid-February 2024 to mid-February 2025. Net shift in Thai arrivals is -0.98 CIF (01); applied at FOB and resident share. Contract terms could change the sign.
