Importers value CIF. Bulk reefer freight and insurance over a median 38-42 day voyage to Thailand is taken as 6% of the mirror (range 3-10%) and removed, giving FOB at the point of sale. No freight rates are in the pack.

Flag-coded mirror holds all Kiribati-flag catch. Register-address hours (8.5k, up 15%) point to a slightly larger resident minority. About 14% of the FOB mirror (range 4-30%) is taken as resident-operated; the rest, fish sold between non-residents, is removed.

If a Kiribati-resident operator runs vessels under other flags (locally based foreign-flag vessels, reflagging among Kiribati, Nauru, Tuvalu), importers code that fish elsewhere. Sized at a quarter to a third of resident Kiribati-flag fish, with a long upper tail.

Resident fish reaching buyers outside the monthly series: annual-only reporters (Comtrade annual total is 7.05 above the monthly sum), non-reporting partners, fresh or other HS lines. Thai share of 70% matches the chain share, so no extra gap-fill.

Small net removal: resident-operated fish sent to affiliated plants abroad for processing without change of ownership is not a goods export, and merchanting is recorded net. No processing data exist, so the range spans removal and a small addition.

Timing. The mirror counts arrival; ownership passes about 40 days earlier. January-February arrivals fell year on year, so replacing this year's with next year's, applied to the resident share, gives a small reduction.

Importers value imports CIF (P3). Thailand takes 68.75 of 97.57; remove about 7.5% of CIF for long-haul reefer freight and insurance, and about 4% on the larger non-Thai part (28.82), mostly landings and shorter hauls. Ranges 4-11% and 1-8%.

If the operator is not resident in Kiribati, a sale between non-residents is not a Kiribati export (P1). Resident-address hours are small (8,496) and the mirror does not follow them (P4), so about 11% of the FOB mirror is treated as resident-run; the rest is removed.

Resident operators may run vessels flagged elsewhere (Nauru and Tuvalu registers move with Kiribati in the fish-transfer chain) or land fish coded to a processing country (P5). No direct count; set near 29% of the resident-run amount in the mirror, wide range.

Resident sales at sea to carriers, landings in third countries, fresh or chilled fish under other HS codes, and partners reporting annually only (gap 7.05, resident share only) are outside the monthly series (P5). Not measured; sized near one third of the resident mirror amount.

Goods sent for processing without change of ownership are not goods exports, and merchanting is recorded net (P6). Nothing shows either is large for resident operators; a small net removal, with a range that includes a small addition.

Timing: ownership changes at sea about 42 days before the importer records arrival (P6). Resident flows grew only modestly from 2023, so the calendar-year shift is near zero after allowing for possible double counting where one lot passes two importers.

P1: importers record CIF (files 00, 05). About 7% for the Thai route and 5% for direct landings, weighted by a 71% Thai share (file 06), gives 6.8% of the raw mirror. Sized from model knowledge; plausible range 4-10%.

P2, P3, P8: resident share of the FOB mirror set at 25% (range 9-45%). Resident-pattern hours rose to 8.5k (file 02) and the non-Thai route share rose to 29% (file 06). The other 75% is a sale between non-residents and is removed.

P4: if a Kiribati-resident operator runs vessels under another flag, importers code the fish to that flag (files 03, 05). No direct count exists, so about 1.7% of the FOB Nauru and Tuvalu series (file 03) is added; the range runs down to near zero.

P4, P5: adds resident fish the series misses: destinations outside the seven reporters (about 15% of resident mirror), annual-only partners (Comtrade annual 104.62 less monthly 97.57, file 06) and products outside the HS codes (about 1.2).
P7: the pack cannot size tolling, merchanting or re-export effects and the question counts fish residents caught, so the layer is centred on zero with a symmetric range rather than a guessed value.

P6, P8: timing. Importers record at arrival, about 40 days after sale (file 02). Thai-route arrivals in early 2025 were below early 2024 (file 01), so the year-end carry-over is slightly negative. Applied to the resident share, FOB.

Importers record CIF. Remove freight and insurance: about 7% of Thai-bound value (70% of the 2024 mirror) and 3% of other partners' value (mostly direct landings, a larger share this year). Thai and non-Thai split from file 06.

Resident-operated share set at 33% (80% range 12-62%); the remaining 67% of FOB fish is a sale between non-residents. Address-hint hours were 8,496, a little above 2023. Residence is a matter of fact, not flag.

If Kiribati-resident operators also run vessels under other flags (Nauru and Tuvalu carry large coded volumes), that catch is outside the Kiribati-origin series. Set at 10% of the resident-operated amount, range 0-35%; nothing in the pack sizes it directly.

Adds resident fish the monthly series misses: partners reporting annually only (annual total 7.05 higher, taken at FOB and resident share), non-reporting hubs (10% of resident fish) and fresh tuna under other codes (1%). Reporter coverage was broader than in 2023.

Customs recorded 0.59 FOB of tuna exports. Taking 30% as fish bought from non-resident vessels and processed locally (a processed-goods export, not resident catch) gives a small removal. Toll processing and merchanting are unsized; range is wide.

Early-2025 Thai arrivals were close to early 2024 in January (6.13 against 6.07) and lower in February (5.81 against 8.45), so matching sales to a lagged window gives a small negative, scaled to Thai-bound resident fish.

official.note: 2025 BOP value is the compiler's estimate

rationales.text: Importers record CIF (P4). Sea-to-port freight and insurance, including about 38 days to Thai ports, are removed at 5% of the raw total (range 2-9%). Applied first, so L2 onward is on an FOB basis. Rate is a prior, not observed.

Kiribati-flagged catch run from abroad is not a Kiribati export (P2, P3). Resident-operated share of FOB mirror taken as 33% (80% range 17-62%), from 22,237 resident-pattern hours and 43 of 116 register vessels with address hints (02, P5). Rest removed. Customs tuna also rose in 2025 (06).

The mirror follows the flag (P3). Allows for 2.9% (0.9-8%) of the 197.9 USD m of Nauru- and Tuvalu-flagged imports (03) being run by Kiribati residents, as the three registers form one fleet family (02). No file shows operators of those flags; range is wide and bounded below by zero.

Resident sales by routes the partner series misses (P6): buyers outside the importers listed, fresh air-freighted fish, products outside the codes. Taken as 11% (4-30%) of the resident catch identified in L2 and L3. No direct data (01, 02).

Small deduction (P7): resident fish sent abroad for processing with no change of ownership, or resold as merchanting, is not a gross goods export. Central 3% of resident flow, range from +3% to -10%. Not observable in the pack, so kept small (05).

Timing (P7): importers record fish about 38 days after hand-over. Moving the monthly series back by that lag lowers the year by 3.05 on the whole mirror (01); scaled to the resident share of fish. Lag comes from 2018-2021 chain data (02).

Remove freight, insurance and carrier handling to reach FOB at the vessel: about 8.5% on the Thai route (61.71 of 86.93) and 6% on other routes. No freight data in the pack; rates are model knowledge. P3.

Keep Kiribati-flag fish only where the operator is resident (P1, P2). Resident-address hours jump to 22,237 (2.6 times 2024) and customs tuna rises, so about 18% of the FOB mirror is kept, 82% removed. Range keeps 8% to 35%. P4, P6.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels flagged elsewhere, importers code that fish to the other flag (P2). No residence data for other registers in the pack; taken as 15% of resident fish in the mirror, range from zero.

Adds (a) annual-only reporters' extra 1.26 CIF, scaled to resident share and FOB, and (b) 25% of resident fish sold by routes outside the partner series: other buyers, fresh or other HS codes, at-sea chains not reaching Thailand. P5.

If resident fish goes to affiliated plants abroad under retained title, or moves under a lease, it is not a goods export on arrival (BPM6 10.17(f), Table 5.1). Taken as 5% of retained resident fish, negative, with a positive tail. P7.

Timing: ownership passes at the at-sea sale, the mirror records arrival about 42 days later. Fewer arrivals in early 2026 than early 2025 imply a downward cut-off adjustment on the larger resident share. P7.

Importers record CIF (P2, file 05). Remove freight and insurance at 5.5% of the Thai value (61.71) and 7.5% of the rest (25.22); longer routes to the Americas sit at the high end. Applied to the whole mirror.

If the operator is not resident, the sale is between non-residents (P1, P3). Resident share of the FOB mirror taken as 20.2% (22,237 resident-pattern hours, file 02); the rest, 65.15, is removed. Band 10%-35%.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels on other registers, importers code that catch to the other flag (P1, P4). Take 3% of Nauru and Tuvalu coded imports at FOB plus 0.1% of five other flag states (file 03). Weakly evidenced; wide band.

Resident sales missed by the partner series (P5): 12% of the resident base for carriers, destinations and products outside the series; resident share of annual-only partner returns (1.26); 35% of annualised customs tuna (4.13, file 06).

No evidence sizes processing without change of ownership, merchanting, sales between residents or fish kept in the economy (P6). Centre set at zero with a symmetric band; a negative tail is possible if exported fish was bought from non-residents.

Timing: importers record arrival about six weeks after the at-sea sale, so the mirror year and sale year differ slightly (P8, file 02). With roughly flat flows the net effect is set to zero with a narrow band.
Importers record CIF; exports are FOB. Removing sea freight and insurance at 5.5% of CIF (range 3 to 8.5%), the same rate as other years.

Origin follows the flag, so fish from Kiribati-flagged vessels run by non-resident operators is not a Kiribati export. Resident-run share lifted to 19% of Thai-coded and 48% of other flows (27% overall) because resident-pattern hours rose 2.6-fold; the rest removed.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels under other flags, importers code that fish to the flag state. Allowance raised a little as resident-pattern activity and local customs tuna exports (3.44) both grew; still indirect evidence.

Resident-pattern hours rose 2.6-fold yet the mirror fell, so more resident fish probably moved by routes the series does not show (non-listed processors, other ports). Includes the resident share of annual-only partners (1.26 USD m). Wide range.

Small deduction for resident-run fish delivered for processing where ownership does not pass until after processing, and for any merchanting. Larger than earlier years because resident-run volumes appear higher. Range includes zero.

Timing: imports follow sales at sea by about six weeks. Early-2026 imports are well below early-2025 imports, so calendar-year sales in 2025 sit slightly below calendar-year imports for the resident portion. 2026 months are partly reported.
Importers value CIF. Freight, insurance and trader margin taken as 7.5% of the raw mirror (range 5-11%) to reach FOB at the point ownership passes.

Resident-run share of the FOB mirror raised to 28% (range 16-49%): resident hours rose 2.6 times and official goods exports doubled, but the mirror fell 11%, so the share rises less than hours. The rest is non-resident-run.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels under other flags, importers code that fish to those flags. Assumed about 1% of Nauru and Tuvalu coded value plus a little elsewhere, FOB. No operator data, so wide range.
Resident sales at sea to carriers for non-reporting markets, fresh fish and other codes: 30% uplift on resident in-mirror fish (6.75), plus resident share of annual-only reports (1.26 CIF, 0.33).

Small net deduction for resident fish retained or toll-processed without change of ownership, partly offset by merchanting margins. Wider than earlier years as resident activity grew; otherwise near zero.
Timing: ownership passes about 38 days before the importer records arrival. Early-2026 flow is well below early-2025 flow; the whole-mirror shift of -3.3 is applied to the resident share.

Importers value CIF. I take 7% off Thai-bound fish (61.71) and 2.5% off other destinations (25.22). Ranges 4-10% and 1-5%. Fewer carrier port calls this year (111 vs 165) do not change the per-tonne freight assumption.

After FOB the mirror is 81.98. If operators are resident in Kiribati for about 18.00 of it (roughly 22%, range 9-42%), the rest is a sale between non-residents. Resident-pattern hours rose to 22,237 yet the mirror fell, so I cap the share.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels on other flags, importers code that fish to those flags. Resident activity jumped in 2025 without a rise in the mirror, so I add more than in earlier years, with a wide range.

Resident hours nearly tripled and Kiribati customs tuna exports rose (0.59 to 3.44 in 10 months), but the mirror did not rise. I add fish sold by routes the partner series misses: annual-only partners (1.26), other buyers, products outside the HS codes.
Small allowance for resident fish on consignment or processed without change of ownership, a little larger as resident activity grew. No pack evidence on size; the range includes zero.
Timing: sale at sea precedes the port record by about 6 weeks. Early-year Thai imports keep falling, but early-2026 data are incomplete, so I use a moderate adjustment scaled to the resident part.
Importers value CIF; the at-sea sale is FOB. Carrier freight and insurance on frozen tuna hauled for weeks assumed 5.5% of CIF (range 3-9%), same rate each year. P2, P4; files 01, 05.

Removes Kiribati-flagged catch run by non-residents. Resident-run share of the FOB mirror set at 28% (about 16-48%) from 22.2k register-address hours. Hours rose 2.6 times but the mirror fell, so only part is passed through. P2, P3, P4; files 02, 01.
Adds fish run by Kiribati residents under other flags, coded to those flags. 1.5% of Nauru plus Tuvalu imports (197.9 USD m), as FOB; range 0.5-4.5%. Evidence thin, kept small. P6; files 03, 02.

Adds the resident-run share of partner gaps: annual-only reporters (1.26 USD m, observed) and unlisted buyers (6% of raw, inferred), as FOB, plus 1.5 USD m fresh or chilled tuna outside the HS codes. P5; files 06, 01.
Deducts 10% (range 0-20%) of the resident-run total for catch owned by non-residents under charter or processing arrangements, and merchanting margins, which are not gross goods exports. P7; file 05.

Timing: sale at sea precedes the importer's record by a median 42 days, so each mirror year holds late sales of the prior year. January-February arrival shift (-3.67 USD m CIF) scaled to resident-run FOB. P4; files 01, 02.

Importers value CIF. Thai-bound fish is 71 percent of the 2025 mirror; about 8 percent is removed for Thai-bound fish and 4 percent for other partners, 6.8 percent blended. Point of sale is at sea or ex-vessel. P4, P1; files 01, 05.

Resident-pattern hours jump to 22,237 (2.6 times 2024) while the mirror fell 11 percent; customs tuna and the goods total rose. Resident share raised to about 30 percent of the FOB mirror (range 12 to 55), not scaled fully with hours. P2, P5, P8; files 02, 03, 06.

Resident operators may run vessels flagged elsewhere and importers code by flag. Other-flag imports are large (Nauru and Tuvalu 198) but no link to Kiribati residents is observed; kept slightly higher given more resident activity. Wide range from zero. P2, P3; files 03, 05.

Hours grew faster than the mirror and customs tuna rose, so more resident catch likely left by routes the mirror misses: 25 percent of resident-operated catch plus the resident share of annual-only returns (gap 1.26). Wide range. P5, P6, P8; files 01, 02, 06.

If the resident operator is paid for fishing and the catch belongs to a non-resident owner, it is a service, not a goods sale. Taken as 10 percent of the larger resident catch (range 0 to 25). Customs tuna of 3.44 covers only visible routes. P7, P8; files 05, 06.

Ownership changes about 38 days before Thai arrival, so the year's exports are arrivals shifted by that lag. Thai January arrivals fell from 2025 to 2026 (2026 months near-complete), trimming 2025 after scaling by the resident share. P1; files 01, 02.
Importers value CIF. Remove about 6% freight and insurance on Thai-coded fish (61.71) and 8% on other partners (25.22) (P3). Range is 3-10% of the mirror; no freight data in the pack.

Remove fish of Kiribati-flag vessels with a non-resident operator. Resident-operated part raised to about 35% of the FOB mirror (47% of Thai-coded) as resident-address hours reached 22,237, tempered because register coverage and address hints are partial (P1, P4).

Resident-address hours rose 2.6 times to 22,237 while the mirror fell. If that added effort is sold under another flag or origin is coded to the landing country, it sits here; part may be a register-coverage effect. Widest range (P2, P4, P5).

Annual-only reporters add 1.26 (annual 88.19 versus 86.93), taken at 25% resident. Allowance raised for resident fresh or chilled lines and non-reporting destinations: customs tuna rose to 3.44 in 10 months (P5, P8).
Slightly larger deduction as resident activity grew: processing abroad without change of ownership and merchanting-type resales (P6). Scale unobserved; range spans zero.
Timing: January to mid-February imports fall sharply into 2026, which would cut 2025 sales; shrunk because early-2026 months may be incomplete and flows are lumpy (P7).
Importers record CIF; exports are FOB. Freight and insurance taken as 4% of Thai-coded value (71% of the mirror) and 3% of other partners' value. Smaller if a resident operator carries its own fish.

Removes non-resident-operated fish. Resident-pattern hours rose to 22.2k (2.6 times 2024) while the mirror fell, and customs tuna rose to 3.44. Resident share taken as 30% of the FOB mirror; hours-only scaling would give about 39%. A sale between non-residents is not an export.

Adds resident-operated fish carried under other flags, taken as a quarter of resident Kiribati-flag fish, which is larger in 2025. Nauru and Tuvalu are coded at 149 and 49 USD m, so some resident fish may sit there. No hours exist for other flags.

Adds resident fish outside the seven importers' monthly series: about a fifth of resident fish for other buyers, third-country landings and other HS lines, plus the resident share of annual-only reporters (1.26 gap, the smallest). Inferred.

Deduction (3.5% of resident fish) for fish not sold to a non-resident in the year: processing without change of ownership and fish kept in the economy. Larger resident base than in earlier years. Merchanting and re-exports taken as negligible.

Calendar timing: fish sold at sea reaches the importer about 42 days later. Thai-coded January-February arrivals fall from 7.87 (2025) to 4.11 (2026), so 2025 sales sit below 2025 arrivals. Applied to the resident part only.

Importers value at CIF, Kiribati exports are FOB (P4). Freight and insurance taken at 7% of the Thai-bound part (71% of the mirror) and 6% of the rest; about 6.7% overall. Range 4-11% Thai, 3-15% other.

Mirror follows flag, not residence (P2, P3). Resident-pattern hours rose 2.6 times (22,237) while the mirror fell, so a higher resident share is assumed: 28% of FOB mirror value (range 10-50%); the rest removed. Fleet turnover between flags is one possible reason (P5).

Resident operators may run vessels under other flags, including the neighbouring registers, or have fish coded to a landing or processing country (P3, P5). Sized at 18% of resident fish in the mirror, which is larger in 2025. Wide range.

Resident-pattern hours rose 2.6 times while mirror value did not rise, so more resident fish probably took routes the series misses (P5, P6). Annual-only gap is small (1.26); uplift raised from 30% to 42% for sales at sea, third-country landings and non-reporting buyers.

If a resident unit manages catch for a non-resident owner, or fish is processed abroad without change of ownership, there is no Kiribati sale (P8, P1). Taken as 8% of resident fish in L2-L4; larger base in 2025. No contract data; range 1-20%.

Cut-off timing: at-sea sales reach the importer's record about 38 days later (P8). Thai arrivals in January to mid-February 2026 were well below 2025, so 2025 sales were below 2025 arrivals for the resident share. Early 2026 data are less complete.
Importers value imports CIF. Removing about 3.5 percent of Thai-bound fish and 5 percent of other buyers' fish gives value at the point of sale. Range 1.4 to 7.7 percent of the mirror.

If the operator is not resident in Kiribati, the sale is between non-residents. Resident share raised to 34 percent (range 13 to 60): resident-pattern hours are 2.6 times 2024, and customs tuna and goods exports rose. Discounted because address coverage may have grown.

If Kiribati-resident operators also run vessels flagged elsewhere, importers code that fish to other origins. No direct evidence; sized at about 18 percent of the larger resident core with a wide range.

Resident sales at sea to carriers bound for non-reporting buyers, third-country landings, fresh product and unlisted species sit outside the mirror. The mirror fell while resident hours rose, consistent with more resident fish on unrecorded routes. About 20 percent of the core.

If some resident-owned fish is consigned for processing without change of ownership it is not a goods export; resident merchanting adds only a net margin. Larger resident activity widens the range; small net negative.

Timing. Sale at sea precedes the importer's record by about six weeks. Early-2026 Thai flows are far below early-2025, so the 2025 mirror carries more 2024-made sales than 2025 sales landing in 2026; net negative, applied to the resident Thai-bound share. Early-2026 data are thin.
Importers value at CIF. Freight and insurance after the sale point come out: about 6% on Thai-bound fish, 7% on others, wide for carrier margins and trader terms. Applied to the whole mirror.

Resident-address hours jumped to 22,237 (2.6 times 2024) while the mirror fell. Resident share is raised to 37% but damped, since hours cannot become value without total fleet hours. Band very wide, about 16% to 66%.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels under other flags, importers code the fish to those flags (Nauru plus Tuvalu series 198). About 2.5% is assumed, higher with the 2025 rise in resident hours. No direct evidence.

Annual-only reporters add little (1.26). Resident hours tripled but the mirror did not rise, so 18% of resident-operated fish is assumed to move by unseen routes (non-reporting ports, third-country landings, non-HS products). Customs tuna of 3.44 hints at activity.

Net small. Processing without change of ownership is not a goods export (negative); resident merchanting margins add a little (positive). Slightly larger negative as resident volume rises. Nothing in the pack sizes either.
Timing. Importers record on arrival, about 38 days after the at-sea sale. Late-2025 sales arrive in 2026, and early-2026 data are thin, so the shift is uncertain; applied to the resident share only.
Freight and insurance in CIF values: 6.0% of Thai-coded 61.71 and 2.5% of other partners' 25.22. Blended wedge 5.0%; the Thai share fell, so the amount is the smallest of the three years.

Keeps only the resident-operated part of the FOB mirror: 32% (15-53%), 26.43 of 82.60. Resident-pattern hours 22,237 are 3.0x 2023 while mirror is 1.06x, implying 39%; pulled back toward earlier shares because the hint is weak.

Fish of Kiribati-resident operators on vessels flagged elsewhere: 1.5% of Nauru/Tuvalu-coded fish (197.9 CIF) plus 0.1% of other Pacific flags, converted to FOB. Higher share reflects larger resident fleet.

One-third of resident-run mirror catch (8.81) for sales at sea or landings no partner coded to Kiribati, plus 0.39 for annual-only reporters (gap 1.26 at 32% resident share, FOB). Scales with the larger resident share.
No evidence of processing without change of ownership or merchanting by residents; centred on zero. Range widest in 2025 because resident activity is largest and customs tuna exports (3.44) rose.

Timing: ownership passes at sale, about 38 days before the Thai import date. Monthly Thai data give -2.08 on all Thai-coded fish at 60% weight (early-2026 data may be incomplete); resident share 32% and FOB applied.

CIF to FOB: freight and insurance of about 6.5% on Thai-bound carrier fish (61.71) and 3% on other partners (25.22). Rates are from model knowledge, ranges 4.5-9% and 1.5-4.5%. Handling margins may sit inside the range.

Removes Kiribati-flag fish whose operator is probably not resident (charter, foreign-run, flag of convenience). Inferred resident share of the FOB mirror 40% (80% range 15-60%). Resident-address hours 22,237 are a hint only; no fleet total is given.

Adds fish of Kiribati-resident operators on vessels of other flags. Raised slightly because resident-address hours rose 2.6 times; Nauru and Tuvalu series show vessels change register. No address data for other flags, so the range is wide with a floor at zero.

Two parts. About 0.48 for partners reporting annually only (annual total 1.26 above the monthly sum, converted to FOB and resident share). About 6.00 for sales to non-reporting partners, fresh or chilled fish outside the listed HS codes, and third-country landings. Larger in 2025 as resident hours outgrew the mirror.

Small allowance for resident catch sent for processing without change of ownership or kept at home, partly offset by possible net merchanting margins. Evidence cannot size it, so the centre is near zero with a wide two-sided range.

Timing of ownership change (named). Ownership changes at sea about 42 days before the importer records the fish. With arrivals falling between January-February 2025 and 2026, sales in the calendar year are lower than arrivals. Scaled by chain share 68%, FOB factor and resident share.
CIF to FOB (P3). About 5% off Thai-bound 61.71 and 8% off other 25.22, 5.9% overall. Range 3-7% on Thai-bound and 5-12% on other fish.

Charged on the FOB mirror, 81.82. Resident-pattern hours tripled to 22.2k while the mirror fell, and customs tuna exports rose; I take about 24% resident-operated (range 9-42%), damped from the hours ratio (P4). Remaining 76% is removed (P1, P2).

Same rule as before (P5) with a 1.35 uplift for expanded resident activity: 1% of Nauru and Tuvalu coded imports (197.9) and 0.1% of other flags (787.9), at FOB. No address data for these flags; wide range.

About 30% of recorded resident catch (P5). Higher in level because resident activity grew; if the extra resident fishing is sold by routes the partner series misses, the true value is higher. Annual-only gap is small (1.3). Wide range.

Small and two-sided (P7): fish kept in the economy, processing without change of ownership, merchanting margins and re-exports. Centre at minus 3% of larger resident exports; the range allows a positive sign.

Timing (P8): arrival month against sale at sea about six weeks earlier. Shifting the series back lowers 2025 by 4.1% (weak early-2026 months); applied to the at-sea share of resident exports, about 2.9% of them.
Remove freight and insurance: 5% of Thai-recorded value (71% of mirror) and 3.5% of other partners. Blended rate about 4.6%. Ranges 3-7.5% and 2-5.5%; same principles as other years.

Remove fish from non-resident operators. Resident share raised to 25% (range 10-45%): register-address hours jumped to 22,237, but Thai and other mirror values both fell about 10%, so only part of the extra hours can sit inside the flag-coded mirror.

Add resident-operated catch under other flags or coded elsewhere. Raised from 4.00 because the part of the 2025 hours increase not visible in the mirror, and the rise in customs tuna, may sit outside Kiribati-flag coding. Weakly anchored; wide range.

Add resident-operated sales missed by the monthly series: annual-only gap 1.26 (resident share only, 0.30) plus 25% of the resident part, raised because a larger domestic channel in 2025 implies more fresh or chilled and third-country sales.

Small net treatment effect: processing without change of ownership removes, merchanting margins add. Range widened because the resident part and domestic activity are larger in 2025. No data, so near zero.

Timing: 2025 sales arriving in January 2026 against 2024 sales arriving in January 2025, from monthly arrivals and the 38-day median lag. Net reduction on the resident part, larger than earlier years because early-2026 arrivals are low.
Importers value CIF. Freight and insurance taken as about 6.5% of Thai-coded 61.71 and 6% of other partners' 25.22. Ownership changes at the vessel, before freight. Range 4-9%.

If the operator is not resident, the sale is between non-residents. Resident-pattern hours rose to 22,237 (2.6 times 2024) while the mirror fell, so about 16% is resident-operated (range 8-26%); 84% of the FOB mirror (81.41) is removed.

Resident operators may run vessels flagged elsewhere, coded to those flags. Nauru and Tuvalu flagged imports (197.9 CIF) are 2.2 times the Kiribati series; about 1.9% of them is assumed resident-operated, given the higher resident hours.

Resident fish sold by routes the series misses: fresh or chilled fish outside the HS codes, non-reporting destinations, and annual-only partners (gap 1.3). Taken as 22% of resident-operated fish. Customs non-tuna exports rose in 2025, consistent with this.

No material treatment adjustment: direct sales to non-residents are a change of ownership, and processing without ownership change, merchanting and re-export are not evidenced. Range leans up for processing-contract cases at higher volumes.

Timing: Thai-coded January-February 2026 imports (4.2) are far below the same months of 2025 (11.9), which lowers 2025 sales by date; rising resident hours through 2025 partly offset this. Small net negative, wide range.
Importers record CIF; strip freight, insurance and brokerage. About 8.5% for Thai-bound fish (71% of the 2025 mirror) and about 6% for other buyers, 7.8% overall. Margin is assumed, not observed.

If the operator is not resident in Kiribati, the sale is between non-residents. Resident share raised to about 30% (10-55%): resident-address hours rose 2.6 times to 22,237, but the Kiribati-coded mirror fell, so only part of the rise is taken. The rest is removed.

Add fish caught by Kiribati-resident operators on vessels of other flags, coded to those flags. Taken as 2% (0-7%) of the FOB Nauru- and Tuvalu-coded series, which fell in 2025. No residence data exist for those flags; range is wide.

Resident share of the small annual-only gap (1.26), plus 15% of the resident base for at-sea sales and other routes, plus 2.0 (0-8) because resident-address hours rose 2.6 times while Kiribati-coded imports did not. Inferred.

Remove about 10% of resident-operated flows where the catch may be owned by a non-resident (contract fishing or toll processing), so only the fee is a service, not a good. Upper end allows a small merchanting margin.
Timing: sales at sea precede import recording by about 38 days; early-2026 imports were low, so the calendar-year shift is larger, scaled to the resident share. No other item identified.

Importers value CIF; exports are FOB where ownership changes (P4). Freight and insurance on frozen tuna, 71% of the mirror going to Thailand and the rest on shorter hops, taken at 5.2% of the mirror, range 3% to 8%.

Removes 64% of the FOB mirror as Kiribati-flag fish run by operators not resident in Kiribati (P1, P2). Resident share 36%, range 15% to 56%: address-pattern hours tripled to 22,237 while the mirror fell, so only part of that effort shows in the mirror (P6).

If Kiribati-resident operators run ships under Nauru, Tuvalu or other flags, importers code that fish elsewhere (P3, P7). About 2% of Nauru- and Tuvalu-coded imports (198 million USD CIF) is 3.8; raised to 5.5 for the 2025 jump in resident hours. Wide range.

Resident sales the monthly series misses (P5): annual-only reporters' extra 1.3 million, scaled by resident share (0.4); 18% of resident-run mirror fish by routes with no partner record, higher as hours rose but the mirror did not (5.3); fresh chilled fish outside tuna codes (2.0).

Some resident-run fish may be consigned for processing abroad without change of ownership, and the same fish can be recorded by two importers after landing in one and re-export to another (P1). Taken as about 3.7% of resident-run fish.

Timing: importers record arrival, a median 38-42 days after the at-sea sale (P5). Moving Thai arrivals back to sale dates lowers 2025 by 3.8 million, about 6%, but early-2026 Thai months look incomplete; about three quarters of the shift on the resident share is used.
Importers value CIF. Freight and insurance taken as 6% of Thai-recorded value (61.71) and 3.5% of other partners (25.22). P3; files 01, 06.

If the operator is not resident, the sale is between non-residents. Resident-operated share taken as 30% of the FOB mirror (24.70) because resident-pattern hours rose to 22,237 while the mirror did not; 70% is removed. Wide range. P1, P2, P4; file 02.

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels flagged to other Pacific states, importers code that fish elsewhere. No register data for those flags; taken as 1% of the FOB value of Nauru- and Tuvalu-coded imports. P2, P5; file 03.

Three parts: partners reporting annually only (1.26 CIF, resident share) 0.36; resident fish reaching buyers or codes outside the series, 15% of resident fish in the mirror, 3.71; fresh or chilled tuna outside the HS codes, 1.20, higher as recorded exports rose. P5, P7; files 01, 06.

No evidence of toll processing or merchanting by residents; Kiribati has no tuna processing of scale, and fish kept for local use is neither exported nor in the mirror. Zero, with a range for unknown joint-venture contracts. P8; model knowledge.

Timing: importers record fish one to two months after the sale at sea. Thai monthly values give -3.47 for 2025 (early 2026 months look thin), applied to the resident share at half weight. P6; files 01, 02.
Thai-bound fish (61.71) at about 6% freight and insurance, other partners (25.22) at about 3%. Importers record CIF; an export is valued at the point of sale (P3, P2). Contract terms are unobserved.

Resident share raised to 33% (range 15-65%): address hours triple to 22.2k although the mirror falls, so resident activity rose, but not in proportion since that fish is not visible in the mirror (P4). 67% of the FOB mirror removed (P1).

Catch of resident operators on vessels flagged elsewhere is coded to other flags (P2, P6). Somewhat larger than earlier years because resident activity expanded in 2025 without a matching rise in the mirror. Wide range.

Annual-only records add little (+0.4); chilled fish outside the HS codes and unreported routes +1.6; a further +2.0 allowance because resident hours tripled without a mirror rise (P4, P5). Wide range.
About 3% of resident fish may move within a group, go for toll processing without change of ownership, or stay in the economy (P8). Merchanting by resident traders could offset. Thin evidence.

Timing: Thai arrivals fall into early 2026, so fewer 2025 sales at sea are carried by next-year arrivals than 2025 arrivals carried from 2024. Resident share of the net shift is negative (P5). February 2026 looks incomplete.
Remove freight and insurance: about 6.5% of the 61.71 Thai-recorded value and 5% of the 25.22 other-partner value, importers valuing CIF.
FOB mirror 81.66. Resident-operated share set near 26% (resident-pattern hours 22,237, 2.6 times 2024; customs tuna up to 3.44), so about 74% is catch of non-resident operators. Share range is wide.
Resident operators with vessels flagged elsewhere would be coded to other origins. No direct data; set at about 30% of the larger resident-coded amount, range from near zero.
Annual-only partners add 1.26 CIF (observed), scaled to the resident share; plus about 25% of resident-coded fish for omitted destinations, fresh tuna codes and sales at sea not coded to Kiribati.
About 5% of the resident total removed for fish kept locally, processing without change of ownership and merchanting, which are not ordinary goods exports.
Timing: with resident activity rising fast, fish sold at sea late in 2025 reaches import records about 6 weeks later, in 2026. Sale-year exports exceed import-year records.
Importers value CIF. Freight and insurance taken as 5% of the CIF mirror (range 2.8-7.2%). Thai buyers are 71% of value; non-Thai months are lumpy bulk shipments (P3, P4).

Flag does not fix residence (P2). Judged 50% of Kiribati-flag value resident-operated (80% range 25-75%). Resident-pattern hours rose to 22,237 and customs tuna and goods exports rose, but the mirror fell 11%, so the share rises only part way (P5, P8).

Resident operators running Nauru- or Tuvalu-flagged vessels. About 2.4% of the FOB Nauru and Tuvalu mirror (USD 198m CIF), higher than earlier years because resident activity grew. No residence data for those flags (P3, P5).

Thai share of 71% matches the carrier-chain share, so few missed destinations. Allowance for sales at sea to non-reporting destinations and for forms outside the HS set, larger than 2024 as resident activity and non-tuna customs exports grew (P6, P8).
Processing before sale and merchanting margin net to a small amount, taken as about 2% of resident-operated catch, sign uncertain. Larger base than 2024 because the resident share is higher (P7).
Timing of ownership change. Sales at sea in late 2025 arrive in early 2026, which was lower than early 2025 arrivals (2026 months are provisional); resident share applied (P7).

Importers record CIF (P4). Freight, insurance and any trader margin taken as 6 percent of the mirror, range 3.5 to 10 percent. Thai share is about 71 percent, similar to 2024, so the same rate and range are used.

Resident-pattern hours rose to 22.2k, about 2.6 times 2024, but the mirror fell 11 percent, so hours do not map one-for-one (P5). Share raised to 34 percent of FOB mirror (15 to 60); the other 66 percent is removed (P2, P3).

If Kiribati-resident operators run vessels on Nauru or Tuvalu registers, importers code that fish to those flags (P3, P6). Those flags carry 198 USD m; 2 percent gives 4.0. Lower range top because more resident capacity now shows on the Kiribati register (file 02).

Annual-only gap is small, 1.26 CIF, about 0.4 at FOB and resident share. Add about 4.0 for expanded resident activity (hours tripled, customs tuna returns rose): landings abroad, sales to carriers bound for non-reporting ports, fresh fish outside the HS set (P5, P6, P7).

Goods for processing without change of ownership and merchanting are not gross goods exports (P1). No evidence of material resident tolling or trading. Zero, with a wider upside range as resident operations expand and may sell processed product.

Cut-off timing (P8): early-January 2026 arrivals in the Thai series are lower than early January 2025, so fish sold late in 2025 is not yet in 2025 import records. Net shift for the resident share, plus a small double-count allowance.

Importers value imports CIF (05). Carriage and insurance come off at about 8% for carrier cargo to Thailand (Thai share 71% of the mirror, 01) and 5% for other routes, 7.1% overall. Rates are model knowledge. P3, P8.

Coded by flag (P1; 05), but vessels run from abroad sell between non-residents (P2). Resident-run share 26% of the FOB mirror: 22,237 resident-address hours (02) imply about 34%, shaded down because hours are not catch value and officially recorded tuna stays small (06). P4.

Fish caught by Kiribati-resident operators on vessels under other flags is coded to those flags, so the mirror misses it (P1, P5; 03, 05). No direct evidence; set at 18% of resident-run Kiribati-flag catch, wide range. Inferred.

Adds the annual-versus-monthly partner gap (88.19 vs 86.93; 01, 06) at FOB and resident share (0.30), plus 16% of resident catch for sales at sea bound for ports that do not report, third-country landings, and fresh or other products outside the HS codes. P5.

Small deduction for merchanting margins and for fish processed abroad without change of ownership, neither a full goods export (P6; 05). Set at 4% of resident-run catch; direction fairly clear, size not. Inferred.

Sale at sea precedes arrival by a median 42 days (P6; 02), so 2025 sales map to arrivals from mid-February 2025 to mid-February 2026. Net shift in Thai arrivals is -4.27 CIF (01); applied at FOB and resident share. Contract terms could change the sign.

Importers value CIF. Bulk reefer freight and insurance over a median 38-42 day voyage to Thailand is taken as 6% of the mirror (range 3-10%) and removed, giving FOB at the point of sale. No freight rates are in the pack.

Resident-pattern hours rise 2.6-fold (22.2k) while the mirror falls, so the share is raised but damped: about 21% of the FOB mirror (range 7-38%) is resident-operated. Customs tuna and goods exports also rise. The rest, fish sold between non-residents, is removed.

If a Kiribati-resident operator runs vessels under other flags (locally based foreign-flag vessels, reflagging among Kiribati, Nauru, Tuvalu), importers code that fish elsewhere. Raised for 2025 given the hours jump and the rise in customs-recorded tuna; long upper tail.

Resident fish reaching buyers outside the monthly series: annual-only reporters (small gap in 2025), non-reporting partners, fresh or other HS lines. Thai share of 71% matches the chain share, so no extra gap-fill. Scales with the larger resident base.

Small net removal: resident-operated fish sent to affiliated plants abroad for processing without change of ownership is not a goods export, and merchanting is recorded net. Larger resident base widens the range; no processing data exist.

Timing. The mirror counts arrival; ownership passes about 40 days earlier. Early-2026 arrivals are well below early-2025 and are partly incomplete, so the reduction on the resident share is larger but uncertain.

Importers value imports CIF (P3). Thailand takes 61.71 of 86.93; remove about 7.5% of CIF for long-haul reefer freight and insurance, and about 4% on the non-Thai part (25.22). Rates are model knowledge: ranges 4-11% and 1-8%.

If the operator is not resident in Kiribati, a sale between non-residents is not a Kiribati export (P1). Resident-address hours rose to 22,237 but the mirror fell (P4), so the resident share is raised only to about 21% of the FOB mirror; the rest is removed. Very wide range.

Resident operators may run vessels flagged elsewhere (Nauru and Tuvalu registers move with Kiribati in the fish-transfer chain) or land fish coded to a processing country (P5). Higher than 2024 as resident hours and official exports rose; set near 29% of the resident mirror amount.

Resident sales at sea to carriers, landings in third countries, fresh or chilled fish under other HS codes, and partners reporting annually only (gap 1.26, resident share only) are outside the monthly series (P5). Not measured; sized near 29% of the resident mirror amount.

Goods sent for processing without change of ownership are not goods exports, and merchanting is recorded net (P6). Nothing shows either is large; slightly bigger removal than earlier years because resident activity is larger, with a range that includes a small addition.

Timing: ownership changes at sea about 42 days before the importer records arrival (P6). Resident flows rose sharply in 2025, so calendar-year sales exceed arrivals by a small amount, net of possible double counting where one lot passes two importers.

P1: importers record CIF (files 00, 05). About 7% for the Thai route and 5% for direct landings, weighted by a 71% Thai share (file 06), gives 6.8% of the raw mirror. Sized from model knowledge; plausible range 4-10%.

P2, P3, P8: resident share of the FOB mirror set at 36% (range 15-65%). Resident-pattern hours tripled to 22.2k (file 02) but the mirror did not rise and the address is a hint, so hours are damped; customs tuna rose (file 06). The rest is removed.

P4: if a Kiribati-resident operator runs vessels under another flag, importers code the fish to that flag (files 03, 05). About 1.7% of the FOB Nauru and Tuvalu series (file 03) is added; lower than 2023-24 because more resident hours sit under the Kiribati flag (file 02).

P4, P5: adds resident fish the series misses: destinations outside the seven reporters (about 15% of a larger resident mirror), a small annual-only gap (88.19 less 86.93, file 06) and products outside the HS codes (about 1.5, with a larger resident fleet).
P7: the pack cannot size tolling, merchanting or re-export effects and the question counts fish residents caught. Centred on zero; range widened because the resident base is larger in 2025.

P6, P8: timing. Importers record at arrival, about 40 days after sale (file 02). Thai-route arrivals in early 2026 were well below early 2025, but those months are incomplete (file 01), so the effect is damped and the range widened.

Importers record CIF. Remove freight and insurance: about 7% of Thai-bound value (71% of the 2025 mirror) and 3% of other partners' value (mostly direct landings). Thai and non-Thai split from file 06.

Resident-operated share raised to 55% (80% range 22-85%): address-hint hours roughly tripled to 22,237 and tuna passing customs rose. Hours are only a hint and the mirror did not rise, so the share stays well below hours-proportional.

If Kiribati-resident operators also run vessels under other flags (Nauru and Tuvalu carry large coded volumes), that catch is outside the Kiribati-origin series. Set at 10% of a larger resident-operated amount, range 0-35%; nothing in the pack sizes it directly.

Adds resident fish the monthly series misses: partners reporting annually only (annual total 1.26 higher, taken at FOB and resident share), non-reporting hubs (10% of resident fish) and fresh tuna under other codes (1%).

Customs recorded 3.44 FOB of tuna exports, up from 0.59. Taking 30% as fish bought from non-resident vessels and processed locally (a processed-goods export, not resident catch) gives a small removal. Toll processing and merchanting are unsized; range is wide.

Early-2026 Thai arrivals fell sharply (January 4.09, February 0.09 against 6.13 and 5.81 a year earlier), so lagged 2025 sales are lower. Part may be rerouting rather than timing, hence a wide range. Scaled to Thai-bound resident fish.

principles.statement: True exports are goods whose economic ownership passes from a Kiribati resident to a non-resident, valued free on board at the point of hand-over. Fish caught by ships operated by residents and sold abroad directly counts, whether sold in a foreign port or at sea to a carrier, and wherever the fish was caught.
principles.source: 05 bop_goods_fish (BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e); IMTS 2010 1.31 and F.19)
principles.uncertainty: Low on the concept. Moderate on where ownership really passes in each supply chain (at the vessel, at the carrier, or on arrival), which no file observes.

principles.statement: Residence follows the operator, not the flag. Flags of convenience and place of registration do not decide residence; a legal entity is resident where it is incorporated or registered and has significant operations, and the operator can differ from the owner or charterer. A Kiribati-flagged ship run from abroad has a non-resident operator; a Kiribati-incorporated operator running its own ship is resident.
principles.source: 05 residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136)
principles.uncertainty: High in application. The register address in 02 is a hint only: a locally incorporated company with foreign owners can be resident, and a Kiribati address can belong to an agent.

principles.statement: Importers record origin by the catching vessel's nationality (wholly obtained fish, Kyoto Annex K 2(f)), in practice the flag. The raw mirror therefore follows the flag: it holds the catch of every Kiribati-flagged vessel whoever runs it, and misses resident-operated catch carried under other flags (for example Nauru and Tuvalu, whose flagged series are large in 03).
principles.source: 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports; 03
principles.uncertainty: Low on the coding rule (stable 2014-2025 for the seven importers). Very high on how much Nauru- and Tuvalu-flagged fish is run by Kiribati residents; no file shows it.

principles.statement: Importers value imports CIF, while a goods export is valued at the point of hand-over, so freight and insurance after that point come out. Fish sold at sea to a carrier and shipped to Thai ports (median about 38 days) carries a real charge. I size it at 2-9% of CIF, centre 5%.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis (CIF); 02 chain lag; model knowledge on reefer freight rates
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. The rate is not in the evidence; it varies by route (bulk carrier to Thailand versus air-freighted fresh fish).

principles.statement: Only a minority of Kiribati-flagged catch is resident-operated, but the share is uncertain and higher in 2025. Of 116 register vessels only 43 carry an address hint, and resident-pattern fishing hours were 7,415 (2023), 8,496 (2024) and 22,237 (2025) while the Kiribati-flag mirror stayed flat. I take about one fifth of fish value in 2023-24 and one third in 2025.
principles.source: 02 hours and register counts; model knowledge that much of the Kiribati-flagged fleet is foreign-run or chartered
principles.uncertainty: High. Hours are a partial hint (no foreign-pattern or total hours are given) and the 2025 jump may partly reflect better register matching.

principles.statement: The partner series covers a few importers and fish coded to the flag. Resident sales to other buyers (non-reporting processing countries, fresh air-freighted fish, products outside the codes) are not in it, and about one third of at-sea transshipments do not end in a Thai port, so route coverage is not guaranteed. This adds a modest share to resident exports.
principles.source: 01; 02 chain facts; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: Very high. Scale is a prior of roughly 4-30% of resident flow, with no direct evidence.

principles.statement: Fish sent for processing abroad with no change of ownership, and merchanting, are not gross goods exports. Also, importers record fish about 38 days after hand-over, so some fish sold late in one year appears in the next year's mirror. Both effects are small next to residence and flag coding.
principles.source: 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (BPM6 Compilation Guide table 5.1); 02 lag; 01 monthly series
principles.uncertainty: Moderate on timing (lag comes from AIS chains mostly before 2022). High on how much resident fish is processed without a sale.

principles.statement: Official statistics show what compilers recorded, which differs from true exports by concept, timing and coverage. Customs cannot see fish sold at sea or landed abroad, so other sources are needed. Goods exports (8.07, 8.49, 17.34) and part-year customs tuna (0.00, 0.59, 3.44) are consistent with partial coverage of resident fish. They give a floor for the customs-visible part and a direction (a 2025 step-up), not a level.
principles.source: 06; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation
principles.uncertainty: High. The compiler's methods are not documented, balance-of-payments goods include non-fish items, and customs months are partial (7, 10, 10 of 12).

principles.statement: A catch is a Kiribati export only if the operator who owns the fish when it is sold is resident in Kiribati. Flag and registration do not decide residence; a charterer's residence follows its own base of operations. Direct sales at sea or in foreign ports by resident operators are goods exports whatever the flag or catching area. Access fees paid by foreign fleets are not goods and stay outside this bridge.
principles.source: 05 residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136); 05 bop_goods_fish (BPM6 10.17(e); IMTS 2010 1.31, F.19)
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. A locally incorporated company with foreign owners and no local base may or may not be treated as resident, depending on compiler practice; register address is only a hint.

principles.statement: Importers record partner by origin, and for fish caught at sea origin follows the catching vessel's flag. So the raw mirror is fish from Kiribati-flagged vessels whoever operates them, and it omits resident-operated fish on other flags. Thai import rules also key to the flag state.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports (Kyoto Annex K 2(f); IMTS 2010 6.25)
principles.uncertainty: Low for the coding rule; moderate for how each importer treats chartered or reflagged vessels and processed products.

principles.statement: Importers value at their border including freight and insurance (CIF). The export concept values the fish where ownership changes, alongside the vessel for sales at sea (FOB). A deduction for freight, insurance and carrier handling is needed; it is larger on the long reefer route to Thailand than on nearer or air-freighted routes.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis (imports CIF, exports FOB); model knowledge of reefer freight and carrier costs
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. No freight data in the pack; a plausible deduction is 4.5% to 11.5% of the raw mirror.

principles.statement: The Kiribati register is mostly foreign-run vessels using the flag for access, with a resident minority. Kiribati register addresses (a hint, possibly agents) cover few vessels, and their fishing hours rise sharply in 2025; no hours denominator is given. The resident share of Kiribati-flag catch value is therefore a minority: low in 2023 and 2024, higher in 2025.
principles.source: 02 (address hints for 43 of 116 vessels; resident-pattern hours 7,415, 8,496, 22,237); model knowledge of the Kiribati-flag fleet
principles.uncertainty: High, and the largest source of uncertainty: most vessels have no usable address, the hint may be an agent, and value per hour differs by gear.

principles.statement: The mirror misses resident-operated fish coded to another flag, sold to buyers outside the partner set or reporting annually only, falling outside the HS codes (fresh or chilled fish), or sold at sea to carriers that do not end in a reporting port. About two thirds of at-sea encounters by register vessels are followed by a Thai port call within 120 days.
principles.source: 02 AIS chain facts; 06 reference block (annual returns exceed monthly sums); 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation
principles.uncertainty: High for sizes. The third without a Thai call may still reach other reporting buyers, and the encounter counts are sparse after 2021.

principles.statement: Official statistics show what the compiler recorded. Fish sold or landed abroad never passes home customs, so a compiler needs fisheries-administration or company sources to see it. Without them official tuna goods are a floor for resident sales; they can sit above true exports only if fish of non-residents is counted. They give direction, not size.
principles.source: 06 how_to_read; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (Compilers Manual 24.9, Norway case)
principles.uncertainty: High. The compiler's sources and methods are not documented in the pack, and customs returns cover only 7, 10 and 10 months in 2023-25.

principles.statement: Treatment and timing. Goods sent abroad for processing without a change of ownership, and goods under operating leases, are not goods exports on crossing; merchanting is recorded net. Ownership of at-sea sales changes when sold, while the mirror records arrival about six weeks later (median 42 days), a small cut-off effect.
principles.source: 05 bop_goods_fish (BPM6 10.17(f)); 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (Table 5.1); 02 lag facts
principles.uncertainty: Low to moderate in size; there is no direct evidence of processing or lease arrangements.

principles.statement: Whether a sale of fish counts as a Kiribati goods export depends on the residence of the operator and a change of economic ownership to a non-resident, not on the vessel's flag or registry. Catch of resident operators sold abroad directly, in port or at sea, is included.
principles.source: BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e), 4.131-4.136; IMTS 2010 F.19 (file 05: bop_goods_fish, residence_vs_flag)
principles.uncertainty: Residence of each operator is not observed in the pack; register addresses are only a hint. The test is substantive: significant production from a Kiribati base.

principles.statement: The raw mirror is a flag-based count valued CIF. Importers record origin as the country of the catching vessel's flag, and Thai fisheries law keys fish imports to the flag state. FOB is lower by freight and insurance: about 5.5% on the Thai route and 7.5% on other routes on average (ranges 3.5%-8% and 4%-11%).
principles.source: file 05 (partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports); file 01 description; model knowledge of frozen-tuna carrier freight
principles.uncertainty: Freight rates are not in the pack. Routes to the Americas cost more than routes to Thailand or Japan.

principles.statement: Most Kiribati-flagged fishing is done by operators not resident in Kiribati (chartered, foreign-run or foreign-owned vessels), so their sales are between non-residents. The resident share of the flag-based mirror is set at 12% in 2023 and moved with resident-pattern fishing hours relative to the mirror, damped by a square root: 12.0%, 11.8% and 20.2% for 2023, 2024 and 2025.
principles.source: BPM6 4.136 (file 05); file 02 (register address hints for 43 of 116 register vessels; resident-pattern hours 7,415, 8,496 and 22,237); model knowledge of chartering practice
principles.uncertainty: Large. The 2023 level (5%-25%) is a judgment; hints cover about one third of vessels; hours are not value. The 2025 band is wider (10%-35%).

principles.statement: Fish caught by Kiribati-resident operators on vessels flagged elsewhere is true exports even though importers code it to another flag. The neighbouring registers analysed alongside Kiribati's (Nauru, Tuvalu) are the main candidates; other flag states are minor. Central resident share: 4% of the FOB value of Nauru and Tuvalu coded imports in 2023-24 and 3% in 2025 (as resident hours move onto the Kiribati register), plus 0.1% of five other flag states.
principles.source: BPM6 4.136 (file 05); file 03 (Nauru 180.8 and Tuvalu 54.1 USD m in 2023); file 02 (three registers followed as one chain); model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: Very large and mostly unobserved: 1%-9% of Nauru and Tuvalu value (1%-7% in 2025). This is the weakest link in the bridge.

principles.statement: Resident sales missing from the partner series: (a) partners that report annually only (annual returns exceed monthly sums by 3.71, 7.05 and 1.26 USD m); (b) carriers and destinations outside the seven reporters, and products outside the listed HS codes, taken as 12% of the resident base; (c) fish passing through Kiribati's own customs, taken at 35% of annualised customs tuna to allow for overlap with the mirror and non-resident catch. A sale at sea to a carrier is a goods sale at transfer.
principles.source: BPM6 10.17(e); IMTS 2010 1.31; file 06 (annual vs monthly totals, customs tuna); file 02 (about 32% of at-sea transfers not followed by a Thai port call within 120 days)
principles.uncertainty: Share (b) 4%-25%; the customs overlap is unknown; annual-only partners are assumed to carry the same resident share as the monthly ones.

principles.statement: Treatment items do not change the level on balance: goods sent for processing without change of ownership are not exports, sales between residents are not exports, and merchanted fish or fish kept for local use sit outside the partner series. No evidence sizes them, so the central value is zero with a symmetric band.
principles.source: BPM6 10.13, 10.41-10.49; BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1 (file 05: customs_vs_bop_compilation)
principles.uncertainty: Band of about plus or minus 1.3 USD m (1.8 in 2025) is a judgment.

principles.statement: Official statistics are evidence about compiler coverage, not a measure of true exports. Fish sold at sea or landed abroad bypasses home customs by construction, so a customs or goods figure can sit below true exports; it can also contain fish that is not resident-caught. Customs tuna exports (0.00, 0.59, 3.44 for 7, 10, 10 months reported) and BOP goods (8.07, 8.49, 17.34, which include non-tuna goods) are used for the customs term in P5 and as a direction signal: the 2025 rise fits the 2025 rise in resident hours.
principles.source: file 06; file 05 (customs_vs_bop_compilation, Compilers Manual 24.9 and the Norway case)
principles.uncertainty: Composition of BOP goods and compiler methods are not documented; customs months are missing in all three years.

principles.statement: The calendar-year concept follows the sale, while importers record arrival, a median six weeks after an at-sea transfer. With roughly flat flows the timing effect on a year's total is small and is set to zero with a narrow band. Payments for access rights are income, not goods, and sit outside this bridge.
principles.source: file 02 (chain lag median 42 days, quartiles 22 and 53); BPM6 change-of-ownership rule (file 05)
principles.uncertainty: Timing shift within about plus or minus 0.45 USD m; larger if flows turn sharply at year end.

principles.statement: A BPM6 goods export needs a change of economic ownership between a resident and a non-resident. Fish caught by ships operated by residents and sold abroad directly, including sales at sea to foreign carriers, is included. The test is the operator's residence and who owns the catch at sale, not the flag or the route.
principles.source: BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e); IMTS 2010 1.31, F.19 (file 05, bop_goods_fish)
principles.uncertainty: Low on the concept. The point at which title passes (at sea, at the cannery gate) is a contract matter not seen in the pack.

principles.statement: Operator residence is set by where the operator is based and engaged in significant production, not by flag or registration; a chartered or foreign-run vessel flying the Kiribati flag has a non-resident operator, while a Kiribati-incorporated unit operating its own vessel is resident. Only the second kind produces Kiribati exports.
principles.source: BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136 (file 05, residence_vs_flag)
principles.uncertainty: High in application. Operator residence is not observed; a register address in Kiribati is only a hint and may be an agent's address.

principles.statement: Importers record partner by country of origin, and for fish caught at sea origin follows the nationality of the catching vessel, in practice its flag. The raw mirror is therefore a flag-coded series: it mixes resident-run and foreign-run Kiribati-flagged fish, and it omits resident-run fish landed under other flags.
principles.source: IMTS 2010 6.6, 6.25; Kyoto Annex K 2(f); Comtrade metadata for seven reporters; Thai fisheries ordinance s.95-96 (file 05)
principles.uncertainty: Medium. The nationality test is left to each importer, though the pack shows it stable for 2014-2025.

principles.statement: Importers value imports CIF while exports are FOB. For frozen tuna carried by reefer carrier from the catch area to Thailand and other ports, sea freight plus insurance is about 3 to 8.5 percent of CIF value, central 5.5 percent.
principles.source: Comtrade metadata (imports CIF, file 05); model knowledge of reefer freight and tuna prices
principles.uncertainty: Medium. Freight depends on route, season and price; the range is judgement.

principles.statement: The resident-operated share of Kiribati-flag fish is small and uncertain. Resident-pattern register hours (7.4k, 8.5k, 22.2k) do not track the flat mirror, so hours cannot size it directly. Thai-bound fish moves by carrier from industrial vessels (about two thirds of register encounters reach a Thai port, median lag 42 days) and is likelier foreign-run; other flows are likelier resident. Taken as 15 percent of Thai-coded and 40 percent of other flows, raised about 25 percent for 2025.
principles.source: Files 01, 02, 03; model knowledge of Pacific fleet ownership
principles.uncertainty: Very high. 80 percent range of overall share: 7-33 percent (2023), 8-38 percent (2024), 9-45 percent (2025). Encounter data show almost no events after 2022.

principles.statement: Fish sold at sea or landed abroad does not pass home customs, and the standard remedy is a fisheries-administration source. Partner series capture it only if the importer is among those reported, codes origin as Kiribati, and uses the listed HS lines. Some partners report annually only (annual returns exceed monthly sums by 3.71, 7.05 and 1.26 USD m), and processors in other Pacific states, fresh or chilled lines and non-listed importers sit outside the series.
principles.source: IMTS Compilers Manual Box XXIV.2 (file 05); files 01 and 06; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High. Size of out-of-series routes is not observed; allowance is judgement.

principles.statement: Official figures show what the compilers recorded. Customs tuna exports are near zero (0.00, 0.59, 3.44 USD m, 7 to 10 months) and the goods line (8.07, 8.49, 17.34) includes non-tuna goods, so both sit far below the mirror. This is consistent with resident catch sold at sea being outside customs, and says little about the true level. The 2025 rise in both gives a direction check only.
principles.source: File 06; IMTS Compilers Manual para 24.9; BPM6 Compilation Guide table 5.1
principles.uncertainty: High. The tuna content of the goods line is not documented in the pack.

principles.statement: Treatment and timing matter at the margin. Goods processed abroad without a change of ownership and merchanting are not general merchandise exports; ownership changes at the sale, about six weeks before the import is recorded, so calendar-year sales differ slightly from calendar-year imports. Fish kept for local use never enters the mirror and needs no adjustment.
principles.source: BPM6 Compilation Guide table 5.1; BPM6 10.13; file 01 and file 02 chain lags
principles.uncertainty: Low to medium in size, but no direct evidence on how much resident fish is processed under tolling terms.

principles.statement: True exports are the FOB value of fish caught by operators resident in Kiribati and sold to non-residents in the year, whatever the vessel flag or route. Operator residence and change of ownership decide, not flag, landing place or customs record. Sales at sea to foreign carriers count.
principles.source: 05 bop_goods_fish (BPM6 10.17(e), IMTS 1.31) and residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136)
principles.uncertainty: The concept is firm. Applying it needs operator-residence facts that the pack gives only as hints.

principles.statement: Importers code origin by the catching vessel's flag (Kyoto Annex K 2(f); Comtrade partner is origin; Thai import control keys to flag state). The raw mirror therefore tracks flag-state catch: it includes Kiribati-flag fish run by non-residents and leaves out resident-run fish under other flags.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. Origin practice of the non-Thai partners is documented only by metadata.

principles.statement: Importers value imports CIF. True exports are valued FOB at the point ownership passes (alongside a carrier at sea or in port). For frozen tuna carried across the Pacific, freight, insurance and any trader margin between first sale and importer are about 5-11% of CIF, central 7.5%.
principles.source: 01/05 partner_basis (CIF); model knowledge for the percentage
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. Rate varies by route and market; fresh or air-freighted fish carries more.

principles.statement: Most Kiribati-flag vessels are chartered or run by foreign parents; some are run by Kiribati-incorporated operators. Register address hints (43 of 116 vessels) and resident-pattern fishing hours (7,415 in 2023; 8,496 in 2024; 22,237 in 2025) show resident-run activity exists and rose sharply in 2025. Hours cannot be turned into value (longline versus purse seine). I set the resident share of the FOB mirror at 18%, 17% and 28%, with the 2025 rise damped.
principles.source: 02 fleet aggregates; model knowledge on fleet ownership
principles.uncertainty: High. Share range is roughly 9-36% (2025: 16-49%). Register address is a hint, not a finding.

principles.statement: Flags move. Nauru-coded imports went from 0 (2018) to about 181 (2023) and Tuvalu-coded from about 8 (2017) to about 54, while Kiribati-coded fell from 140 (2017) to 86-105. Some fish caught by Kiribati-resident operators therefore carries another flag and is coded to other states. I assume about 1% of Nauru and Tuvalu coded value plus a little elsewhere.
principles.source: 03 flag-state series; 02 chain facts cover three registers
principles.uncertainty: Very high. No direct operator data for non-Kiribati flags; flag change alone does not show operator residence.

principles.statement: Resident operators sell to carriers at sea; 68% of register-fleet encounters are followed by a Thai port call within 120 days (median lag 38 days). Ownership passes at sea, so these are Kiribati exports even though Kiribati customs never sees them. The mirror reaches them only where the importer is one of seven reporting partners, reports monthly and uses the listed HS codes. Fresh fish, other markets and annual-only reporters sit outside the raw mirror.
principles.source: 02 AIS chain facts; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation; 06 note (annual returns exceed monthly sums by 3.71, 7.05, 1.26 USD m)
principles.uncertainty: High. Uncaptured share of resident fish taken as a 30% uplift on the resident in-mirror part (range 10-55%).

principles.statement: Official figures show what the compiler recorded. Customs cannot see fish sold at sea or landed abroad, and the BOP compiler needs extra sources for it. Official totals cover all goods, so recorded resident fish is small in 2023-24; the 2025 step-up in BOP, customs tuna and resident hours moves together. Official figures are coverage evidence only; true exports can sit above or below them.
principles.source: 06 official statistics; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation
principles.uncertainty: Compiler methods are not documented in the pack, so how much of the gap is concept, timing or coverage is unknown.

principles.statement: Ownership passes at sea or on landing, about 5-6 weeks before importers record the arrival. Calendar-year sales differ from calendar-year imports by the change in early-year flow. After applying the resident share this is a small negative item.
principles.source: 02 chain lag (median 38 days); 01 monthly series
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. Lag differs for non-Thai routes and for the 2025 resident ramp-up.

principles.statement: A fish sale is a Kiribati goods export only if the operator who catches and sells it is resident in Kiribati and ownership passes to a non-resident. The vessel's flag and registration do not decide residence. Direct sales at sea or in foreign ports by resident operators count.
principles.uncertainty: Boundary cases are hard: a Kiribati-incorporated entity with foreign owners counts as resident only if it has significant operations from Kiribati. The register address is a hint, not a finding.

principles.statement: Importers code origin by the nationality of the catching vessel, in practice its flag. So the raw mirror follows flag, not operator residence. It includes fish of non-resident operators on Kiribati-flag vessels and leaves out fish of resident operators on other flags.
principles.source: Kyoto Annex K 2(f); IMTS 2010 6.6, 6.25; Comtrade metadata for seven reporters; Thai fisheries ordinance (file 05)
principles.uncertainty: The nationality test is left to each country and customs practice at landing or processing may differ. The metadata shows stable origin coding but not how each declaration was made.

principles.statement: Importers value imports CIF. FOB at the point where ownership changes is lower by freight and insurance. Fish moved by carrier over weeks to Thailand carries more freight than catch landed directly by the catching vessel. I size this at roughly 4-10% for Thai-bound fish and 1-5% for other destinations.
principles.source: File 05 (imports CIF, exports FOB); file 02 (carrier chain, median lag 38-42 days); model knowledge of reefer freight rates
principles.uncertainty: Freight rates, fish price and the share of each route are not in the pack. The size of the adjustment is a judgement.

principles.statement: Resident operators are only part of the Kiribati-flag fleet. Resident-pattern fishing hours move little with the mirror: the mirror stays within 82-130 while those hours range from about 3,000 to 22,000. So most mirror fish comes from vessels without a resident-address pattern. I set the resident share low to moderate and keep a wide range.
principles.source: File 02 (register address hints, 43 of 116 vessels; hours by year); file 01; BPM6 4.136
principles.uncertainty: The pack gives no hours for non-resident or unclassified vessels, so no share can be computed. Vessel types differ in value per hour. The link between hours and mirror is weak (about 0.4 correlation before 2025).

principles.statement: The mirror leaves out resident-operator fish in four ways: vessels on other flags (the Nauru and Tuvalu series rose sharply while Kiribati's did not); buyers outside the seven reporters; partners that file annually only; and products or routes outside the HS codes, such as fish sold at sea to carriers heading elsewhere. These belong in true exports under BPM6 10.17(e).
principles.source: File 03; file 01 and file 06 (annual vs monthly totals); file 02 (67.5% of Kiribati-register encounters followed by a Thai call); BPM6 10.17(e)
principles.uncertainty: The pack has no residence data for operators on other flags. The high 2023 Thai share (87%) may mean unseen non-Thai routes or simply fewer non-Thai sales that year.

principles.statement: The official goods line follows customs returns closely in years with full data, and Kiribati's recorded tuna exports are small. Fish landed or sold abroad never passes home customs, so such a line is expected to differ from true exports in concept, timing and coverage. I use the official figures as evidence of what was recorded, not as the target.
principles.source: File 06 (BOP vs customs 2017, 2018, 2020; customs tuna by year); IMTS Compilers Manual Box XXIV.2 and para 24.9 (file 05)
principles.uncertainty: The compiler's methods are not documented in the pack. Months missing from customs in 2023-2025 mean the customs figures are partial.

principles.statement: Goods sent for processing without change of ownership, merchanting, fish that stays in the economy and re-exports change what counts as a goods export. Little of this should sit inside a flag-coded fish mirror, so I allow only a small adjustment with a range that includes zero.
principles.source: BPM6 10.13, Compilation Guide Table 5.1 (file 05)
principles.uncertainty: The pack has no evidence on consignment, tolling or local processing, so the size and sign are uncertain.

principles.statement: Ownership changes at the sale (often at sea), while the importer records the fish on arrival in port weeks later. A calendar-year cut-off therefore moves a small amount of value between years. I allow a small adjustment based on the median lag.
principles.source: BPM6 10.17(e); file 02 (lag median 38-42 days, quartiles 22-53); file 01 monthly series
principles.uncertainty: Lags vary by route and the early-2026 months are incomplete, so the sign and size are uncertain.

principles.statement: True exports are goods whose economic ownership passes from a Kiribati resident to a non-resident in the year, valued FOB. The test is where the operator and owner of the catch are resident, not the vessel's flag. Fish sold directly at sea by resident-operated ships counts.
principles.source: BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e), 4.136 (file 05: bop_goods_fish, residence_vs_flag); IMTS 2010 1.31
principles.uncertainty: Concept is clear. Residence of a Kiribati-incorporated entity run largely from abroad is open (4.131 significant production versus 4.134 place of incorporation).

principles.statement: The partner series assigns fish to Kiribati because importers use origin rules that, for sea fish, follow the catching vessel's flag, and value imports CIF. The mirror therefore measures flag-state catch recorded by seven reporting importers, not sales by residents. Flag and residence differ for chartered or flagged-in ships.
principles.source: File 05: partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports; Kyoto Annex K 2(f); IMTS 6.25
principles.uncertainty: Documented for the seven reporters. Practice of buyers outside the set is not shown.

principles.statement: Most Kiribati-flagged catch is run by operators based abroad (chartered, foreign-run or foreign joint-venture ships). Residents run a minority. Register addresses in Kiribati give a hint: 7.4k, 8.5k and 22.2k fishing hours in 2023-25, with only 43 of 116 register vessels carrying a usable address. I set the resident-run share of the Kiribati-coded mirror at 17%, 19% and 28%, lifting 2025 only partly because the mirror did not rise with the hours.
principles.source: File 02 (hours, register counts); model knowledge of flagging-in and charter practice in Pacific purse-seine fleets
principles.uncertainty: Very high. Hours have no denominator and no gear split, and a register address is a hint of residence, not proof. Central 80% range about 10-29% in 2023.

principles.statement: Fish sold to carriers at sea becomes an export when ownership changes. About two-thirds of at-sea encounters on the Kiribati register are followed by a Thai port call, median 42 days later. So Thai-bound mirror flows are sales at sea, valued FOB at the sale, recorded by the importer about six weeks later; calendar years need a small timing shift.
principles.source: File 02 (ais_chain_facts_kiribati_register); BPM6 10.17(e); file 01 monthly series
principles.uncertainty: Encounter-to-call links are a pattern, not a matched shipment. Lag spread is 22-53 days (quartiles). Freight share of CIF is model knowledge, 3-9%.

principles.statement: The monthly partner series leaves out partners that report annually only (annual returns exceed monthly sums by 3.71, 7.05 and 1.26 USD m), buyers outside the seven, and fresh or chilled tuna outside the listed HS codes. These gaps count toward true exports only for the resident-run share.
principles.source: File 06 (raw_mirror_tuna_by_year_for_reference note); file 01 (n_reporters_fish); model knowledge on buyers such as non-reporting or unlisted markets
