principles.uncertainty: Annual-only gap is observed but may include revisions. Unlisted-buyer gap (6% of the raw mirror, range about 2.5-13%) and fresh fish (about 1-1.5 USD m) are inferred.

principles.statement: Fish caught by Kiribati-resident operators under other flags is coded by importers to those flag states, so it is absent from the mirror. The Nauru and Tuvalu series (198-235 USD m a year) and the reflagging pattern show the flags are mobile, but nothing in the pack names residents as operators there. I add only a small fraction.
principles.source: File 03 (Nauru, Tuvalu series); file 05 origin_of_fish note on reflagging; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High. Fraction set at 1.5% of Nauru plus Tuvalu imports, range about 0.5-4.5%. Direction is clear, size is not.

principles.statement: Not every resident-run catch is a gross goods export: catch owned by a non-resident charterer or sent for processing without change of ownership is excluded, and merchanting counts only the margin. I deduct a modest share of the resident-run total.
principles.source: BPM6 10.13, 10.17(f); BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1 (file 05: customs_vs_bop_compilation); model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High. Deduction 10%, range about 0-20% of the resident-run total.

principles.statement: Official goods exports (8.07, 8.49, 17.34 USD m) cover all goods, not only tuna. Customs tuna lines (0, 0.59, 3.44 USD m, 7-10 months reported) cover what passes through Kiribati's own ports. Neither source is built to capture resident catch sold at sea or landed abroad, so recorded values show compiler coverage, not the economic total.
principles.source: File 06 how_to_read and annual table; file 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation; IMTS Compilers Manual 24.9
principles.uncertainty: The compiler's sources and methods are not documented in the pack. A recorded figure can sit below or above true exports.

principles.statement: True exports are goods whose economic ownership passes from a Kiribati resident to a non-resident in the year, valued FOB at the point of sale (at sea, alongside, or ex-vessel). Fish caught by resident-operated ships and sold abroad directly counts, including sales at sea. Flag, customs territory and the importer's arrival date do not decide it; the date of the ownership change does.
principles.source: File 05 bop_goods_fish (BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e); IMTS 2010 1.31, F.19); file 02 AIS chain lag (median 38 days from at-sea transfer to Thai port call).
principles.uncertainty: Low on the concept. Moderate on timing: the transfer date is not observed, and the 38-day lag comes from vessels on three registers.

principles.statement: Residence of the operator decides whose catch it is, not flag or registration. A Kiribati-flagged ship run from abroad has a non-resident operator; a Kiribati-incorporated operator with real activity in Kiribati is resident even if the owner is abroad or the flag is elsewhere. The sale between two non-residents is not a Kiribati export.
principles.source: File 05 residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136); file 02 register address hints.
principles.uncertainty: High in application: only 43 of 116 register entries carry an address hint, and an address in Kiribati does not prove substantial operations there.

principles.statement: The partner series measures the flag nationality of the catch, not residence. Importers record origin by their own rules, normally the flag of the catching vessel, and value imports CIF. So the raw mirror includes non-resident-operated Kiribati-flag fish and omits resident-operated fish carried under other flags.
principles.source: File 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports (IMTS 6.25; Kyoto Annex K 2(f); Thai fisheries law keyed to flag state); file 03 flag-state series.
principles.uncertainty: Low to moderate: the seven reporters are documented as using origin, but how each applies the flag test to chartered or re-flagged vessels is not shown.

principles.statement: CIF includes freight and insurance to the importer's border, which are not part of an FOB sale. Most Kiribati-origin fish (70 to 87 percent) goes to Thailand by carrier after at-sea transfer over a very long route, so the deduction is larger for Thai-bound fish than for fish moved over shorter routes.
principles.source: File 05 partner_basis (imports CIF, exports FOB); file 02 AIS chain facts; file 01 Thai share; model knowledge of carrier freight and delivered versus ex-vessel prices.
principles.uncertainty: Moderate: about 8 percent for Thai-bound fish (range 5 to 11) and 4 percent for other partners (range 2 to 7) are judgments, not observed rates.

principles.statement: The resident-operated part of the mirror must be sized as a share of value, with a wide range. Resident-pattern fishing hours are a hint of operator residence, not a value measure: across 2017 to 2025 they move between about 3,000 and 22,000 while the mirror stays between roughly 85 and 140. Resident-operated fish is therefore a minority of the Kiribati-flag mirror, and hours pass into value only partly.
principles.source: File 02 hours by address pattern; file 03 Kiribati row; file 01 monthly totals.
principles.uncertainty: Very high: there is no total-hours denominator, no gear split, and 73 register entries have no usable address.

principles.statement: Resident sales that the partner series does not capture are still goods exports: sales at sea to carriers bound for non-reporting destinations, landings in third countries, partners that report only annually, and fish under codes outside the mirror (fresh, chilled). The usual remedy is a fisheries-administration source, which is not in the pack.
principles.source: File 05 bop_goods_fish, customs_vs_bop_compilation (IMTS Compilers Manual Norway example); file 06 note on annual versus monthly totals (gaps of 3.71, 7.05, 1.26).
principles.uncertainty: High: no test of coverage by destination or product; the annual-only gap is observed but its Kiribati-origin split by operator is not.

principles.statement: Not every resident-operated catch is a goods export. If the resident operator fishes for a non-resident owner of the catch and is paid for the work, or the fish is handled for another's account without change of ownership, the transaction is a service. Fish kept in the economy is not exported. Merchanting and goods for processing follow separate BPM6 rules.
principles.source: File 05 bop_goods_fish (BPM6 10.13, 10.17(f)); customs_vs_bop_compilation (Compilation Guide Table 5.1).
principles.uncertainty: High: contract terms and who owns the catch at the moment of transfer are not observed.

principles.statement: Official figures show what the compilers recorded, in their coverage and timing, and are a different concept from true exports. Customs cannot see fish sold at sea or landed abroad, so recorded tuna is a floor-type signal of visible resident exports and a direction-of-change indicator. The goods total also holds non-tuna items, and months reported are incomplete, so levels are not read across.
principles.source: File 06 (BOP goods exports, customs tuna, months reported); file 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation.
principles.uncertainty: High: composition of the BOP goods line is not documented and the 2025 BOP value is an estimate.

principles.statement: A goods export needs a change of economic ownership from a resident to a non-resident. Fish caught by ships operated by residents and sold abroad directly, in a foreign port or at sea to a foreign vessel, is included. The test is the operator's residence and who owns the catch, not the vessel's flag.
principles.uncertainty: Medium. Whether a locally incorporated one-vessel company with little on-island activity counts as resident (legal test, BPM6 4.134, versus production test, 4.131) is a judgment, so the resident share is wide.

principles.statement: Importers code origin by the catching vessel's flag (Thai fisheries law keys to the flag state; Comtrade partner is origin; wholly-obtained fish belongs to the vessel's country). The raw mirror is therefore all catch of Kiribati-flag vessels whatever the operator's residence, and it omits resident-operated catch under other flags. Flags of convenience do not fix residence.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports, residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.136)
principles.uncertainty: Medium-low for Thailand (about 70-87% of the mirror); higher for the other six importers, which may apply landing-based tests to some flows.

principles.statement: Import values are normally CIF while exports are FOB. Freight and insurance from the fishing grounds to the importing port are a few percent of fish value. I use about 6% for the long reefer chain to Thailand (median 38 days from at-sea meeting to Thai port) and about 8% for other partners (chilled or air-freighted lines carry more).
principles.source: 05 partner_basis (imports CIF, exports FOB); 02 chain lag; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: Medium. The pack holds no freight data; plausible range is 3-10% of the mirror.

principles.statement: The resident share of Kiribati-flag catch is bounded but not measured. Only 43 of 116 register vessels carry an address hint. Resident-address hours moved from 3,066 (2021) to 7,415, 8,496 and 22,237 (2023-25) while the Kiribati mirror stayed at 85-140 in all years, so the mirror is not mainly driven by resident-address vessels. Hours understate (vessels without a hint, local-incorporation test) and may overstate (agent addresses, register coverage). Fish landed by Kiribati-flag vessels in other partners' home ports is less likely resident-operated than Thai-bound at-sea sales.
principles.source: 02 address-pattern hours and register counts; 03 Kiribati row; 01 Thai versus non-Thai split; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High. This is the main driver of the bridge; the 80% range for the resident-operated part spans roughly 14-60% of the FOB mirror.

principles.statement: The partner series misses some resident sales: partners that report annually only (annual Comtrade totals exceed the monthly sums by 3.71, 7.05 and 1.26), tuna lines outside the listed HS codes (fresh or chilled fish), destinations that do not report or do not code by flag, and resident-operated vessels under other flags (Nauru and Tuvalu flagged flows are large and grew). No pack data shows who operates those other-flag vessels.
principles.source: 06 raw_mirror_tuna_by_year_for_reference note; 03 rows; 05 bop_goods_fish (10.17(e)); model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High for other-flag vessels (could be near zero or sizeable); medium-low for the annual-only gap, which is observed.

principles.statement: Treatment rules narrow what counts as a good: goods sent for processing without a change of ownership are excluded, merchanting is recorded as a net item, and fish retained at home is not exported. Any resident catch processed abroad under such terms is not a sale of fish to a non-resident in the year landed.
principles.source: 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1); BPM6 10.41-10.49
principles.uncertainty: High on size, low on direction. No evidence of the scale of such arrangements; kept small with a range spanning zero.

principles.statement: Timing differs by concept: the sale is dated when ownership changes (often at sea) while the importer dates arrival, a median 38 days later (quartiles 23-53). Calendar-year sales therefore sit about 1.5 months ahead of the mirror year; the effect is the difference between the January-to-mid-February imports of the following year and of the same year.
principles.source: 02 ais_chain_facts; 01 monthly series
principles.uncertainty: Medium. Monthly flows are lumpy and early-2026 months may be incomplete; effect kept small.

principles.statement: Official figures are evidence of what the compilers recorded, not of true exports. Goods exports follow customs returns closely (2017: 15.24 and 15.25; 2018: 8.40 and 8.28; 2020: 9.67 and 9.30), and customs see goods crossing Kiribati's border, not fish sold at sea or landed abroad. Recorded tuna is 0.00, 0.59 and 3.44 against a mirror of 82-98. Differences are differences of concept, timing and coverage; the 2025 rise signals more resident activity passing through customs.
principles.source: 06 annual rows and how_to_read; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (IMTS Compilers Manual Box XXIV.2, 24.9)
principles.uncertainty: Medium. The compiler's methods are not documented in the pack; 2025 values are estimates and customs covered 7, 10 and 10 months.

principles.statement: True tuna exports are the FOB value of fish caught by ships operated by Kiribati residents and sold to non-residents, whatever the flag, route or statistical record. A sale at sea to a foreign carrier counts. A sale between two non-residents does not. Fish sent for processing without change of ownership, or kept in the economy, does not count until it is sold abroad; merchanting counts only as a margin.
principles.source: 05 bop_goods_fish and customs_vs_bop_compilation (BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e); IMTS 2010 1.31, F.19; Compilation Guide Table 5.1)
principles.uncertainty: Low on the concept. Operator residence of individual vessels cannot be seen in the pack.

principles.statement: Residence follows the operator's base of operations or place of incorporation, not the flag. A Kiribati-flagged vessel run from abroad or chartered by a non-resident is a non-resident operation. If a Kiribati-incorporated company really operates its own vessel, it is resident whatever the vessel's flag.
principles.source: 05 residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136)
principles.uncertainty: Medium. A locally incorporated company with little local activity could be judged resident or not, which moves the resident share.

principles.statement: The raw mirror follows the catching vessel's flag (all seven importers record origin; fish caught at sea is wholly obtained in the vessel's country) and is normally valued CIF. It therefore follows the Kiribati flag, not operator residence: it includes fish from non-resident operations and omits resident-operated fish under other flags.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports; 01 header
principles.uncertainty: Low for the seven importers. Individual customs offices may code origin differently case by case.

principles.statement: Importers value at CIF and the export concept is FOB. For frozen tuna carried by reefer or container from the central Pacific to Thailand, Japan, Korea, the Philippines, Indonesia or Latin America, freight and insurance are roughly 3-5% of CIF, higher on the long Thai and Latin American hauls and lower where a resident operator carries its own fish.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis (imports CIF, exports FOB); model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: Medium. Rate range 1.5-6% of CIF; carrier contracts are not seen.

principles.statement: Most Kiribati-flagged catch is taken by vessels whose operators are not resident (flag held for access; foreign owners and charterers). Resident-pattern register hours were 7.4k (2023), 8.5k (2024) and 22.2k (2025), only 43 of 116 register vessels have an address hint, and the mirror did not rise in 2025. I take the resident share of Kiribati-flag fish as 14% in 2023 and 2024 and 30% in 2025.
principles.source: 02 kir_flag_fishing_hours, register_counts; 01 annual sums; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High. Hours have no denominator, a hint is not a finding, and a Kiribati address can belong to an agent. Range 6-30% (2023-24) and 12-48% (2025).

principles.statement: If Kiribati-resident operators also run vessels under other flags, importers code that fish to other origins (the pack's chain facts group the Kiribati, Nauru and Tuvalu registers; importers code Nauru at 149-181 and Tuvalu at 49-63 USD m a year). Some resident fish also reaches buyers outside the seven importers, third-country landings or other HS lines. I size other-flag resident fish at a quarter, and unseen routes at a fifth, of resident fish. Annual-only reporters add 3.71, 7.05 and 1.26 to Comtrade totals; only their resident share counts.
principles.source: 02 ais_chain_facts_three_registers; 03 Nauru, Tuvalu rows; 06 raw_mirror note; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High. Ratios are judgement: other-flag fish 4-55% and unseen routes 6-45% of resident fish.

principles.statement: If a resident operator sells fish at sea to a foreign carrier, the export occurs at that sale. For Kiribati-register vessels 67.5% of carrier encounters are followed by a Thai port call, median 42 days later (22-53). The Thai-coded mirror therefore largely records sales at sea that reach the importer about 1.3 months later, so calendar-year allocation differs slightly.
principles.source: 02 ais_chain_facts_kiribati_register; 05 bop_goods_fish; 01 monthly Thai series
principles.uncertainty: Medium. Encounters in file 01 fall to 4, 1 and 1 in 2023-25, so the chain facts are earlier patterns applied to later years.

principles.statement: Official goods exports and customs returns record what passed through Kiribati's customs or the compiler's other sources. Fish caught by resident ships and sold at sea or landed abroad never passes home customs, and the standard remedy is a fisheries-administration source not described for Kiribati. Official tuna can sit below resident exports for that reason. The 2025 rise fits the rise in resident-pattern hours, but the figures size no layer.
principles.source: 06 how_to_read and annual; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation; 02
principles.uncertainty: High. Compiler methods are not documented, only 7, 10 and 10 months were reported, and goods exports include non-fish items.

principles.statement: A tuna export is a change of economic ownership from a Kiribati resident to a non-resident. Fish caught by vessels operated by residents and sold abroad directly, in foreign ports or at sea to carriers, counts, whatever the flag and whether or not any customs record exists.
principles.source: 05 bop_goods_fish (BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e); IMTS 2010 para 1.31, Annex F.19)
principles.uncertainty: Low on the concept. The point at which ownership passes (at sea, in port, on arrival) is not observed, and contract terms are unknown.

principles.statement: Residence follows the operator's base of operations, not the vessel's flag or register. A Kiribati-flagged vessel run or chartered by a non-resident gives a sale between non-residents; a Kiribati-incorporated unit with real operations that runs its own vessel is resident.
principles.source: 05 residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136)
principles.uncertainty: Medium. The line between a genuine local operating unit and a nominal local entity with little local production is a judgement the pack cannot test.

principles.statement: The raw mirror is a flag series. Importers record origin by the catching vessel's nationality (wholly-obtained rule), so it follows registration, not residence. Moves of vessels between the Kiribati, Nauru and Tuvalu registers shift the mirror without changing who operates them.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports; 03
principles.uncertainty: Medium. Seven importers were checked for origin basis; some products (processed fish, loins) may be coded to a processing country, and flag and registration tests may differ in a few cases.

principles.statement: Importers value fish at CIF; Kiribati exports are FOB. Freight and insurance on reefer carriage from the Pacific to Thailand is a mid-to-high single-digit share of the CIF value. Shorter hauls cost less; fresh air-freighted fish costs more. A higher Thai share therefore means a larger valuation layer.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis (imports CIF, exports FOB); 00 README; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: Medium. No invoice or freight data in the pack; carrier rates and trader margins vary by year and route.

principles.statement: Register addresses are a hint of operator residence, not a finding. Only 43 of 116 register vessels have a usable address, and resident-pattern Kiribati-flag hours (7,415 / 8,496 / 22,237) are a floor on resident effort. Most Kiribati-flagged fish in the mirror comes from chartered or foreign-run vessels, so residents are a minority of mirror value, larger in 2025.
principles.source: 02 fleet aggregates; model knowledge of flag-in and charter arrangements
principles.uncertainty: High. The remaining effort is foreign or unclassified in unknown proportions, the pack gives no total hours, and the minority claim is model knowledge, not data.

principles.statement: Resident catch is often sold at sea to carriers. About two thirds of at-sea transfers on the three registers were followed by a Thai port call (median 38 days), so one third went elsewhere. Some resident fish therefore reaches buyers or routes where it is not coded to Kiribati or not in the monthly series, for example partners reporting annually only.
principles.source: 02 ais_chain_facts; 06 annual versus monthly mirror totals; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation
principles.uncertainty: High. Transfer counts are near zero in 2023-2025, so chain facts come from earlier years; the destination of the non-Thai third is unknown.

principles.statement: Official figures record what customs and balance-of-payments compilers could observe. Fish landed or sold abroad does not pass home customs, so their coverage of resident catch is probably thin. They are evidence about coverage and concept, not an estimate of true exports, which can sit above or below them.
principles.source: 06 how_to_read and annual lines; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation
principles.uncertainty: Medium. The compiler's sources and methods are not documented in the pack; the BOP lines cover all goods, not tuna alone.

principles.statement: Treatment and timing matter. Goods processed abroad without change of ownership are not exports, fish owned by a non-resident principal but managed by a resident unit is not a Kiribati sale, and merchanting is recorded separately. Exports belong to the year of sale, while the mirror records arrival about five to six weeks later.
principles.source: 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1); 02 lag facts; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High on size (no contract or consignment data); low on direction.

principles.statement: True exports are the FOB value of fish caught by operators resident in Kiribati and sold to non-residents in the year, whatever the flag or route. Sales at sea to foreign carriers count; sales between two non-residents do not.
principles.source: File 05 bop_goods_fish (BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e); IMTS 2010 1.31, F.19)
principles.uncertainty: Low on the concept; the residence test can only be applied with limited evidence.

principles.statement: The raw mirror records origin by the catching vessel's flag (Kyoto Annex K 2(f); Thai fisheries law keys imports to the flag state), not by operator residence, and imports are valued CIF. It therefore needs a freight and insurance strip and a residence filter.
principles.source: File 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports; model knowledge on carrier freight
principles.uncertainty: Freight and insurance on frozen tuna carried from the central Pacific is about 1 to 7 percent of CIF; assumed 3.5 percent for Thai-bound fish and 5 percent for other buyers.

principles.statement: Flag and registration do not decide residence (BPM6 4.136, 4.134). A Kiribati-flagged vessel run by a charterer based abroad has a non-resident operator; a Kiribati-incorporated operator is resident even if foreign-owned. Register addresses in Kiribati are a hint only, available for 43 of 116 register vessels.
principles.source: File 05 residence_vs_flag; file 02 register counts and resident-pattern hours (7.4k, 8.5k, 22.2k hours in 2023-2025)
principles.uncertainty: High. Resident-operated share of Kiribati-flag value taken as about 22, 21 and 34 percent (80% range 8 to 42; 2025: 13 to 60). Address coverage may grow over time, which could overstate the 2025 rise.

principles.statement: The mirror covers frozen tuna under listed codes from seven reporting buyers. Resident sales at sea to carriers bound elsewhere, third-country landings, non-reporting partners, fresh product, other species, and vessels run by Kiribati residents under other flags fall outside it or are coded to other origins. About two thirds of at-sea transfers by Kiribati-register vessels are followed by a Thai port call within 120 days.
principles.source: File 02 chain facts; file 03 Nauru and Tuvalu series; file 05; model knowledge of Pacific tuna logistics
principles.uncertainty: High. No direct evidence on resident operators' routes or other-flag fleets; additions sized at roughly 15 to 20 percent of the resident core each, range 0 to about 50 percent.

principles.statement: Official figures show what compilers recorded, not the target. Customs does not see fish sold at sea or landed abroad unless a fisheries source is added. Balance-of-payments goods exports tracked customs exports closely in 2017, 2018 and 2020, suggesting a customs-based line. Tuna in customs was 0 to 0.6 in 2023-24 and 3.4 in 2025, far below the mirror.
principles.source: File 06; file 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation
principles.uncertainty: Compiler methods undocumented; customs months incomplete in 2023-25 (7, 10, 10 of 12); non-tuna goods make up much of the goods line.

principles.statement: Goods sent abroad for processing with no change of ownership are not goods exports; merchanting counts only the net margin; fish that stays in the economy is not an export. Resident output affected by these treatments is small and unsized.
principles.source: File 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1); model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High, but small in value; range about -6 to +3 USD m.

principles.statement: Ownership passes when the fish is sold, often at sea, about six weeks (median 42 days) before the port call that triggers the importer's record. Annual mirror values therefore lag the true sale year; the net annual effect is early-next-year flows minus early-this-year flows.
principles.source: File 02 chain lag; file 01 monthly Thai series
principles.uncertainty: Depends on contract terms (sale at sea or on arrival); early-2026 Thai data are thin.

principles.statement: The same method applies to all years. Differences come from data: resident-pattern fleet hours (much higher in 2025), the Thai share of the mirror (87, 70, 71 percent), and official returns (customs tuna and goods exports higher in 2025). Lumpy non-Thai landings in 2024-25 are more likely foreign-run than resident-run.
principles.source: Files 01, 02, 06; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: Moderate to high; hours and official returns move together in 2025 but each is an imperfect proxy.

principles.statement: A tuna sale is a Kiribati goods export only if the operator who caught and sold the fish is resident in Kiribati and ownership passes to a non-resident. Flag and registration do not decide residence; the operator may differ from the owner (charter, lease). Direct sales at sea or in foreign ports count.
principles.source: File 05: bop_goods_fish (BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e); IMTS 1.31, F.19) and residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136)
principles.uncertainty: Low on the rule. High on application: operator residence is not observed for each vessel, and a nominally incorporated operator may have little real base in Kiribati.

principles.statement: Importers record origin by the catching vessel's flag (wholly obtained at sea in the vessel's country). The raw mirror is therefore all flag-coded Kiribati catch sold to reporting partners, whoever runs the vessel, and it leaves out resident operators' catch under other flags.
principles.source: File 05: partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports (Kyoto Annex K 2(f); IMTS 6.6, 6.25); file 03 for other flag series
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. Flag is stable across the seven buyers, but some buyers may code processed or re-exported product to the landing or processing country.

principles.statement: Mirror values are mostly CIF. The balance-of-payments value is taken where ownership passes (alongside the carrier or on landing). Freight and insurance after that point, and any trader margin, come out. I take about 6% for Thai-bound frozen fish and 7% for other partners, with a wide band.
principles.source: File 01 README (values as published, normally CIF); file 05 (imports CIF, exports FOB); file 02 (median 38 days from at-sea encounter to Thai port); model knowledge on reefer freight rates
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. Plausible range 3% to 12% of value depending on carrier terms, trader margins and air freight for fresh fish.

principles.statement: The share of flag-coded fish run by Kiribati-resident operators cannot be observed. Register address hours (resident pattern) are 7,415, 8,496 and 22,237 in 2023-25, but only 43 of 116 register vessels carry any address hint and total fleet hours are not given. I infer a resident share of about 20%, 22% and 37%, damped in 2025 because the mirror did not rise with hours. Most flag-coded catch is assumed chartered or foreign-run.
principles.source: File 02 (hours, register counts, how_to_read); file 03 and file 01 (mirror not rising in 2025); model knowledge on Kiribati-flag chartering
principles.uncertainty: Very high. This is the main driver of the result; the 80% band is roughly 8% to 40% of the mirror in 2023-24 and wider in 2025.

principles.statement: The partner series misses some resident sales: partners reporting annually only add 3.71, 7.05 and 1.26 beyond the monthly sums; some destinations do not report; fresh or chilled fish and landings in third countries fall outside the HS list or the partner set; and 2023 non-Thai flows look thin (13% of the mirror against 24-34% in 2017-22, with only 2-5 reporters in many months). About a third of at-sea encounters are not followed by a Thai port call.
principles.source: File 06 (annual versus monthly totals); file 01 (monthly Thai and non-Thai split, reporter counts); file 02 (AIS chain facts); file 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation
principles.uncertainty: High. The unseen share of resident fish is an assumption (about 15-18%); non-Thai levels vary a lot year to year for real reasons.

principles.statement: Other-flag series are large (Nauru and Tuvalu 198-235 in 2023-25). If Kiribati-resident operators run some vessels under those or other flags, their sales are Kiribati exports that the mirror codes elsewhere. Treatment items (processing without change of ownership, merchanting margins) and arrival-versus-sale timing are small and roughly offsetting.
principles.source: File 03; file 05 (BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1; BPM6 4.136 on flags of convenience); file 02 (38-day lag)
principles.uncertainty: High for the other-flag add-on (no direct evidence; 0 to about 2.5% of those series). Low in size for treatment and timing.

principles.statement: Official goods exports follow customs returns in years when customs are available (2017, 2018, 2020 within 0.4), and customs tuna is 0.00, 0.59 and 3.44 in 2023-25. Fish sold at sea or landed abroad by residents does not pass home customs, so recorded values describe what the compiler could observe and sit below the resident-sale concept by the part not collected.
principles.source: File 06; file 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (Norway example, IMTS Compilers Manual 24.9)
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. The compiler's methods are not documented here; part-year customs coverage in 2023-25 (7, 10, 10 months) limits comparison.

principles.statement: Bridge layers apply in order: valuation first, then removal of non-resident-operated fish from the FOB mirror, then additions for resident fish the mirror does not carry. Additions are scaled to the resident share and to the resident fish base, so they move with P4, not independently of it.
principles.source: Model knowledge; internal consistency of P1 to P6
principles.uncertainty: Low on logic; the dependence means the band on true exports is driven mainly by P4.

principles.statement: A Kiribati goods export is a change of economic ownership from a Kiribati resident to a non-resident. Fish caught by ships operated by residents and sold abroad directly, at sea or in foreign ports, is included. The tests are operator residence and ownership of the catch, not flag, route or customs record.
principles.source: File 05 bop_goods_fish (BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e); IMTS 2010 1.31, F.19)
principles.uncertainty: Operator, owner and charterer are not observed directly; the moment ownership passes at sea is not observed.

principles.statement: Flag and registration do not decide residence (BPM6 4.136). A Kiribati-flag vessel run from abroad has a non-resident operator, and its sales to non-residents are not Kiribati exports; a Kiribati-incorporated unit operating its own vessel is resident (4.134). The register address pattern (resident-pattern fishing hours 7,415 / 8,496 / 22,237 for 2023 / 2024 / 2025) is the only residence hint. I set the resident share of the FOB Kiribati-coded mirror at 14% (6-30%) in 2023 and 13.5% (6-29%) in 2024; 2025 follows hours growth (3.0x against mirror 1.06x, implying 39%) but is pulled back to 32% (15-53%).
principles.source: File 05 residence_vs_flag; file 02 hours and register counts; model knowledge on catch per fishing hour
principles.uncertainty: Only 43 of 116 register vessels have an address hint; an address can belong to an agent; hours of other vessels are not in the pack; catch value per hour differs greatly by gear (about USD 3,500 purse seine, about USD 400 longline). The share is inferred, not measured. Cross-check only: hours at a mixed USD 2,300 per hour give 17 / 19 / 50 USD m.

principles.statement: Importers record origin by the catching vessel's flag (Kyoto Annex K 2(f); Thai import law keys to the flag state; Nauru and Tuvalu reflagging series show buyers do not use an EEZ test). The mirror therefore holds Kiribati-flag fish of any operator and omits fish caught by Kiribati residents on vessels flagged elsewhere. Pool assumption: residents operate 1% (0.2-3%) of fish coded to Nauru or Tuvalu (1.5% in 2025, 0.5-4.5%) and 0.1% (0-0.3%) of fish coded to other Pacific flags.
principles.source: File 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports; file 03; file 02 chain facts across three registers
principles.uncertainty: No vessel-level evidence of resident operators under other flags; the shares are assumptions bounded only by the size of the other-flag pools.

principles.statement: Importers value imports CIF, while true exports are FOB at the point of ownership change. Thai-coded fish (about 70% of the mirror) travels by carrier from the fishing grounds (about two-thirds of tracked at-sea encounters were followed by a Thai port call, median 38-42 days), so freight and insurance are material. I remove 6.0% (3.4-7.8%) of Thai-coded values and 2.5% (1-4.5%) of other partners' values.
principles.source: File 05 partner_basis; file 01 header note (normally CIF); file 02 chain facts; model knowledge on carrier rates
principles.uncertainty: Contract terms (CFR versus ex-vessel) and carrier rates vary. Tracked encounters are almost absent in 2023-25, so chain facts show structure, not recent levels.

principles.statement: Resident catch sold at sea to carriers or landed in third countries never meets home customs, and a partner series sees it only if the destination reports and codes it to Kiribati (BPM6 10.17(e); IMTS 1.31; fisheries-administration remedy in the Norway example). I assume 25% (10-45%) of resident-run catch is outside the mirror, plus the share of annual-only reporters' imports missing from monthly sums (annual returns exceed monthly sums by 3.71 / 7.05 / 1.26 USD m), taken at the resident share.
principles.source: File 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation, bop_goods_fish; file 06 raw-mirror note; file 02
principles.uncertainty: The 25% is inferred. About 32% of tracked encounters were not followed by a Thai call, but not all of that fish is unrecorded by partners.

principles.statement: Goods processed abroad without change of ownership are not exports at the border; the export is the principal's final sale. Merchanting is recorded net, and fish used locally is not exported. The pack shows no such arrangement for Kiribati residents, so the treatment layer is centred on zero with a range that grows with resident activity.
principles.source: File 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1); BPM6 10.13
principles.uncertainty: No evidence either way; a processing or trading arm owned by residents could move the figure in either direction.

principles.statement: Ownership of fish sold at sea passes at the sale, typically 5-8 weeks before the importer's customs date (median lag 38 days). Calendar-year totals therefore shift slightly. I apply the shift to Thai-coded monthly values with 60% weight that the sale precedes arrival, then to the resident share only.
principles.source: File 05 bop_goods_fish (change of ownership); files 01 and 02
principles.uncertainty: Consignment sales (ownership at arrival) would remove the shift; early-2026 Thai data may be incomplete.

principles.statement: Official figures record what a compiler captured under its own concept, sources and coverage; they are not the target. Customs tuna exports (0.00, 0.59, 3.44 USD m over 7, 10, 10 months) and goods exports (8.07, 8.49, 17.34) sit far below the mirror, as expected if customs-based records miss resident catch sold at sea (P5). Annualised customs tuna (0, 0.7, 4.1) is a floor for resident exports, and the 2025 rise supports a larger resident share. They may sit below or above true exports.
principles.source: File 06 how_to_read and annual table; file 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation
principles.uncertainty: Compiler methods are not documented in the pack; customs months are incomplete; BOP 2025 values are estimates.

principles.statement: Fish caught by ships operated by Kiribati residents and sold abroad, at sea to foreign carriers or in foreign ports, is a goods export when economic ownership passes to a non-resident. The flag, the landing port and whether home customs saw the fish do not decide this.
principles.uncertainty: Rule is clear. Whether ownership passes at the at-sea transfer or later (consignment) cannot be seen in the data.

principles.statement: The operator's residence, not the flag or register, decides. A Kiribati-flagged vessel run by a non-resident (charter, foreign-run, foreign partner) makes a sale between non-residents. A Kiribati-incorporated operator running its own vessel is resident.
principles.source: 05 residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136)
principles.uncertainty: The resident share of the Kiribati-flag fleet is not observed. The register address is known for 43 of 116 vessels and may be a local agent or a foreign owner, so it can mislead in either direction.

principles.statement: Importers record partner by origin, and for fish caught at sea origin follows the nationality of the catching vessel. The raw mirror is therefore a count by flag: it includes Kiribati-flag fish of non-resident operators and omits fish of resident operators on vessels of other flags.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports (IMTS 6.25; Kyoto Annex K 2(f))
principles.uncertainty: Origin tests differ by importer. An importer using the landing or processing country would move fish out of the mirror; the pack shows the main buyers use origin by vessel.

principles.statement: Importers value imports CIF, while true exports are valued where ownership changes, on a FOB basis. Freight and insurance are removed. The share is higher for carrier-borne fish bound for Thailand (about 6.5% of CIF, 80% range 4.5-9%) than for other partners with more direct landings (about 3%, 1.5-4.5%).
principles.source: 05 partner_basis metadata (imports CIF, exports FOB); 01 header; model knowledge on reefer freight
principles.uncertainty: Rates come from model knowledge, not the pack. Handling and trader margins between the first sale and the importer's value may sit inside the range.

principles.statement: Much Kiribati-coded fish moves by carrier. 67.5% of register-fleet encounters are followed by a Thai port call within 120 days, median lag 42 days. Such fish changes ownership at sea or abroad, does not pass home customs, and is recorded by the importer about six weeks later.
principles.source: 02 ais_chain_facts_kiribati_register; 05 bop_goods_fish, customs_vs_bop_compilation
principles.uncertainty: Encounter counts in 2023-2025 are very low in file 01, so the chain statistics rest mainly on earlier years and AIS coverage may be partial.

principles.statement: Resident-operated output is a minority of the Kiribati-coded mirror. Resident-address fishing hours rose 15% in 2024 and 2.6 times in 2025 while the mirror fell 11% in 2025, so the 2025 resident share is higher and part of the extra activity is probably sold by routes the mirror misses. Nauru and Tuvalu series show vessels move between registers, so a small resident share may sit under other flags.
principles.source: 02 hours by address pattern; 03 flag-state series; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: No fleet total of hours is given and the address is a hint, not a finding. Resident share of the FOB mirror set at about 29-30% in 2023-24 and 40% in 2025, with wide ranges.

principles.statement: Official figures show what the compiler recorded with the sources used. Goods crossing customs are captured; resident sales at sea or abroad need fisheries or vessel records. Differences between official figures and true exports are differences of concept, timing and coverage, and can run in either direction.
principles.source: 06 how_to_read and annual table; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (IMTS Compilers Manual 24.9, fish-landed-abroad example)
principles.uncertainty: The compiler's methods are not documented in the pack. The 2025 step-up (goods exports 17.34, customs tuna 3.44) may reflect more resident activity or wider sources.

principles.statement: Mirror coverage and treatment. The monthly sum leaves out partners that report only annually (annual totals are higher by 3.71, 7.05 and 1.26) and fish outside the listed HS codes, such as fresh or chilled tuna. Goods processed without change of ownership, merchanting and fish kept at home are not ordinary exports, and re-exports from third countries are not Kiribati's.
principles.source: 06 raw_mirror_tuna_by_year note; 05 BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1; BPM6 10.41-10.49
principles.uncertainty: Sizes of the unlisted routes and treatment cases are not observed. They are set small with wide ranges.

principles.statement: A fish sale is a Kiribati goods export only if the seller is a Kiribati-resident operator, the buyer is a non-resident and economic ownership changes hands, wherever the sale happens (at sea, in a foreign port, or at home). The vessel's flag or registration does not decide the operator's residence; a locally incorporated company operating its own vessels is resident, a foreign-run operator on a Kiribati flag is not.
principles.source: 05 bop_goods_fish and residence_vs_flag (BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e), 4.131, 4.134, 4.136; IMTS 2010 1.31, F.19)
principles.uncertainty: Concept is clear. Whether a Tarawa-registered company has enough local operations to be resident (4.131 against 4.134) cannot be tested with the pack; low-to-moderate.

principles.statement: The raw mirror measures the flag of the catching vessel, not the residence of its operator. Fish is wholly obtained in the vessel's country, all seven importers record origin, and Thai fish-import law keys on the flag state. So the mirror holds all Kiribati-flag catch that reaches a reporting importer, whoever runs the vessel, and none of the catch of Kiribati-resident operators fishing under other flags.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports; 03
principles.uncertainty: Low on concept; how importers code chartered or recently reflagged vessels cannot be checked.

principles.statement: Importers value imports CIF, while a goods export is valued FOB at the point where ownership changes. Freight and insurance must come out. For frozen fish moved by carrier to Thailand I take about 5% of CIF; for fish going to Japan, Korea, the Philippines, Indonesia, Colombia and Ecuador (more chilled, longer or air legs) about 8%. The Thai share of the mirror (87%, 70%, 71%) sets the blend.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis (imports CIF); 01; model knowledge of reefer and air freight rates
principles.uncertainty: Moderate; each rate could be 2-3 points either way.

principles.statement: Kiribati-resident operators are a minority of the Kiribati-flag mirror. Register-address hours for resident-pattern vessels were 7.4k, 8.5k and 22.2k in 2023-25 against 3k-10k in 2015-22, while the Kiribati-coded mirror stayed in an 85-140 band; only 43 of 116 register vessels carry any address hint. I therefore take the resident-operated share of the Kiribati-flag mirror as about 11% in 2023, 12% in 2024 and 24% in 2025 (hours tripled, damped because the mirror did not rise), each with a wide range.
principles.source: 02 (hours, register counts); 03; model knowledge that much of the Kiribati-flag fleet is chartered or foreign-run
principles.uncertainty: High: hours are not catch, the total flag-fleet hours are not given, and a Kiribati address is a hint of residence, not a finding.

principles.statement: Resident catch missing from the partner series comes from four places: vessels run by Kiribati residents under other flags (no address data; I assume 1% of Nauru and Tuvalu coded imports and 0.1% of other Pacific flags); sales at sea or landings with no reporting importer (about a third of register-vessel sales at sea are not followed by a Thai call); fish outside the HS lines used; and importers that report annually only. Together I add about 28-30% to recorded resident catch.
principles.source: 02 ais_chain_facts; 03; 06 (annual vs monthly totals); model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High: no operator data for other flags and no destination data for the unmatched third.

principles.statement: Official figures record what Kiribati's compilers could see, not true resident exports. Customs tuna exports were 0.0, 0.59 and 3.44 (partial years) and the goods line was 8.1, 8.5 and 17.3, including non-fish goods. In 2017, 2018 and 2020 the goods line sat within about 4% of customs totals, so it appears customs-based, and fish sold at sea or landed abroad never meets home customs. They give a floor for fish that crosses customs and a direction (2025 up), not a level.
principles.source: 06; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (Norway example, Table 5.1)
principles.uncertainty: Moderate: the compiler's methods are not documented in the pack.

principles.statement: Treatment items change what counts as a good: fish kept in the economy, goods sent for processing without change of ownership, merchanting margins, and the same frozen fish recorded by two importers as a re-export. None can be sized from the pack, so I treat them as small, two-sided and proportional to resident exports (centre about minus 3%).
principles.source: 05 bop_goods_fish, customs_vs_bop_compilation (BPM6 10.13, Table 5.1); model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High on sign and size; the range allows a small positive.

principles.statement: The mirror counts the arrival month, while ownership changes at the sale at sea, a median 42 days (six weeks) earlier for about 70% of the flow. Moving the monthly series back about 1.4 months gives calendar-year sales; this lowers each year by 1.8%, 2.3% and 4.1% of the series (weak early-2026 months), applied only to the at-sea share of resident exports.
principles.source: 01 monthly series; 02 chain lag (median 42, quartiles 22-53 days)
principles.uncertainty: Low to moderate: lag spread and incomplete early-2026 months.

principles.statement: True exports are the FOB value of fish caught by vessels operated by Kiribati residents and sold to non-residents in the year, whatever the flag, route or recording. Fish caught by resident operators and sold abroad directly, at sea or in foreign ports, is a goods export; IMTS 2010 agrees on scope.
principles.uncertainty: Low on the concept; high on how much of the fleet is resident-operated.

principles.statement: Operator residence follows BPM6 4.131-4.136 (incorporation or registration plus significant production from the territory), not flag, registration or charter paperwork. A Kiribati-flagged vessel run from abroad has a non-resident operator, so its sale is between non-residents. A Kiribati-incorporated unit operating its own vessel with substantial local operations is resident.
principles.source: 05 residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136)
principles.uncertainty: High: operator facts are not in the pack and the register address in file 02 is only a hint.

principles.statement: Importers code origin by the catching vessel's flag state and value imports CIF. The raw mirror therefore (i) includes freight and insurance, (ii) counts fish by flag whatever the operator's residence, and (iii) omits resident-operated fish carrying another flag or coded to the landing or processing country.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports; 03 (Nauru and Tuvalu series show reflagged catch follows the new flag)
principles.uncertainty: Flag basis is firm for the main buyers. Freight and insurance of 3-8% of CIF is model knowledge, lower for short hauls.

principles.statement: About 68% of at-sea transshipment encounters on the Kiribati register are followed by a Thai port call within 120 days (median 38 days), matching the 70-87% Thai share of the mirror. Most mirror fish is sold or consigned at sea to carriers and discharged in Thailand. For a resident operator that is an export at the point of sale; the CIF value at discharge includes the carrier leg.
principles.source: 02 ais_chain_facts; 01 Thai and non-Thai series; 05 bop_goods_fish
principles.uncertainty: Moderate: the point where ownership passes is not observed. The lag shifts a small part of each year's sales into the next year's import records.

principles.statement: No file states the operator's residence for Kiribati-flagged catch. The only hint is register-address fishing hours (7,415, 8,496 and 22,237 in 2023-25). They moved far less than the mirror over 2017-2024 (2021: 3,066 hours against a mirror of about 86), so most mirror fish comes from operators outside that group. Model knowledge: most flagged effort is run under charter or foreign ownership and the Kiribati-owned fleet is small. The resident-operated part is a minority, with a wide range.
principles.source: 02 kir_flag_fishing_hours; 01; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High: an address can be an agent's address, and hours are not mapped to value or gear.

principles.statement: Published goods exports (8.07, 8.49, 17.34) and customs tuna (0.00, 0.59, 3.44 in 7-10 reported months) come from customs returns and other sources. Customs cannot see fish sold at sea or landed abroad, so these series show the channel the compiler can observe, and a larger domestic channel in 2025. They are not a measure of resident catch sold abroad. Differences from true exports are differences of concept and coverage, in either direction.
principles.source: 06 annual and how_to_read; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (IMTS Compilers Manual Box XXIV.2, 24.9)
principles.uncertainty: Compiler methods are not documented and customs months are partial.

principles.statement: Resident operators sell through routes the monthly seven-reporter series misses: partners that report annually only (annual totals exceed monthly sums by 3.71, 7.05 and 1.26), buyers outside the seven reporters, third-country landings, and fresh or chilled tuna outside the HS lines. Resident catch under another flag is coded to that flag, not to Kiribati.
principles.source: 06 raw_mirror note; 03; 05 origin_of_fish; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High on size. The share of resident catch outside the seven reporters (5-35% of the resident part) is model-based.

principles.statement: Goods sent for processing without change of ownership and merchanted goods are not general merchandise, and fish kept in the economy is not an export. For resident catch these items are expected to be small and two-signed: processing arrangements remove, merchanting margins add. Sales are dated at change of ownership, imports by arrival month.
principles.source: 05 bop_goods_fish (BPM6 10.13), customs_vs_bop_compilation (Compilation Guide Table 5.1)
principles.uncertainty: No data in the pack; sized as near zero with a wide, slightly negative-leaning range.

principles.statement: A Kiribati goods export of fish needs a change of economic ownership from a Kiribati resident to a non-resident. Fish caught by ships operated by residents and sold abroad directly, in foreign ports or at sea to foreign vessels, counts. The test is the operator's residence and who owns the catch, not the flag or the route.
principles.uncertainty: Concept is firm. The exact point of sale (at sea, in port, after processing) depends on contracts that are not observed.

principles.statement: Residence of the operator is decided by where it is incorporated or does significant production, not by flag or registration. If a Kiribati-flagged vessel is operated by a non-resident (charter, operating lease, foreign joint-venture partner), its catch sold to non-residents is not a Kiribati export. A Kiribati-based operator is resident whatever the flag.
principles.source: 05 residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136)
principles.uncertainty: Boundary cases (local shell units, agent addresses, joint ventures with mixed control) cannot be sorted from the pack.

principles.statement: Importers record partner as origin, and fish caught at sea is wholly obtained in the vessel's country, in practice the flag. The raw mirror is therefore a flag series: it holds all fish of Kiribati-flagged vessels whoever operates them, and it omits resident-operated fish under other flags. The Nauru and Tuvalu series show origin following the flag.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports; 03
principles.uncertainty: The nationality test is left to each importer; some may code to landing or processing country in part.

principles.statement: Importer values are CIF, while a BPM6 export is valued where ownership changes, at the catching vessel. Fish moves by refrigerated carrier, with a median 38-42 days from sale at sea to a Thai port call and about 68% of carrier encounters ending in Thailand. Freight and insurance are therefore about 6-7% of the mirror (range 4-9%).
principles.source: 05 partner_basis (imports CIF); 02 AIS chain facts; model knowledge on reefer rates
principles.uncertainty: Rate per tonne and the mix of destinations vary by year; plus or minus 2 points on the percentage.

principles.statement: Most Kiribati-flagged output is foreign-operated (chartered or foreign-run vessels). Register addresses in Kiribati cover few fishing hours (7,415 in 2023, 8,496 in 2024, 22,237 in 2025) against 85 identified Kiribati-flag vessels, most with no usable address hint. Scaling by hours puts the resident-operated share of the mirror at about 7% in 2023-24 and about 16% in 2025.
principles.source: 02 fleet aggregates; model knowledge on Pacific fleet structure
principles.uncertainty: Large (about a factor of two). The address is a hint, may be an agent address, and hours are not catch value. The 2025 rise may partly reflect register changes.

principles.statement: Resident-operated fish exists outside the mirror: vessels of Kiribati-resident operators flagged elsewhere (Nauru and Tuvalu flagged imports are 2.2-2.7 times the Kiribati series), fresh or chilled fish outside the listed HS codes, sales to destinations that do not report, and partners that report annually only (Comtrade annual totals exceed the monthly sum by 3.7, 7.1 and 1.3 USD m).
principles.source: 03; 06 raw_mirror note; 01; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High. Each channel is sized by assumption, from the resident share and from other-flag series, not observed.

principles.statement: Official figures are evidence of what was recorded, not of what happened. Customs tuna exports (0.00, 0.59, 3.44 USD m over 7-10 months) form a loose floor for recorded resident sales; total BOP goods exports (8.07, 8.49, 17.34) include copra and other goods. The 2025 step-up matches the rise in resident-operator hours, and coverage of sales at sea looks thin in 2023-24.
principles.source: 06; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation
principles.uncertainty: The mix inside BOP goods and the compiler's sources are not documented in the pack.

principles.statement: Treatment effects are small. Ownership changes at the date of sale, which is about six weeks before the partner record, so calendar years shift slightly. Goods for processing without change of ownership are excluded in BPM6, merchanting is netted, and fish eaten at home is not an export. Kiribati has no large cannery, so none of these is large.
principles.source: 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (Table 5.1); 02 lag; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: Low to moderate. Processing contracts with foreign canneries could change what counts as a good, but are not evidenced.

principles.statement: True exports are the FOB value of fish whose economic ownership passes from a Kiribati resident to a non-resident in the year. Fish caught by ships operated by residents and sold abroad directly, including at sea or in foreign ports, is included. The test is the operator's residence and who owns the catch, not the flag, the route or whether any statistic recorded it.
principles.source: BPM6 10.13 and 10.17(e); IMTS 2010 1.31 and F.19 (file 05, bop_goods_fish)
principles.uncertainty: Low on the concept; high on applying it, because operator residence and catch ownership are not observed in the pack.

principles.statement: An operator's residence follows where the operating entity is incorporated or does significant production, not the flag, the registration or the ship owner. A Kiribati-flagged vessel run from abroad has a non-resident operator, so its sale is between non-residents and not a Kiribati export. A Kiribati-incorporated operator is resident whatever the flag. The flag-coded mirror therefore mixes resident and non-resident fish.
principles.source: BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136 (file 05, residence_vs_flag); register hints in file 02
principles.uncertainty: High on the resident share: only 43 of 116 register vessels carry an address hint, and resident-address hours (7,415; 8,496; 22,237 in 2023-25) come without a total to divide by.

principles.statement: Importers code origin as the country of the catching vessel (wholly obtained, flag or registration test), so the mirror follows the flag, not the operator. Fish caught by Kiribati-resident operators on vessels of other flags is coded to those flags. Nauru-coded imports rose from 0 in 2018 to 109 in 2020 and Tuvalu-coded imports rose in 2022 while Kiribati-coded imports eased from 140 in 2017, which fits vessels moving between registers.
principles.source: Kyoto Annex K 2(f), IMTS 2010 6.6, Thai fisheries ordinance ss.95-96 (file 05); file 03
principles.uncertainty: Very high: no operator-residence data exist for non-Kiribati flags, so the resident share of those series is an assumption from model knowledge.

principles.statement: Importers record imports CIF while export value is FOB. Freight, insurance and brokerage between the point of sale and the importing port are a margin of roughly 6-10% for frozen tuna, higher on the long haul to Thailand, which supplies 70-87% of the mirror.
principles.source: Comtrade metadata (file 05, partner_basis); Thai shares from file 06; freight margin from model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: Moderate: the margin is not observed and moves with the freight market and product form.

principles.statement: The partner series misses some routes. Some importers report annually only: Comtrade annual totals exceed the monthly sums by 3.71, 7.05 and 1.26 in 2023-25, and monthly reporters numbered 2-5 for much of 2023 against 6-11 in 2024-25. Resident sales at sea to carriers, landings in third countries and fish outside these HS codes are also goods exports. Fish sold at sea never passes home customs. Detected carrier encounters of register vessels are near zero in 2023-25, so recent at-sea sales cannot be confirmed.
principles.source: Files 01, 02, 06; BPM6 10.17(e); IMTS Compilers Manual (file 05, customs_vs_bop_compilation)
principles.uncertainty: Moderate for the annual-only gap (observed); high for the other routes (inferred).

principles.statement: Only a change of economic ownership makes a good an export. Where a resident operator fishes or processes fish owned by a non-resident (contract fishing, toll processing, no change of ownership), the fee is the export and the fish is not. Merchanting is recorded at net margin. Part of resident-operated catch may therefore not count as goods in full.
principles.source: BPM6 10.13 and 10.41-10.49; BPM6 Compilation Guide table 5.1 (file 05)
principles.uncertainty: High: contracts and ownership of the catch are not observed.

principles.statement: Published goods exports (all goods) and customs tuna show what the compiler's sources recorded. BOP stayed within 0.4 of customs in 2017, 2018 and 2020 when 12 months were reported, so BOP leans on customs where it exists. Fish sold at sea or landed abroad does not pass home customs unless a fisheries source feeds the compiler, which the pack does not document. Official figures are therefore a partial record of resident sales, useful for direction and coverage (the 2025 step-up fits the rise in resident-address hours), not a bound on or a target for true exports.
principles.source: File 06 (how_to_read and annual rows); file 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation
principles.uncertainty: High: the compiler's methods and sources are not documented.

principles.statement: Exports are recorded when ownership changes (at sea or at landing) while imports are recorded on arrival. The median lag from carrier encounter to Thai port call is 38 days (quartiles 23 and 53). A calendar-year mirror therefore covers sales from about mid-November of the previous year, so the year-end shift is a small timing difference.
principles.source: File 02 (AIS chain facts); file 01 monthly series; BPM6 10.17(e)
principles.uncertainty: Moderate: the lag comes from earlier years and the Thai chain only; if ownership passes on arrival the effect is zero.

principles.statement: A Kiribati goods export needs a change of economic ownership from a Kiribati resident to a non-resident. Fish caught by ships operated by residents and sold abroad directly, in foreign ports or at sea, counts. Fish processed abroad without change of ownership is excluded, and merchanting is shown net.
principles.source: BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e); IMTS 2010 1.31 and F.19; BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1 (file 05: bop_goods_fish, customs_vs_bop_compilation)
principles.uncertainty: The concept is clear. When ownership of the catch passes inside joint ventures or charters is rarely visible, so applying it vessel by vessel is hard.

principles.statement: Residence follows the operator's own base of operations or legal incorporation, not the vessel's flag or registry. A Kiribati-flagged ship run or chartered from abroad has a non-resident operator, so its catch is not a Kiribati export. A resident operator with substantial operations in Kiribati is resident even if its ships fly another flag.
principles.source: BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136 (file 05: residence_vs_flag)
principles.uncertainty: A thin local company set up by a foreign parent may or may not pass the test. The register address in file 02 is only a hint of residence.

principles.statement: Importers record the origin of fish caught at sea as the catching vessel's nation, and the main buyers have done so every year 2014-2025. The raw mirror is therefore a flag series: it includes Kiribati-flag fish run from abroad and omits resident-run fish under other flags.
principles.source: Kyoto Annex K 2(f); IMTS 2010 6.6-6.26; Comtrade metadata; Thai fisheries ordinance (file 05: partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports)
principles.uncertainty: How each importer treats chartered or recently reflagged ships is not shown. The nationality test is left to each country.

principles.statement: Importers value imports CIF, while exports are valued FOB where ownership changes. Freight and insurance on frozen tuna carried by refrigerated ship from the central Pacific to Asia are about 3% to 8% of CIF value, near 5.5% for Thailand and nearer 4.5% for shorter hops.
principles.source: Comtrade metadata, imports CIF (file 05: partner_basis); model knowledge of reefer freight rates
principles.uncertainty: No freight data in the pack. Some invoices may already be on a cost-and-freight basis, and unit prices vary by year.

principles.statement: Resident sales happen where ownership passes, often at sea to a carrier, and importers record the fish on arrival, a median 38-42 days later. About 68% of at-sea carrier meetings by Kiribati-register ships are followed by a Thai port call within 120 days. Home customs cannot see these sales. Annual-only reporters, other destinations and fresh fish outside the tuna codes fall outside the monthly series.
principles.source: File 02 (AIS chain facts); file 01 (monthly series); file 06 (annual totals differ from monthly sums); file 05: customs_vs_bop_compilation
principles.uncertainty: The other third of carrier meetings may end in reporting partners already in the mirror. AIS coverage and the 120-day window are imperfect.

principles.statement: Hours fished by Kiribati-flag ships with a Kiribati owner or operator address are a hint, not a finding. The mirror per such hour fell from about 28,000 USD (2021) to about 4,000 (2025), so most mirror value comes from ships outside this pattern. I take about 28-30% of 2023-24 mirror value as resident-run, more in 2025 when such hours tripled.
principles.source: File 02 (hours by address pattern); file 03 (annual Kiribati-coded imports); file 01
principles.uncertainty: Very high. An address is not residence, gear mix and catch per hour are unknown, and hours for non-resident ships are not in the pack.

principles.statement: Operators change flags. Imports coded to Nauru rose from nil in 2018 to 181 million USD in 2023 and Tuvalu from 8 (2017) to 54 while Kiribati-coded imports fell from 140 (2017) to 86-110. Some Kiribati-resident operators may therefore have fish coded to other flags, and some Kiribati-flag fish is run from elsewhere.
principles.source: File 03; file 05: origin_of_fish note on reflagging
principles.uncertainty: No operator data. The share of Nauru- and Tuvalu-coded fish run by Kiribati residents is an assumption, about 2% with a wide range.

principles.statement: Official figures record what compilers can see through customs and other sources. Customs tuna exports (0.0, 0.6, 3.4 USD m; 7, 10, 10 months) and balance-of-payments goods exports (8.1, 8.5, 17.3) are far below the mirror. This fits resident sales at sea or abroad that never pass customs (P5). They are a visible floor, and the 2025 step-up fits more resident activity.
principles.source: File 06; BPM6 10.17(e); IMTS Compilers Manual 24.9 and Box XXIV.2 (file 05)
principles.uncertainty: Compiler methods and sources are not documented in the pack. Differences between records are differences of concept, timing and coverage.

principles.statement: A Kiribati goods export needs the catch to be owned and sold to a non-resident by an operator resident in Kiribati. The vessel's flag or registration does not decide residence: a locally incorporated operator is resident, while a foreign-run operator of a Kiribati-flagged vessel is not. Sales at sea or in foreign ports count.
principles.uncertainty: Medium. Whether a locally registered company with little activity on shore counts as resident in practice is a judgement, and the register address is only a hint.

principles.statement: Importers record origin as the catching vessel's flag, because fish taken at sea is 'wholly obtained' in the flag country. The raw mirror therefore holds all Kiribati-flag catch, whether or not the operator is resident, and leaves out resident-run catch under other flags.
principles.source: File 05 (IMTS 2010 6.6 and 6.25; Kyoto Annex K 2(f); Thai fisheries law sections 95-96)
principles.uncertainty: Low for the rule. How each importer treats landings or processing in a third country is not shown.

principles.statement: Importers value imports CIF, while Kiribati exports are measured FOB at the point ownership passes, so carrier freight and insurance come out. Fish moved by reefer carrier to Thailand carries more freight (taken as 6% of delivered value) than fish landed directly by the catching vessel (taken as 3.5%).
principles.source: File 05 (imports CIF, exports FOB); model knowledge of reefer freight rates
principles.uncertainty: Medium-low. Rates vary by voyage; 80% ranges are 3-9% for Thai-recorded value and 1-6% for other partners.

principles.statement: Only a minority of Kiribati-flag fishing is run by operators with a Kiribati address. Resident-pattern hours were 7,415 (2023), 8,496 (2024) and 22,237 (2025); 43 of 116 register vessels have a usable address. Total flag hours are not given, so the resident share of Kiribati-flag fish is assumed 14% in 2023-24 and 30% in 2025 (22,237 over 8,496/0.14 plus 13,741 added hours).
principles.source: File 02; model knowledge that many Kiribati-flag vessels are chartered or foreign-run
principles.uncertainty: High. Hours are not catch value, addresses are hints that may be applied across a vessel's whole tenure, and the denominator is assumed. 80% ranges: 5-32% (2023-24) and 13-50% (2025).

principles.statement: Resident-run catch can be missing from the mirror: fish under other flags (the Nauru and Tuvalu series show large flag shifts), buyers outside the seven reporting importers, fresh or chilled tuna outside the HS codes, and partners that report annually only (annual totals exceed the monthly sums by 3.71, 7.05 and 1.26 in 2023-25).
principles.source: Files 03 and 06; model knowledge of Pacific tuna trade
principles.uncertainty: High. None of these can be seen directly; each is sized as a share of the resident-run fish.

principles.statement: Importers record fish on arrival, one to two months after the sale at sea (AIS: about two thirds of at-sea encounters are followed by a Thai port call, median 38 days). The calendar-year mirror therefore differs slightly from sales made in the year. Encounters of register vessels are near zero in 2023-25, so a missing encounter is treated as non-detection, not as no transshipment.
principles.source: Files 01 and 02
principles.uncertainty: Medium for the lag; the effect on the annual level is small.

principles.statement: Official figures show what the compiler recorded. Goods exports cover all goods, and customs tuna returns cover only 7, 10 and 10 months. Fish sold at sea by residents does not cross Kiribati customs, although BPM6 wants it in goods exports, so an official figure can sit below true exports. The 2025 rise in recorded tuna matches the rise in resident-pattern hours. Customs tuna is used as a floor check only.
principles.source: File 06; File 05 (IMTS Compilers Manual Box XXIV.2, para 24.9; BPM6 10.17(e))
principles.uncertainty: Medium. The make-up of the goods total (copra, seaweed, fish estimates) and the compiler's methods are not documented in the pack.

principles.statement: Kiribati has no tuna processing of scale, so toll processing and merchanting by residents are taken as negligible. Fish landed for local use is not an export and is not in the mirror.
principles.source: BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1 (File 05); model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: Medium. Joint-venture contract terms and any processing arrangements abroad are unknown.

principles.statement: A Kiribati goods export needs a change of economic ownership from a Kiribati resident to a non-resident. The operator's residence decides, not the vessel's flag. Fish caught by resident-operated ships and sold abroad directly, including at sea, counts; a sale between two non-residents does not.
principles.source: 05 bop_goods_fish (BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e)); 05 residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.131-4.136); IMTS 2010 para 1.31
principles.uncertainty: Residence of each operator is not observed. A register address is only a hint, and a locally incorporated owner directed from abroad sits between the 4.131 and 4.134 tests.

principles.statement: Importers code origin by the catching vessel's flag (fish is wholly obtained in the vessel's country) in every year. The raw mirror therefore holds all Kiribati-flagged catch whoever operates it, and holds none of the catch of resident operators whose vessels fly another flag.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports
principles.uncertainty: Each importer's own origin rule is not published in detail; Colombia and Ecuador may apply different tests; reflagging dates can blur years.

principles.statement: Importers value imports CIF, while an export is valued at the point of sale. Freight and insurance from the Western Pacific to Thailand is a mid-single-digit share of fish value; shorter hauls to other buyers cost less.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis metadata (imports CIF, exports FOB); 01 header; model knowledge on reefer freight
principles.uncertainty: Contract terms (cost-and-freight versus free-on-board; ownership passing at sea or at discharge) and freight rates are not in the pack. About 6% for Thai-bound and 3% for other fish is a judgement.

principles.statement: Most Kiribati-flagged catch is probably run by operators not resident in Kiribati, so the resident-operated share of the mirror is a minority: about one fifth in 2023-24 and higher in 2025. Register-address hours are small (7.4k, 8.5k) and do not track the mirror over 2015-2024, then rise to 22.2k in 2025 while the mirror falls.
principles.source: 02 address-pattern hours and register counts; 03 Kiribati row; model knowledge of the flag fleet
principles.uncertainty: Very high. There is no total-hours denominator, hours are not catch, gear mix is unknown, and the 2025 jump may partly reflect register updates.

principles.statement: Fish sold at sea to carriers reaches the importer weeks later (median 38 days), and about two thirds of chains end in a Thai port. The dominant route is inside the mirror and year-end timing shifts a little. For resident operators the mirror misses late or annual-only partner records, non-reporting destinations and fish outside the HS codes.
principles.source: 02 ais_chain_facts; 01 reporter counts and Thai/non-Thai split; 06 annual Comtrade totals versus monthly sums
principles.uncertainty: Chain facts come from encounter samples, not values. 2023 had few monthly reporters. Sizes of unreported routes are inferred.

principles.statement: Under BPM6 a charterer's residence follows its own base of operations, not the flag. Resident operators may therefore run vessels flagged elsewhere, whose catch importers code to other flags. The pack has no register evidence on this, so the layer is small with a wide range.
principles.source: 05 residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.136); 03 other flag rows (Nauru and Tuvalu large); model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: No address data for other registers. The true size could be near zero or several USD m.

principles.statement: Official goods exports follow customs returns (BOP close to customs in 2017, 2018 and 2020) and customs-recorded tuna is small (0.0, 0.6 and 3.4 for 7 to 10 months), so the compiler mainly sees fish that clears Kiribati customs. Resident sales at sea or landings abroad sit outside that net unless a fisheries source is used. Official figures are a coverage check, not the target; they could sit above true exports if customs tuna belongs to non-residents.
principles.source: 06 annual and how_to_read; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (Norway example; IMTS Compilers Manual 24.9)
principles.uncertainty: Compiler methods are undocumented; BOP may include estimates (2023 BOP exceeds the customs sum); the owner of customs-recorded tuna is unknown.

principles.statement: A good counts only when ownership changes. Fish sent for toll processing or moved within one group without a change of ownership, fish kept in the economy, and merchanting sit outside general merchandise exports. They touch only a small slice of resident sales.
principles.source: 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1); BPM6 10.13, 10.17(f); model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: No evidence on contract structures. The sign could be positive (merchanting by resident traders) or negative.

principles.statement: Importers record origin by the catching vessel's nationality (flag), while a Kiribati goods export needs the operator to be resident in Kiribati and ownership to pass to a non-resident. Flag and residence are different tests, so the raw mirror measures flag-coded catch, not resident exports.
principles.source: 05 origin_of_fish (Kyoto Annex K 2(f)); 05 residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.136, 4.134); 05 partner_basis
principles.uncertainty: Concepts are firm; what share of Kiribati-flag catch has a resident operator is the main unknown.

principles.statement: Importers value imports CIF and exports are FOB, so freight and insurance must be removed. For reefer carriers from the western Pacific to Thailand this is roughly 4-9% of value, and less (about 2-8%) for nearer or air-freighted destinations.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis (imports CIF); model knowledge on reefer freight
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. Rates are not in the pack; range 4-9% (Thai) and 2.5-8% (other).

principles.statement: The resident-operated share of the Kiribati-flag mirror is sized from register address hints and fishing hours. Resident-pattern hours were 7,415, 8,496 and 22,237 in 2023-2025 and only 43 of 116 register vessels carry an address hint, with total fleet hours not given. This points to a low share in 2023-24 (about 11-12%) and a higher one in 2025 (about 26%).
principles.source: 02 fleet aggregates; 05 residence_vs_flag (4.134, 4.136); model knowledge on chartered fleets
principles.uncertainty: Very high. The address is a hint about the operator, not a finding, and totals are missing. This is the dominant uncertainty: 80% range about 4-33% (2023-24), 10-52% (2025).

principles.statement: Fish caught by Kiribati-resident operators on vessels flagged elsewhere (chartered-in or joint-venture vessels) is coded by importers to the other flag and is absent from the mirror. The flag-state series show catch moving across registers, so such fish can exist.
principles.source: 05 residence_vs_flag; 05 origin_of_fish; 03 flag-state series; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: Very high. No data size it; it is set as a fraction of the resident-coded amount with a range that starts at zero.
