principles.statement: Fish sold by resident operators at sea to carriers, or landed abroad, is a goods export when sold, yet may be missing from the partner series: the seven reporters omit other destinations, some partners report only annually (annual totals 85.48, 104.62 and 88.19 against monthly sums 81.77, 97.57 and 86.93), and fresh or chilled tuna codes may be outside scope.
principles.source: 05 bop_goods_fish (BPM6 10.17(e), IMTS 1.31); 06 raw_mirror note; 01 reporter counts; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High. The annual-only gap is observed; the other-destination and scope shares are inferred.

principles.statement: Goods sent for processing without change of ownership, merchanting, and fish kept in the economy do not count as goods exports in the usual way. For a small resident fleet these treatment effects are small and mostly negative.
principles.source: 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (Compilation Guide Table 5.1); model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: Moderate to high. Size is a judgement of about 5% of the resident total.

principles.statement: Official goods figures show what the compilers captured from customs returns and other sources. Fish landed or sold abroad by resident operators does not cross home customs by construction, so the official series can sit below true exports. Customs tuna (0.00, 0.59, 3.44) and 2025 hours move together, which fits more resident activity in 2025.
principles.source: 06 official statistics; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (Norway example); 02
principles.uncertainty: Compiler methods are not documented; customs months reported were 7, 10 and 10 of 12, so levels are partial.

principles.statement: Partners record fish at the date of import, while a sale at sea happens earlier. The median lag from carrier encounter to a Thai port call is 38-42 days, so sale-year exports differ from import-year records when resident activity is changing quickly, as in 2025.
principles.source: 02 ais_chain_facts; 01 monthly series
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. The lag is observed; the share of resident fish sold at sea and the monthly profile are inferred.

principles.statement: True exports are the FOB value of fish caught by vessels operated by Kiribati residents and sold to non-residents in the year, whatever the flag, route or recording office. The tests are the operator's residence and a change of economic ownership, not the vessel's flag or the customs border.
principles.source: 05 bop_goods_fish (BPM6 10.13 and 10.17(e); IMTS 2010 para 1.31 and Annex F.19)
principles.uncertainty: Low on the concept. The point where ownership passes (at sea to a carrier, or on arrival) is not documented and may differ by buyer.

principles.statement: An operator's residence follows its incorporation and base of operations, not the flag. A Kiribati-flagged vessel run, chartered or leased by a foreign operator is nonresident-operated, and a sale between two non-residents is not a Kiribati export. A Kiribati-incorporated operator with real operations is resident.
principles.source: 05 residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136)
principles.uncertainty: High in practice: register addresses are hints only, an agent's local address does not make an operator resident, and joint ventures run from abroad are a judgement call.

principles.statement: Importers record the partner as origin, and for fish caught at sea that means the flag of the catching vessel, valued CIF. The raw mirror therefore holds every Kiribati-flagged catch whatever the operator's residence (to remove), omits resident-operated catch under other flags such as Nauru or Tuvalu (to add), and includes freight and insurance (to remove).
principles.source: 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports; 03 flag-state series
principles.uncertainty: Moderate: a few importers may use a landing-country or EEZ test. The main buyers (about 70% Thai) key on the flag.

principles.statement: Freight and insurance on frozen tuna carried from Pacific transshipment points to Asian or Latin American canneries are about 3-8% of the CIF value, central 5%. Air-freighted fresh fish costs more but is a small share.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis (imports valued CIF); model knowledge of reefer freight rates
principles.uncertainty: Plus or minus about 2 points. The pack has no freight data.

principles.statement: The resident-operated share of Kiribati-flag catch value is sized from fleet evidence: only 43 of 116 register vessels carry an address hint, and resident-pattern hours are 7,415 (2023), 8,496 (2024) and 22,237 (2025) with no denominator. I take about one-third in 2023, 36% in 2024 and 50% in 2025. Hours tripled in 2025 while the mirror fell, so the share rises only part of the way.
principles.source: 02 register_counts and kir_flag_fishing_hours; 01 and 03 mirror totals
principles.uncertainty: Very high: hours carry no gear mix, catch rate or non-resident hours. 80% range for the share: 15-53% (2023), 17-57% (2024), 25-75% (2025).

principles.statement: Sales at sea to carriers are goods exports and the mirror captures them when the destination importer reports and codes by flag. About 68% of carrier encounters (67.5% on the Kiribati register) are followed by a Thai port call within 120 days (median 42 days), so a complete mirror should be roughly 68-75% Thai. The 2023 mirror is 87% Thai with 2-4 reporting partners a month, so some non-Thai destinations were probably not coded to Kiribati; 2024-25 (70-71%) look complete. Fresh, chilled and other forms outside the tuna HS set add a little.
principles.source: 02 ais_chain_facts; 01 monthly series; 06 raw_mirror_tuna_by_year; 05
principles.uncertainty: Chain shares count encounters, not value. The Thai share ran 66-84% in 2017-2022, so part of the 2023 gap may be ordinary variation.

principles.statement: Treatment and timing: goods sent for processing without a change of ownership are not goods exports, merchanting counts only the margin, and ownership may pass at sea about six weeks before the month the importer records. For resident operators these net to small amounts.
principles.source: 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1); 02 lag facts; 01 monthly series
principles.uncertainty: Cannot be sized from the pack. The sign of the processing effect and the point of ownership transfer are unknown, so ranges span zero.

principles.statement: Official records show what the compilers captured. Customs sees only goods crossing Kiribati's border, and the goods line follows customs totals in years with full customs data (2017, 2018, 2020, within 4%). Customs tuna is near zero in 2023-24 and 3.4 in 2025 (10 months); goods exports are 8.1, 8.5 and 17.3. Resident catch sold at sea or landed abroad is in balance-of-payments scope but needs a fisheries-administration source, so the gap to the mirror reflects concept, timing and coverage.
principles.source: 06 annual and how_to_read; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (Norway example)
principles.uncertainty: The compiler's sources are not documented in the pack, and the 2025 balance-of-payments values are estimates.

principles.statement: A goods export in the balance of payments needs a change of economic ownership from a resident to a non-resident. Fish caught by ships operated by residents and sold abroad directly counts, whether sold in a foreign port or at sea to a foreign vessel. The test is the operator's residence and who owns the catch, not the vessel's flag.
principles.uncertainty: Low on the concept. Moderate on the point of ownership change for at-sea sales to carriers, which sets the price that counts.

principles.statement: Residence of an operator follows its base of operations, not the flag or registry of its ships. A flagged vessel run or chartered from abroad has a non-resident operator, so its catch sold to non-residents is not a Kiribati export. An entity incorporated and substantially operating in Kiribati is resident.
principles.source: 05 residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136)
principles.uncertainty: High in application: the pack does not identify operator residence vessel by vessel. Register addresses may be agent addresses.

principles.statement: Importers code origin of sea-caught fish by the catching vessel's flag (wholly obtained in the country of the vessel). The mirror therefore follows the flag: it contains non-resident-operated fish on the Kiribati flag and leaves out resident-operated fish on other flags.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports; 03 (Nauru and Tuvalu series rise as Kiribati-coded series falls)
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. Some partners may apply landing or processing-country tests to part of the fish; the pack shows no sign of it for the main buyers.

principles.statement: Importers value imports CIF. True exports are valued where ownership changes, a free-on-board type value. Freight and insurance on carrier legs, and any trader margin between first sale and arrival, sit inside the mirror and must come out. Model knowledge puts the freight and insurance share of delivered frozen tuna at roughly 3.5 to 10 percent.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis (imports CIF); model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. Rates vary by route, season and whether first sale was at sea or on delivery.

principles.statement: Only a minority of Kiribati-flag activity looks resident. Register address hints exist for 43 of 116 vessels across three registers, and resident-pattern fishing hours were 7.4k, 8.5k and 22.2k in 2023 to 2025. The 2025 tripling is not matched by the mirror, which fell, so hours cannot be turned into value one-for-one; the resident share of the Kiribati-coded mirror is taken as a wide band.
principles.source: 02 kir_flag_fishing_hours, register_counts; 01 monthly totals
principles.uncertainty: High. Hours mix vessel types with very different catch per hour, and an address is a hint of residence, not a finding.

principles.statement: Resident-operated fish can fall outside the mirror through other flags (Nauru, Tuvalu), partners not in the monthly series (annual-only reporters, non-reporting partners), fresh or chilled fish outside the HS set, landings in third countries, and sales at sea. About two thirds of register-fleet at-sea encounters are followed by a Thai port call, so most at-sea sales are still caught by Thai import records, which limits the unrecorded route.
principles.source: 02 ais_chain_facts; 03; 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation; 06 raw_mirror note (annual versus monthly totals); model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High. No direct measure of resident fish on other flags or in non-reporting partners.

principles.statement: Official customs returns cannot see fish landed or sold abroad unless fisheries-administration data are used, so official goods exports reflect what passed through customs plus the compiler's other sources. They are context on coverage, not the concept. Their level and direction (customs tuna near zero in 2023, higher in 2025; months reported 7, 10, 10) say something about how much resident activity passes through Kiribati, not about total resident sales.
principles.source: 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation; 06 annual block and how_to_read
principles.uncertainty: High. Compiler sources and methods are not documented in the pack.

principles.statement: Timing differs by concept. Ownership changes at the sale, often at sea, while importers record on arrival, a median of about 38 to 42 days later. This shifts some fish across year ends. The net effect is small when flows are stable and larger when they change.
principles.source: 02 ais_chain_facts (lag median 38 days; Kiribati register 42); 01 monthly series
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. The lag applies to carrier-borne fish, mostly the Thai route; other routes are shorter.

principles.statement: The raw mirror measures catch by Kiribati-flagged vessels, not Kiribati-resident catch. Importers record partner by country of origin, and fish taken at sea is wholly obtained in the country of the vessel; the main buyers apply the flag test. So the mirror holds every Kiribati-flag vessel's fish, whoever runs it, and misses resident-run fish carried under other flags.
principles.source: 05 (partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports); 03
principles.uncertainty: Low for the main buyers (Thailand is about 70-87% of the mirror). Individual shipments may be coded to the landing or processing country.

principles.statement: A fish sale is a Kiribati goods export only if the operator who owns the catch is resident in Kiribati and sells to a non-resident. Flag, registration and flags of convenience do not decide residence. Resident-run fish sold at sea or abroad counts; a sale by a foreign-run Kiribati-flag vessel is between non-residents and does not.
principles.source: 05 (residence_vs_flag: BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136; bop_goods_fish: BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e))
principles.uncertainty: Rule is clear; application is hard because incorporation in Kiribati and substantial operations can differ, and operator and owner can differ.

principles.statement: Importers value imports CIF. A true export is valued FOB at the point ownership changes (alongside a carrier at sea, or at a Kiribati port), so freight and insurance to the buyer must come off. Carrier freight to Thailand is a larger share of value than shorter routes to other buyers.
principles.source: 05 (partner_basis metadata: imports CIF, exports FOB); model knowledge on reefer freight
principles.uncertainty: Moderate: single-digit percent of value, varying by year, route and contract terms.

principles.statement: The resident-run share of Kiribati-flag fish is a minority and moves with resident activity. Register addresses are only a hint (43 of 116 vessels have one). I scale the share with resident-address fishing hours (7,415; 8,496; 22,237 for 2023-25) against the FOB mirror, shade toward the direction of official returns, and do not treat hours as catch value.
principles.source: 02; 06; model knowledge on foreign-run and chartered fleets
principles.uncertainty: Very high: hours are not catch, most vessels lack a usable address, and register data can change between years.

principles.statement: The mirror also misses resident exports by routes the partner series does not capture: partners that report annually only (annual totals exceed monthly sums), destinations that do not report, third-country landings, and fresh or other products outside the tuna HS codes. These scale with resident activity and are positive. Resident operators running vessels under other flags are a further addition.
principles.source: 01; 03; 06; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High: there is no direct data on resident sales to carriers bound for ports that do not report.

principles.statement: Ownership of fish sold at sea changes before it arrives (AIS chain: about two thirds of encounters followed by a Thai call, median 42 days), while the mirror is dated at arrival. Merchanting records only a margin, and goods processed abroad without change of ownership are not goods exports. These are small adjustments.
principles.source: 02 (ais_chain_facts); 05 (customs_vs_bop_compilation, BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1)
principles.uncertainty: Moderate for timing (contracts differ); high for the size of merchanting and processing effects.

principles.statement: Kiribati's official goods exports and customs returns record what the compilers could observe. Customs cannot see fish sold at sea or landed abroad (the usual remedy is a fisheries-administration source), covered only 7 to 10 months in 2023-25 and recorded little tuna. Official figures give scale and direction for resident exports, not a ceiling or a floor; they differ from true exports by concept, timing and coverage.
principles.source: 06; 05 (customs_vs_bop_compilation: IMTS Compilers Manual Box XXIV.2, para 24.9)
principles.uncertainty: High: the compiler's other sources are not documented in the pack.

principles.statement: The same rules apply in all three years. Year differences enter only through observed inputs: Thai share of the mirror (freight weighting), resident-address hours (resident share), the annual-versus-monthly gap, monthly arrival timing and official returns. Fees paid by foreign fleets for access are primary income, not goods, and sit outside the bridge.
principles.source: 01; 02; 06; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: Moderate: the shading of the 2025 resident share is a judgement.

principles.statement: True exports are the FOB value of fish caught by Kiribati-resident operators and sold to non-residents, counted when economic ownership passes (loading, at-sea transfer or foreign port), whatever the flag, route or statistic.
principles.uncertainty: Low on the concept. The moment ownership passes depends on sales terms that are not in the pack.

principles.statement: Importers record origin by the catching vessel's flag and value imports CIF; Thai fisheries law also keys imports to the flag state. The raw mirror is therefore all Kiribati-flag catch reaching the seven reporters, resident-operated or not, and it omits resident-operated catch under other flags.
principles.source: 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports; 01 header note
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. Flag-based coding is the common practice but is not written down for every importer.

principles.statement: CIF includes reefer freight and insurance over long voyages (median 38-42 days from at-sea transfer to a Thai port). FOB at the point of sale is lower by a single-digit to low-double-digit share of CIF.
principles.source: 02 AIS chain facts; 01 note (values normally CIF); model knowledge on bulk frozen-tuna freight
principles.uncertainty: About 3-10% of the mirror. No unit values or freight rates are in the pack.

principles.statement: Operator residence follows BPM6 4.131-4.136, not flag or register. A Kiribati-flag vessel run from abroad (charter, foreign partner) has a non-resident operator; a Kiribati-incorporated operator running its own vessel is resident. Register-address hours (7.4k, 8.5k, 22.2k in 2023-25; 43 of 116 vessels with an address hint) show a resident minority but cannot size it.
principles.source: 05 residence_vs_flag (BPM6 4.134, 4.136); 02 fleet aggregates
principles.uncertainty: High. Total fleet hours, gear mix and what an address means for substantial operations are not given.

principles.statement: Sales at sea or in foreign ports by residents are exports when ownership passes. About two thirds of carrier transfers by the three registers are followed by a Thai call, which the flag-coded mirror sees. The monthly series misses annual-only reporters, non-reporting buyers, fish outside the listed HS lines, and resident catch under other flags (reflagging among Kiribati, Nauru, Tuvalu).
principles.source: 02 chain facts; 03 flag series; 05 origin_of_fish; 01 Thai share (87%, 70%, 71%); 06 annual vs monthly sums
principles.uncertainty: High. Detected carrier encounters are near zero in 2023-25, so the route mix is not observed.

principles.statement: Fish processed abroad without change of ownership, merchanting margins and fish kept at home are not goods exports. Ownership passes about 40 days before arrival, so a calendar-year mirror lags sales. Both effects are small next to the residence split.
principles.source: 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (Compilation Guide Table 5.1); 02 lag; 01 monthly arrivals
principles.uncertainty: Moderate. No information on processing arrangements or on sales terms.

principles.statement: Official goods exports and customs returns record what passes home customs or reaches the compiler through other sources. Fish sold at sea does not pass home customs; the standard remedy is a fisheries-administration source. Differences from true exports are differences of concept, timing and coverage. Here the official figures indicate direction (the 2025 rise) and the scale of fish landed at home, not the level of true exports.
principles.source: 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (IMTS Compilers Manual Box XXIV.2, 24.9); 06 how_to_read
principles.uncertainty: High. The compiler's methods and coverage are not documented; customs months reported are 7, 10 and 10.

principles.statement: The same method is used every year. The resident share of the flag-coded mirror moves with resident-pattern hours, damped because the 2025 jump in hours is not visible in the mirror. A Thai share above the chain share (2023) signals partial coverage of non-Thai flows, handled in L4.
principles.source: 02 hours; 01 Thai and non-Thai sums; 06 raw_mirror_tuna_by_year; model knowledge
principles.uncertainty: High. Hours are a proxy; gear, catch per hour and the number of vessels are unknown.

principles.statement: True exports are catch sold by operators resident in Kiribati to non-residents, valued at the point ownership changes (FOB). The vessel's flag and registration do not decide the operator's residence; a Kiribati-incorporated operator running its own vessel is resident and its direct sales at sea or in foreign ports are goods exports. If the operator is based abroad, the sale is between non-residents.
principles.source: File 05 bop_goods_fish and residence_vs_flag (BPM6 10.17(e), 4.131, 4.134, 4.136; IMTS 2010 para 1.31)
principles.uncertainty: The residence of each operator is not observed. Register address is only a hint and 43 of 116 register vessels carry any address hint.

principles.statement: The raw mirror is a flag concept. All seven importers record partner as country of origin, and fish caught at sea is wholly obtained in the country of the catching vessel. Fish caught by Kiribati-flagged vessels is therefore coded Kiribati whoever operates the vessel, and fish caught by Kiribati-resident operators on other flags is not coded Kiribati.
principles.source: File 05 partner_basis, origin_of_fish, thailand_fish_imports (Kyoto Annex K 2(f); IMTS 2010 para 6.25)
principles.uncertainty: Importers may apply registration or other nationality tests in individual cases. Assumed stable over 2023-2025.

principles.statement: Importers value imports CIF. A resident's sale is valued FOB at the vessel or transshipment point, so freight and insurance must come out. Long-haul reefer carriage to Thailand is a larger share of CIF value than shorter hauls or direct landings, so the correction is larger where the Thai share is larger.
principles.source: File 05 partner_basis (imports CIF, exports FOB); model knowledge on reefer freight rates
principles.uncertainty: About 4-11% of CIF for the Thai route and 1-8% for other routes. Rates are not in the pack.

principles.statement: Most Kiribati-flag catch is probably run by operators not resident in Kiribati. The flag-coded mirror stays in a band of roughly 86-140 across 2017-2025 while Kiribati-flag fishing hours with a resident address pattern swing between 3,066 and 22,237. Resident-run catch is therefore a minority of the mirror, and I scale it to hours with damping because an address change can move hours without a change of operator.
principles.source: File 02 hours by address pattern and register counts; file 03 Kiribati row
principles.uncertainty: Value per fishing hour is not observed (about 0.3k to 3.5k USD by gear). The unclassified vessels may include residents. High: resident share of the FOB mirror could lie between 4% and 45%.

principles.statement: A flag-based, monthly, HS-limited partner series misses part of what resident operators sell: vessels flagged elsewhere, sales at sea to carriers that deliver to non-reporting partners, landings in third countries, fresh or chilled fish under other HS codes, and partners that report annually only. BPM6 counts these sales when ownership changes.
principles.source: File 05 bop_goods_fish and customs_vs_bop_compilation; file 02 (Nauru and Tuvalu registers analysed with Kiribati; 32.5% of Kiribati-register fish-transfer events not followed by a Thai call); file 06 annual-only gap
principles.uncertainty: No direct measure. Sized as a fraction of resident-run catch, with wide ranges.

principles.statement: Timing and treatment: ownership changes at sea a median 42 days before a Thai port call, so arrivals lag sales by about six weeks. Fish sent for processing without change of ownership is not a goods export, and merchanting is recorded net. None of these is likely to be large for resident operators.
principles.source: File 02 AIS chain facts (median lag 42 days); file 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation (BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1)
principles.uncertainty: Contract terms are not observed. The timing effect depends on growth in resident flows; treatment effects have no direct evidence.

principles.statement: Official figures record what the compiler could observe under its own sources and methods. Fish sold at sea or landed abroad does not pass home customs by construction, so customs tuna exports (0.0, 0.6 and 3.4 in 2023-2025, for 7, 10 and 10 reported months) cover only a small part of resident sales. Balance-of-payments goods exports (8.1, 8.5, 17.3) cover all goods and mix customs with other sources. They are a cross-check, not a target.
principles.source: File 06 how_to_read and annual table; file 05 customs_vs_bop_compilation; IMTS 2010 Compilers Manual para 24.9
principles.uncertainty: The compiler's coverage and methods are not documented in the pack. A published figure can sit below or above true exports.

principles.statement: The same rules apply in all three years. Years differ only through observed inputs: the Thai share of the mirror (87%, 70%, 71%) for freight; resident-pattern hours (7,415, 8,496, 22,237) for the resident share; the gap between monthly sums and annual returns (3.71, 7.05, 1.26) for partners that report annually only; and the official returns, read as a check on direction.
principles.uncertainty: Medium. The 2025 jump in hours is damped, since the mirror fell in 2025 and the jump may partly reflect register addresses.

principles.statement: Importers in the partner series record the value CIF and the origin by the flag of the catching vessel. A FOB export value therefore needs freight and insurance removed from every mirror dollar, and any fish added from outside the mirror must be stated FOB.
principles.source: Files 00 and 05 (partner_basis: imports CIF, exports FOB; origin_of_fish; thailand_fish_imports); model knowledge on reefer freight.
principles.uncertainty: Freight and insurance share for frozen tuna carried from the Pacific to Thailand or landed elsewhere is not in the pack; I take roughly 4-10% of CIF value, higher for the Thai route.

principles.statement: Residence of the operator, not the flag, decides whether a sale is a Kiribati export. If the operator is resident in Kiribati (incorporated or registered there, with real operations there), its direct sales of catch to non-residents, including at sea, are exports. If the operator is based abroad and only uses the Kiribati flag or a charter, a sale between non-residents is not.
principles.source: File 05 (residence_vs_flag: BPM6 4.131, 4.134, 4.136; bop_goods_fish: BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e); IMTS 2010 F.19, 1.31).
principles.uncertainty: Register address is only a hint; foreign-run vessels can carry a local agent address and resident joint ventures can carry a foreign one. Incorporation versus substance is not observable in the pack.

principles.statement: Most of the Kiribati-coded mirror is expected to come from operators not resident in Kiribati, with a resident minority. The minority should be larger when resident-pattern fishing hours are higher and when the non-Thai route (landings and local-linked sales) is a bigger share of the mirror than the Thai at-sea carrier route.
principles.source: File 02 (resident-pattern hours; AIS chains: about two-thirds of Kiribati-register at-sea encounters are followed by a Thai port call); file 06 (Thai and non-Thai split); model knowledge on charter and flag arrangements.
principles.uncertainty: Very high. Hours have no denominator and no gear split, so they cannot be turned into dollars directly. In 2025 hours tripled while the mirror did not rise. The route-to-residence link is a judgement.

principles.statement: Fish caught by Kiribati-resident operators can sit outside the Kiribati-coded mirror: vessels flagged elsewhere are coded to their flag by the main buyers, some partners report annually only or not at all, some destinations are outside the seven reporters, and some products fall outside the tuna HS codes (fresh or chilled fish, other species).
principles.source: File 05 (origin_of_fish: reflagging series show buyers follow the flag); file 03 (Nauru and Tuvalu series); file 06 note (Comtrade annual totals above monthly sums); model knowledge.
principles.uncertainty: High. The pack gives no operator residence for vessels on other registers, no list of non-reporting destinations, and no non-HS-code trade. Sizes rest on judgement with wide ranges.

principles.statement: The official figures are evidence about what the compilers recorded, not a measure of true exports. Fish landed abroad or sold at sea never passes Kiribati customs, so customs and customs-based balance of payments goods can sit below true resident exports. They could sit above only if fish that is not a resident's were counted, and the pack shows no sign of that.
principles.source: File 06 (how_to_read; BOP goods exports 8.07, 8.49, 17.34 are all goods; customs tuna 0.00, 0.59, 3.44 for 7-10 months); file 05 (customs_vs_bop_compilation; Compilers Manual Box XXIV.2).
principles.uncertainty: Compiler methods are not documented in the pack. Non-tuna goods are in the BOP totals, and customs months are incomplete, so the tuna content of the BOP series is unknown.

principles.statement: BPM6 records a good when economic ownership changes; importers record it at arrival. With a median lag of about 40 days between an at-sea encounter and a Thai port call, the mirror's calendar year is shifted by about six weeks for the Thai route. The year-end effect is small unless flows change sharply.
principles.source: File 02 (AIS chain lag: median 38-42 days, quartiles 22-53); file 05 (BPM6 10.13); file 01 monthly flows.
principles.uncertainty: Lag applies mainly to the Thai route. Early-2026 months are incomplete (file 01), which matters for the 2025 year-end.

principles.statement: Treatment items (goods sent for processing without change of ownership, merchanting, re-exports, fish kept in the economy) can change what counts as a good, but the question counts fish that residents caught and sold. Without evidence on their direction, they are centred on zero with a symmetric range.
principles.source: File 05 (customs_vs_bop_compilation: BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1); model knowledge.
principles.uncertainty: The pack holds no evidence on tolling, merchanting or re-export arrangements, so size and sign are unknown.

principles.statement: The same rules apply in all three years. Year-to-year differences come only from observed inputs: the Thai share, the resident-pattern hours (damped, because the address is a hint and the mirror did not move with hours), the gap between Comtrade annual and monthly totals, and year-end flows.
principles.source: Files 01, 02 and 06; model knowledge.
principles.uncertainty: The weights given to hours and route mix are judgements; different weights would move the resident share by several points.

principles.statement: A Kiribati goods export is fish owned by a Kiribati-resident operator and sold to a non-resident. Residence follows where the operator is incorporated or does significant production, not the vessel's flag; the operator may differ from the owner (charter, operating lease).
principles.source: BPM6 10.13, 10.17(e), 4.131, 4.134, 4.136 (file 05: bop_goods_fish, residence_vs_flag)
principles.uncertainty: Each operator's residence is a matter of fact (incorporation, base of operations) that the pack does not give; an address on a register may or may not meet the test.

principles.statement: The partner series is a flag-based origin series: importers treat fish caught at sea as wholly obtained in the catching vessel's country, and Thailand's fish-import rules key to the flag state. So the mirror holds all Kiribati-flagged catch whoever operates it, and holds no resident-operated catch under other flags.
principles.source: Kyoto Annex K 2(f); IMTS 2010 6.6, 6.7, 6.25; Thai Fisheries Ordinance ss.95-96 (file 05: origin_of_fish, partner_basis, thailand_fish_imports); file 03
principles.uncertainty: Each importer's own rule is not fully documented and 'vessel of that country' is undefined. The Nauru and Tuvalu series show flag coding in practice but not who operates those vessels.

principles.statement: Importers value imports CIF; the balance of payments needs market value at the change of ownership, which for fish sold at sea or landed is close to FOB. Freight and insurance come out first, more for fish carried a long way to Thailand than for direct landings.
principles.source: File 05 partner_basis (imports CIF, exports FOB); BPM6 valuation at change of ownership; model knowledge of reefer freight
principles.uncertainty: The freight share is not in the pack: taken as about 7% of Thai-bound value (80% range 4.5-9.5%) and 3% for other partners (1.5-6%).

principles.statement: The resident share of Kiribati-flag fish can only be hinted at. The register-address hint (owner or operator address in Kiribati) is a proxy for residence, not a finding; I use the movement in hint hours for direction and keep the share wide.
principles.source: File 02: address_resident_pattern hours 7,415 (2023), 8,496 (2024), 22,237 (2025); 43 of 116 register vessels carry an address hint; BPM6 4.134
principles.uncertainty: Total fleet hours and the hours of foreign or unclassified addresses are not in the pack, so a share cannot be computed; the 2025 tripling may partly reflect register changes.

principles.statement: Resident-operated fish can reach buyers by routes the seven-reporter monthly series does not hold: partners that report annually only, landings at hubs or processors that are not reporters, and fresh whole tuna under other codes. Both standards put these sales in scope although they are hard to collect.
principles.source: IMTS 2010 1.31, F.19; BPM6 10.17(e); file 06 (annual totals exceed monthly sums by 3.71, 7.05, 1.26); file 01 (reporters per month)
principles.uncertainty: The annual gap is observed; the share going to non-reporting hubs and other codes is not observed. Only 2-5 reporters a month appear in 2023 against 5-8 later.

principles.statement: Ownership of fish sold at sea changes at transshipment, a median 38 days before the Thai customs record, so a calendar year of sales lines up with Thai arrivals from early February to early February. Landings abroad carry no such lag.
principles.source: File 02 ais_chain_facts (median lag 38 days, quartiles 23 and 53); BPM6 change-of-ownership principle
principles.uncertainty: The lag comes from encounters seen up to 2022; AIS-seen encounters almost vanish in 2023-2025, so the lag is assumed unchanged. Early-2026 arrivals are provisional and may reflect rerouting rather than timing.

principles.statement: Goods sent abroad for processing without a change of ownership are not goods exports; fish bought from non-residents and exported after local processing is a resident export of processed goods but is not resident catch; net merchanting is only a margin. The evidence shows these as small, so they get a small, wide layer.
principles.source: BPM6 Compilation Guide Table 5.1 (file 05); BPM6 10.13; file 06 customs tuna exports 0.00, 0.59, 3.44
principles.uncertainty: No data on toll-processing contracts, merchanting, or the origin of fish that leaves through customs.

principles.statement: Official goods exports follow the same change-of-ownership concept but are built from customs returns and other sources. Fish caught by residents and sold at sea or landed abroad never passes home customs, so a published figure can sit well below true exports; it shows what the compiler could observe. It gives direction, not a target.
principles.source: IMTS 2010 Compilers Manual 24.9 and Box XXIV.2 (file 05, customs_vs_bop_compilation); file 06 how_to_read
principles.uncertainty: The compiler's methods and any confidential fisheries sources are not documented in the pack.

official_use.text: Used only as evidence of coverage and direction. Part-year customs tuna (0.00, 0.59, 3.44) gives a floor for the customs-visible part of resident exports, and the 2025 step-up in customs and balance-of-payments goods supports a higher resident share in 2025. Layer levels were not fitted to these figures.

Coverage evidence only, not a target. Customs tuna exports were near zero in the partial-year 2023-24 returns and the goods line stayed flat near 8, so resident sales at sea are probably mostly unrecorded (P6). The 2025 rise in customs tuna and in the goods line supports the higher resident share used for 2025.

Used as coverage evidence, not a target. Customs tuna exports (0.00, 0.59, 3.44; 7 to 10 months reported) feed a small part of L4 after annualising and a resident-caught haircut. The 2025 rise in BOP goods and customs lines supports the higher resident share that year. BOP goods include non-tuna items, so it sets no floor or ceiling.

Used only to read compiler coverage. Customs tuna exports (0.00, 0.59, 3.44 USD m; 7 to 10 months) and the goods line (8.07, 8.49, 17.34, including non-tuna goods) sit far below the mirror, consistent with catch sold at sea falling outside customs. The 2025 rise supports a higher resident share that year. No layer is tuned to them.

Used only as evidence of compiler coverage. Customs tuna exports (0.00, 0.59, 3.44) and total BOP goods (8.07, 8.49, 17.34) show recorded sales are small, as customs cannot see fish sold at sea or landed abroad. The 2025 step-up matches the rise in resident fishing hours. Not a target or a cap.

Used as evidence of compiler coverage, not as a target. The goods line tracks customs totals in full-data years, and customs tuna is small (0.00, 0.59, 3.44 for 7, 10 and 10 months). Fish sold at sea by residents therefore probably sits outside the recorded line. The 2025 rise supports more resident activity that year.

Used only as a coverage check: customs tuna lines are near zero for 7-10 reported months and goods exports of 8-17 USD m include non-fish goods, so recorded resident tuna is small and landed-only. The 2025 rise in both the goods estimate and register-address hours supports a higher 2025 resident share. No layer is set to match them.

Used for direction and as a visible floor only: customs recorded no tuna in 2023 (7 months), little in 2024, more in 2025, and the goods total roughly doubled in 2025. This tilted the 2025 resident share up. No layer is calibrated to official levels; composition and months reported are incomplete.

Coverage evidence only. Goods exports track customs returns, so they reflect goods crossing the border, not sales at sea; recorded tuna was 0.00, 0.59 and 3.44 (7, 10, 10 months). I read this as a floor on resident landings through customs and a sign that 2025 resident activity rose, not as a level for true exports.

Used as a consistency check, not a target. Customs tuna (0.00, 0.59, 3.44 USD m; 7, 10, 10 months reported) and goods exports (8.07, 8.49, 17.34) suggest little resident fish passes home customs, and the 2025 step-up fits higher resident-pattern hours. This supports a low 2023-24 and higher 2025 resident share. It sizes no layer directly.

Coverage evidence only. Customs tuna returns are near zero (0.00, 0.59, 3.44 in 7-10 reported months) and BOP goods exports (8.07, 8.49, 17.34) cover all goods, so resident catch sold at sea or landed abroad is probably thinly captured. I used the 2025 rise to support a higher resident share and unrecorded-route layer, not as a target.

Used as coverage evidence only. Customs tuna near zero in 2023-24 and goods exports near 8 suggest resident sales at sea are not captured by that line; the 2025 rise in both supports a higher resident share that year. Not used as a target, floor or ceiling for any layer.

Context only. Goods exports track customs when customs exist (2017, 2018, 2020), and customs tuna is near zero in 2023-24, which suggests resident catch sold at sea is largely not collected. The 2025 rise (customs tuna 3.44) mildly supports higher resident activity. No layer is sized from these figures.

Used as a cross-check on compiler coverage, not a target. Customs tuna exports (0.00, 0.59, 3.44) and goods exports (8.07, 8.49, 17.34) are far below the mirror, consistent with customs-based records missing resident sales at sea. Annualised customs tuna sets a floor for resident exports; the 2025 rise supports a larger resident share.

Used only as evidence of compiler coverage, not as a target or cap. Customs tuna exports (0, 0.59, 3.44; 7, 10, 10 months) and goods exports (8.07, 8.49, 17.34, including non-fish goods) are small, consistent with resident sales at sea not crossing the border. The 2025 step-up supports a higher resident share and a larger L4 in 2025.

Coverage check only. Customs tuna exports are near zero (0.0, 0.59, 3.44 for partial years) and the goods line matched customs totals in 2017, 2018 and 2020, which suggests sales at sea or abroad sit outside it (P6). The 2025 rise supports a higher resident share that year. No layer is set equal to an official figure.

Coverage evidence only. Published goods exports (about 8 to 17) and customs tuna (0 to 3.4 in partial years) sit far below the flag-coded mirror, consistent with a customs-based compiler seeing landed fish but not resident sales at sea. The 2025 rise nudges the resident share and L4 up for 2025. Not a target or bound.

Cross-check only. Customs tuna returns (0.00, 0.59, 3.44; 7-10 months reported) and total BOP goods (8.07, 8.49, 17.34, all goods) were read as showing thin recorded coverage of resident sales at sea in 2023-24 and a rise in 2025, matching resident hours. They set a loose floor, not a target.

Cross-check only. Published goods exports (8.07, 8.49, 17.34) cover all goods, and customs tuna (0.00, 0.59, 3.44) covers part-years, so they show what the compiler's sources recorded, not total resident sales. Used for direction (2025 step-up) and as a loose floor; no layer value is set from them.

Evidence about compiler coverage only. Customs tuna returns (0.0, 0.6, 3.4 USD m for 7 to 10 months) and goods exports (8.1, 8.5, 17.3) sit far below the mirror, which fits resident sales at sea never passing customs. I used them as a visible floor and a hint of rising resident activity in 2025, not as a target.

Used as coverage evidence only. Customs tuna returns (0.00, 0.59, 3.44 over 7, 10 and 10 months) give a floor for resident fish crossing Kiribati customs, and their 2025 rise fits the rise in resident-pattern hours. The goods total includes non-fish items and is treated as neither target nor ceiling.

Used only as a coverage check. BOP goods exports track customs returns in full-coverage years, and customs tuna is 0.0, 0.6 and 3.4 for partial years, so the compiler mostly sees fish clearing Kiribati customs. It indicates sales at sea and landings abroad are largely outside it. No layer is anchored to the official level.

Used only as evidence of compiler coverage. Customs tuna (0.00, 0.59, 3.44) and BOP goods exports (8.07, 8.49, 17.34) are small, which fits resident sales at sea or abroad sitting outside recorded flows. The 2025 rise moves with resident-pattern hours, supporting a higher 2025 resident share. Not used as a target.

Context only. The goods line follows customs totals when customs data are complete (2017, 2018, 2020), and customs tuna is near zero in 2023-24, so resident catch sold at sea is probably outside the official records. The 2025 rise in customs tuna and goods exports supports a higher resident share that year. They set no level.

Used only as context on compiler coverage. Customs tuna returns near zero with 7 to 10 months reported fit resident sales at sea or landed abroad not passing customs (P7). The 2025 rise in both series supports a higher resident share and a larger L4 in 2025. No layer was calibrated to official totals.

Cross-check on scale and direction only. Goods exports of 8.07, 8.49 and 17.34, and customs tuna of 0.00, 0.59 and 3.44 over partial months, suggest little resident tuna passes customs and that resident activity rose in 2025. This shaded the 2025 resident share in L2. Not used as a target, floor or ceiling.

Used as context on compiler coverage, not as a target. Customs-recorded tuna is small (0 to 3.4) over 7-10 reported months, while goods exports roughly double in 2025. That fits sales at sea never passing home customs and supports a higher resident share in 2025. No layer's level is set from them.

Coverage check only. Customs tuna exports near zero show resident catch sold at sea or landed abroad mostly bypasses home customs (file 05). Balance-of-payments goods exports (8.1, 8.5, 17.3, all goods) give an order-of-magnitude check and the direction of 2025. No layer was set from them.

Customs tuna (0.00, 0.59, 3.44; 7-10 months) and BOP goods (8.07, 8.49, 17.34; all goods) suggest thin coverage of sales at sea. I read them as a rough floor for locally landed resident fish, not a target. The 2025 step-up modestly supported a higher resident share.

Direction only. Customs tuna exports are near zero (0.00, 0.59, 3.44 FOB; 7 to 10 months reported) and goods exports are 8.07, 8.49, 17.34, so resident sales at sea do not pass customs. The 2025 rise is read as more resident activity (higher resident share) and sizes a small processing adjustment.

audits.text: Checks and fixes. (1) L3 and L4 follow from P3 and P6 only as priors; no file measures them. I kept both as small shares with wide ranges (L3 bounded below by zero) and did not scale L3 by the 2025 hours jump, because 03 shows Nauru- and Tuvalu-flagged imports falling in 2025. (2) L2 is the dominant layer and rests on the resident-pattern hours alone (no total or foreign-pattern hours), so its share is a judgment: 18%, 19% and 33% with wide ranges, not a fit. If the 2025 hours jump is mostly a register-matching effect and the resident share stayed near 19%, 2025 true exports would be about 21, not 34. (3) Order and double counting: L2 is taken on the FOB value after L1; L4, L5 and L6 are scaled on the resident base only, so they cannot remove or add fish that L2 already removed. (4) Official cross-check, not a target: all three results sit above part-year customs tuna scaled to 12 months (0.0, 0.7, 4.1), as P8 requires, and the lower ends of the ranges stay above that floor. (5) Confidence tags are all inferred because no source states the size of any layer. Ranges combine through a joint simulation with shared freight and residence factors, which is why the true-export ranges are wide and skewed upward.

Checks. (1) L1: follows from P3, but the 8.5% and 6% rates are model knowledge, so the layer is tagged inferred with a wide range. (2) L2 carries almost all the uncertainty: P4 gives only resident-address hours with no denominator, so the kept share (8%, 8%, 18%) is a judgement; I tempered 2025 below the 2.6-fold hours jump and set wide ranges. (3) L3 does not follow from evidence in the pack beyond P2; I kept it small and let its range start at zero. (4) Fix applied: L4's annual-only partner gap is scaled to the resident share and FOB, otherwise it would re-add fish L2 removed; L3 (other flags) and L4 (routes for Kiribati-coded fish) do not overlap. (5) The official figures were not used to size any layer; true exports exceed recorded tuna goods each year only because P6 allows resident sales at sea to be unrecorded, and the low ends of the ranges cover the case where the compiler saw most of them. (6) Total ranges come from a simulation of the layer ranges moving together with the resident share, not from adding widths, so they are wide and skewed upward. Same principles and method in all three years.

Checks: each bridge reconciles to 0.01 (start plus six layers equals true_exports). Layers L1, L2, L4 follow from P2, P3, P5 and the files cited. L3 rests on the P4 resident-share assumption with no direct operator-residence evidence; it keeps the widest relative band, and setting it to zero would lower true exports by about 9.5, 9.5 and 6.3 USD m. L5 and L6 are zero by design, not by evidence, and are shown with bands. Fixes made while auditing: (1) a flat 6% freight rate was replaced by route-specific rates so the larger non-Thai share in 2024-25 raises L1; (2) the 2025 resident share uses a damped hours signal rather than the full threefold rise; (3) the customs term in L4 was cut to 35% to avoid double counting with mirror flows and non-resident catch; (4) combined ranges come from a simulation with positively correlated resident-share and other-flag assumptions, not from adding band widths. The lumpy non-Thai months in 2024-25 are given the same resident share as other flows because the pack has no operator evidence for them. True-export ranges are right-skewed because the added layers are positive.

Reconciliation checked in code: start plus six layers equals true exports to 0.01 in all years. Layer check: (1) I first considered scaling the resident share directly from register hours (about USD 3 m per 1,000 hours over 2017-2024); this does not follow, because 2025 hours rose 2.6-fold while the mirror fell, so 2025 gets a 25 percent uplift in share plus a wider L4 allowance instead. (2) L3 and L4 could double count; L3 is limited to fish under other flags, L4 to Kiribati-flag fish by routes outside the series, so they are kept apart. (3) L5 and L6 have little direct evidence, so they stay small with ranges spanning zero. (4) The Thai versus non-Thai split of the resident share (15 and 40 percent) is inferred, not observed, and is the main source of uncertainty; the true-export ranges are right-skewed for that reason (simulated with independent layers). (5) AIS chain facts date mostly from before 2023 and are used only for lag and Thai-bound share, not for sizes. (6) Official figures were used for direction only. Implied resident-run mirror fish at FOB is about 14, 21 and 23 USD m.

Checks. (1) Reconciliation: each year, raw mirror plus the six layers equals true exports to 0.01. (2) L2 and L4 both scale with the resident share, so their errors move together; the true-export ranges come from a joint simulation (resident share, CIF/FOB rate, uncovered-route uplift, other-flag item), not from adding layer widths, and are skewed upward. (3) L3 first looked larger (4-5) when read from the Nauru/Tuvalu flag shift; cut to 2.5-3.0 because flag change does not show where the operator lives. (4) L3 fish already sits in recorded flows under other flags, so the L4 uplift is applied only to the resident Kiribati-flag part: no double count. (5) L5 does not follow from quantified evidence; kept near zero with a wide range instead of invented. (6) 2025: hours rose 2.6 times but the mirror fell, so I let the resident share rise only from 17% to 28%; a larger rise would put 2025 near the top of its range. (7) L1 range widened beyond the simulated 80% band to cover trader margins and fresh-fish freight. (8) The 2024 gap between annual and monthly mirror (7.05) may include revisions as well as annual-only reporters; only the resident share enters L4. (9) Official figures are coverage evidence, not a target; if the resident share is near the low end, true exports approach the recorded level.

Checks. (1) Each bridge reconciles to 0.01. (2) L2 is the complement of an assumed resident share of the FOB mirror; that share is not observed, since the pack has no hours for non-resident or unclassified vessels, so I anchored it on the weak link between resident-pattern hours and the mirror and set wide ranges. (3) L3 first looked larger given the Nauru and Tuvalu growth; I cut it because the pack has no operator residence for those flags. (4) L4 for 2025 draws on official returns only as evidence of resident activity; true exports stay above the official goods line in all years, so the official line is not used as a target. (5) The annual-only partner gap is counted once, in L4, because the starting point is the monthly sum. (6) L5 and L6 have no direct data and are kept small. (7) Total ranges are skewed upward because the resident share and the add-ons move together, and the upper tail covers foreign-owned but Kiribati-incorporated operators that pass the BPM6 residence test.

Weakest links. (1) L2 carries the answer: the resident-run share rests on register-address hours with no denominator or gear split, so I kept a modest central value, a wide range, and lifted 2025 only partly because the mirror did not rise with the hours. (2) L3 first looked larger given the size of the Nauru and Tuvalu series, but nothing in the pack shows residents operating there; cut to 1.5% with a wide range. (3) L4 uses the resident-run multiplier on partner gaps to avoid adding foreign-run fish; the annual-only gap may include revisions. (4) L5 at 10% is judgment from P7, not data. (5) L6 for 2025 uses early-2026 arrivals, which may be revised. Official figures set no layer. Principles were fixed before the numbers; differences between years come only from hours, Thai share, the annual-only gap and timing. Ranges are 10th-90th percentiles of a simulation of the stated parameter ranges, so total ranges are narrower than the sum of layer widths. Reconciliation checked for all three years.

Checks made. (1) I first considered converting resident-pattern hours straight into dollars; hours do not track the mirror across years (for example 2018 against 2021), so L2 uses a share of the FOB mirror with a wide range instead. (2) The 2025 hours jump was not carried fully into value, because the mirror fell and customs tuna is still small; the 2025 share is 30 percent, not the 50 percent or more that hours alone would suggest. (3) L4 applies only the resident share of the annual-only partner gap, so it does not re-add fish L2 removed. (4) L3 covers only resident operators' fish under other flags; third-country landings by Kiribati-flag vessels sit in L4, so nothing is counted twice. (5) L5 is applied after all additions to resident catch and is a single 10 percent judgment. (6) L6 is a timing shift for Thai-bound fish only, scaled by the resident share. (7) Payments to government for access are not goods and enter no layer. (8) Weakest layers: L3 and L4 coefficients and the L2 share are judgments (tagged inferred), and the true-export ranges are wide for that reason. No layer was found that lacks a principle; none changed after this review.

Checks. (1) L2 and the additions are on an FOB basis after L1; L4's annual-only component is scaled to a 25% resident share so non-resident fish is not added back. (2) L3 is for coding or flag issues and L4 for route or coverage issues, to avoid double counting. (3) First draft scaled the resident output linearly with 2025 hours, which implied more resident catch than the whole mirror; that does not follow from P4 (hours are a hint, register coverage is partial), so I capped the 2025 resident share near 35% of the FOB mirror and put the rest in the wide L3 range. (4) L6 is timing on the resident part only, shrunk for 2025 because early-2026 data may be incomplete. (5) L5 is small and unobserved and range spans zero. (6) Ranges for true exports combine layer half-widths in quadrature; resident share and L3 move together, so the upper ends may be slightly narrow. (7) Official figures were used only as coverage evidence (P8).

Checks: each bridge reconciles to 0.01. The resident share (P5) drives L2 and, through ratios, L3 to L6; it cannot be measured in the pack (no hours denominator, hints for 43 of 116 vessels), so ranges are wide and the true-export range comes from combining share and ratio uncertainty, not from adding widths. Hours-only scaling would put the 2025 share near 39%; P5 uses 30% because customs tuna shows little resident fish passes home customs and gear mix is unknown. L3 (a quarter) and L4 (a fifth) are judgement, tagged inferred, with no data on other flags. No overlap: L2 removes only the non-resident share of fish inside the mirror; L4 adds only the resident share of fish outside it; L5 and L6 act on resident fish only. L1 applies one rate to all fish, though a resident operator carrying its own fish would owe no freight deduction; the range allows for it. Result is far below the mirror in all years because the operator test (P2) removes most of it; it sits above official tuna because sales at sea never pass home customs (P8). Official figures and access fees were not used as layers.

Checks. (1) Each bridge reconciles to 0.01 (start plus six layers). (2) L2 is the largest and least observed layer: the 13% / 13% / 28% resident shares rest on P5, which is partly model knowledge; if residents are a larger share, L2 shrinks and true exports rise, and the 80% ranges carry this. (3) I first tried converting resident-pattern hours to value at purse-seine rates; that put 2025 resident catch above the whole mirror, which contradicts a flat 2025 mirror, so hours are used only as a floor and a ratio check. Implied resident catch (resident share of the mirror plus L3 and L4) is 2.05, 2.19 and 1.65 USD thousand per resident-pattern hour, a plausible mixed-gear value. (4) L4 in 2025 leans on hours rising while the mirror did not; if the hours reflect a register refresh or low-value gear, 2025 L2 share and L4 should fall and true exports would sit nearer 10-15. (5) L3 has no direct observation and is kept small with a wide range; L4 is applied to resident fish in the mirror plus the annual-only gap, not to L3, so there is no double count. (6) Official figures are used only as coverage evidence, never as a target or to set a layer. (7) L1 uses one rate by destination; fresh air-freighted fish may carry more. No layer was found to contradict the principles; none changed after sizing.

Reconciliation checked: each bridge sums to its true_exports to 0.01. L2 follows from P2 and P3 and carries most of the uncertainty; the resident share is a judgement anchored on register-address hours and low official tuna returns, not a measured value. L3 and L4 follow from P4 but are the least observed layers; I sized them as shares of the resident core, so they rise and fall with L2's assumption, and I kept their ranges wide. L1 and L6 are small and follow from P2 and P7. Corrections made: I first tried scaling resident hours by a value per hour, which implied a resident share near half in 2025; I discounted it because address hints cover only 43 of 116 vessels and may grow over time, and trimmed the 2025 resident share from 38 to 34 percent. I also fixed the L6 2025 rationale after checking the sign of the early-year flow change. No layer uses licence or access fees. Principles were not changed after sizing the layers.

Checks run. (1) Each bridge reconciles to 0.01. (2) L2 is applied to the FOB mirror after L1, so the order is respected and the resident base is not overstated. (3) L4 has three parts: annual-only reporters, unseen routes, and a 2023 non-Thai shortfall. The 2023 shortfall was sized net of the annual-only gap to avoid double counting, and it rests on a year-to-year comparison that could reflect real changes in buyers, so I kept it modest and wide. (4) The 2025 rates in L3 and L4 (above 2024) follow the resident-hours jump alone; the pack gives no direct evidence, so they are the weakest additions and the band reflects that. (5) I did not size any layer from official figures; I used them only to judge direction. Fixed during drafting: an early version scaled 2025 resident output in proportion to hours, which would exceed the whole mirror; I damped it to a 37% share. (6) Layers L5 and L6 are small and not separately identified, so their bands straddle zero. (7) Access fees are excluded as they are not goods. (8) Remaining weakness: the resident share (P4) drives most of the result; a lower share than assumed would leave true exports near the low end of each band. True exports must also be at least the customs-recorded tuna (0.00, 0.59, 3.44); all three bridges satisfy that.

Checked each layer against P1-P8. L1 is applied to the whole mirror before L2, so L2 and later layers are in FOB terms; consistent. L6 timing was first sized on all Thai-coded fish (-1.10, -0.37, -2.08) but, after L2, only the resident share remains, so it was scaled down; fixed. Customs-recorded tuna exports are treated as already inside the resident share of the mirror and are not added again; resident-run mirror catch (10.81, 12.52, 26.43) exceeds annualised customs tuna (0, 0.7, 4.1) in every year. L3 and the annual-only part of L4 cover different fish (other-flag versus Kiribati-coded), so there is no overlap. Resident-run catch in the bridge (L2 residue plus L3 and L4) is 17.3 / 19.7 / 38.8 USD m, against 17 / 19 / 50 from hours at a mixed per-hour value; 2025 sits lower by design because the register hint is weak and new fishing may not yet be sold. L5 is zero by absence of evidence, not a finding. The resident share in L2 drives most of the result, so true-export ranges are wide and right-skewed. Years use the same principles; differences come from fleet hours, the Thai share and official returns.

Checks made. (1) All three bridges reconcile to 0.01 and use the same eight principles. (2) L2 is the dominant layer and does not follow from observed data: the resident share is inferred from P2 and P6, so its range is wide, and L4 and L6 scale with the same share. True-export ranges come from joint draws of the share, freight rates, L3, L4, L5 and lag, so they are wider than any single layer and skewed upward because shares and additions are bounded below. (3) 2025 share raised from about 30% to 40% because resident hours rose 2.6 times while the mirror fell; the rest of the extra activity is placed in L4, not in L2, to avoid claiming equality. (4) L3 has only indirect support (no address data for other flags), so it is small with a floor at zero. (5) L5 sign is not supported by evidence; a positive merchanting add was dropped and the centre set near zero. (6) L1 removes freight and insurance only; any trader margin between first sale and importer value would add a little more removal, inside the stated range. (7) The annual-only partner gap in L4 was converted to FOB and resident share so that non-resident fish is not added. (8) Official figures were not used as a target or cap. Principles were not changed after numbers; the share parameters were re-centred once during calibration.

Checked each layer against P1-P8. Fixes made: L2 is charged on the FOB mirror so L1 is not double counted; the annual-only reporter gap inside L4 is scaled by the resident share (P1), since the non-resident part is removed anyway; L5 was first zero, but P7 says two-sided and proportional, so a small negative with a range spanning zero is used. No layer is set from an official figure; licence and access fees are excluded. Weakest links: the resident share (hours are a hint, the flag-fleet total is not given, and locally incorporated joint ventures with foreign partners could count as resident under 4.134, which would raise it), the 2025 uplift (hours tripled while the mirror fell, so some extra resident fish may sit outside the partner series, covered by L4's wide range), and the residence rate on other flags (no operator data). Ranges are right-skewed because the resident share cannot fall below zero but could be much higher; true ranges come from combining the layer uncertainties with shared dependence on the resident share, not from adding widths.

Checks. (1) Each bridge reconciles to 0.01. (2) L1 is applied before L2, and L2 keeps the resident share of the FOB mirror, so freight is not removed twice. (3) The annual-only partner gap sits in L4 at the resident share only, so no non-resident fish is added. (4) L3 holds resident fish the mirror cannot see because of flag or landing-country coding; L4 holds resident fish sold through routes outside the seven reporters. I kept these apart to avoid overlap. (5) Timing was first folded into L1; the layer definitions place it in L6, so I moved it. Two choices are weakly anchored: the 2025 rise in L3 (4.00 to 5.00) and the 2025 uplift in L4 (20% to 25%). Both rest on the hours and customs rise in P5 and P6; I kept the values, widened the ranges, and did not tie them to the official figures. The true-export ranges combine the resident share (the dominant, correlated driver of L2 and L4) with the other layers by root-sum-square, not by adding widths. The residence test (P2) cannot be settled from the pack: if more Kiribati-incorporated operators meet the BPM6 tests, true exports sit toward the upper end of each range. No layer was changed after this review.

Checked each layer against the frozen principles. L1 to L5 are sized on the FOB mirror in order, and L2 uses the post-L1 base. L4 was first drafted on the whole annual-only partner gap; it is now scaled by the resident share only, since non-resident fish is already removed in L2. L3 and L4 are assumption-based and kept wide. Official figures were used as a cross-check and not as the target. The 2025 resident share (16%) rests on a hours jump that may partly reflect register changes, so its range is widest. Timing in 2025 depends on low early-2026 imports and is set small. My estimates sit somewhat above total BOP goods exports in each year; that is consistent with BOP covering copra and other goods and with limited coverage of resident sales at sea, and it was not used to tune the layers. Each bridge reconciles to 0.01.

(1) L3 first looked larger from the flag-move pattern in file 03, but no file gives operator residence for Nauru, Tuvalu or other flags, so P3 supports direction only; I cut the central share to 2% and let the range start at zero. (2) L2 rests on one number, the resident share; no total hours are given, so the 7-40% range is wide and 2025 takes only part of the hours rise (P2). (3) The 2.0 extra in 2025 L4 is inferred from hours rising 2.6 times while Kiribati-coded imports fell; range 0-8. (4) The annual-only gap in L4 and the timing in L6 are converted to FOB and scaled by the resident share, avoiding double counting with L1 and L2; L5 applies only to what remains resident. (5) Official figures set no layer; they only confirm the answer sits above the few million of tuna they record. (6) Carrier encounters in 2023-25 are near zero, so the 38-day lag is borrowed from earlier years. After these changes every layer traces to a principle.

Checks and fixes. (1) Annual-only partner fish in L4 is Kiribati-flag coded, so it carries the same non-resident share as the mirror; only the resident share is added, not the full 3.7, 7.0 and 1.3. (2) L6 timing applies only to fish counted as exports, so it is scaled by resident share. (3) L3 covers fish in partner records under other flags; L4 covers fish with no partner record, so no fish sits in both. (4) In 2025 address-pattern hours tripled but the mirror fell; I raised the resident fish outside the mirror (L3, L4) and widened ranges rather than scaling L2 by hours. (5) L3 has no direct evidence and rests on an assumed 2% share of Nauru and Tuvalu coded flows. (6) No positive merchanting term is added in L5 because L2 already removes all non-resident catch. (7) Official figures were not used as a target: central estimates are 3.7, 4.4 and 2.4 times balance-of-payments goods exports, which P5 and P8 explain through coverage. Main driver is the resident share in L2: each 10 points is about 7.7 to 9.3 USD m. Order, signs and reconciliation (start plus six layers equals true exports) were checked for all three years.

Each layer was checked against the principles. (1) L3 has no direct register evidence for other flags; it is kept small (about 1% of the Nauru- and Tuvalu-coded series) with a range down to zero, rather than a larger guess. (2) L4's route gap first looked like 25% of resident fish; it was cut to 15% because the seven reporting importers are the main buyers of Pacific frozen tuna (P5). (3) L6 timing was first applied in full; it is now at half weight because only carrier-borne fish lags. (4) The 2025 resident share (30%) is derived from hours, not copied: 22,237 / (8,496/0.14 + 13,741) = 0.30, and its range is wider. (5) Every bridge reconciles to 0.01. (6) Cross-checks: implied resident exports exceed customs-recorded tuna in all years (floor check, P7). The central true values are about twice the all-goods official total in 2023-24 and 1.8 times it in 2025, which fits fish sold at sea not crossing customs, but this rests on the resident share, the dominant uncertainty, and the lower 80% bounds sit near or below the official total. (7) Near-zero AIS encounters in 2023-25 are treated as non-detection, not as evidence on routes. No layer was left unsupported by a principle.

Checks: (1) L1 is applied before L2 so L2 acts on FOB values. (2) First pass added the whole annual-minus-monthly partner gap in L4; it contains non-resident-run fish, so it is now scaled to the resident share to avoid adding fish that L2 removes. (3) L3 and L4 allowances were tied to resident share, since they only add resident fish. (4) The 2025 resident-hours jump does not fit the falling mirror: I raised the resident share only partly (33%) and put the rest in L3 and L4 with wide ranges rather than scale output to hours. (5) L5 and L6 rest on thin evidence and are small. (6) Official figures were not used to set any layer. The resident share (L2) dominates uncertainty; ranges combine it with linked L3 and L4 and independent L1, L5 and L6, so the true-export range is wide and right-skewed.

Checks: each bridge reconciles to 0.01 and L2 is computed on the FOB value after L1. Findings: (1) L2 rests almost entirely on the resident-share judgement in P3, so its range is wide and the true-export range is built from the share range plus layer ranges, not from summed widths. (2) L3 had no direct data anchor; I tied it to a fraction of the resident-coded amount with a range starting at zero rather than a point claim. (3) L4 and L3 could overlap for fish landed in unreported countries; I kept L4 at about 25% and did not add further. (4) L5 is a small judgement and stays near zero. (5) The 2025 rise reflects hours and customs tuna, not the mirror, which fell; this is why the 2025 range is widest. No layer is left without a principle; the same shares and ratios are used in all three years, differing only where hours, Thai share and annual-only gaps differ.

Checked each layer against the frozen principles. L1 follows P3-P4. L2 follows P2 and P5; the 2025 share was first read from hours alone (about 60%) and lowered to 50% because hours tripled while the mirror fell. L3 rests only on P3 and a judged share of the Nauru and Tuvalu mirror; no residence data exist for those flags, so its lower bound is zero. L4 in 2023 is inferred from the Thai share; I counted about half the implied gap because the Thai share ranged 66-84% in 2017-2022, and kept it separate from L3 and L6 to avoid double counting. L5 and L6 cannot be sized from the pack and straddle zero; L6 assumes ownership passes at sea, and is nil if it passes on arrival. Official figures set no level; they only support a higher resident share in 2025. The true ranges come from simulating the layers with one shared resident-share draw, so they are wider at the bottom than the central sum suggests; the resident share dominates all three years. Each bridge reconciles to 0.01.

Checked each layer against the frozen principles. L2 rests on a judgment share (P5), not a measured one; the 2025 share step was capped because scaling hours one-for-one would put resident value above the whole 2025 mirror, so that approach was rejected. L3 uses a 2 percent share of Nauru and Tuvalu coded imports, a judgment with no direct support; kept but given a wide range. L4 avoids double counting with the mirror by adding only the annual-only gap and routes outside the HS set and reporting partners, since most at-sea sales already reach Thai records. L6 mixes a computed timing shift with a small judged allowance. No layer was fitted to official totals. Each bridge reconciles to 0.01.

Checked each layer against P1-P8. Weakest link is L2: hours are not catch value and only part of the fleet has an address, so its range is wide and L3-L6, which scale with the same share, make the true range skew upward. 2025: hours alone imply about 34% resident-run, but the mirror did not rise and recorded tuna stays small, so I shaded to 26%; this is a judgement. Fixes made while drafting: L4's annual-versus-monthly gap was first all-flag CIF value, now converted to FOB at the resident share; L3's upper bound was first too wide and now follows its simulated 80% range; L1 is applied before L2 so the resident share acts on FOB value. No overlap: L3 is resident catch under other flags, L4 is Kiribati-flag resident routes. L6 uses Thai arrivals only. Official figures set scale and direction, never the answer.

Checked each layer against P1-P8. (1) L2 is applied to the FOB mirror after L1, not to the CIF total, so the two layers do not overlap. (2) L3 covers resident catch under other flags; L4 covers Kiribati-flag or resident fish that reaches buyers, codes or HS lines outside the monthly series. The rise in customs-recorded tuna in 2025 is not added to either, because Kiribati-flag fish that passes customs is already in the mirror; it only supports a higher resident share and a larger L3 in 2025. (3) The 2023 Thai share (87%) is above 2024-25 (70-71%) and the 68% chain share; only the resident fraction of the implied gap is added in L4, and not in 2024-25. (4) The 2025 resident share (21%) is not scaled in line with the 2.6-fold hours, because the mirror fell; that is the main judgement call and the range is wide. (5) L5 and L6 are not sized from numeric evidence beyond the monthly timing shift, so their ranges are wide and include zero. No layer uses access fees, and no official figure is a target. Each bridge reconciles to 0.01.

Checks. (1) Each bridge reconciles: raw mirror plus the six layers equals true exports to 0.01. (2) L1 and L2 are linked: true exports depend on L1 only through the resident FOB amount, so the true-export ranges are built from the resident amount and the L3-L6 ranges, not by adding the L1 width. (3) Fix made: I first considered adding the whole gap between annual returns and monthly sums (3.71, 7.05, 1.26) to L4. That fish is mostly Kiribati-flag catch run by non-residents, so only the resident share is added. (4) Fix made: scaling 2025 resident catch in proportion to hours (about 3 times 2024) conflicts with a falling mirror and with the possibility that the hours jump reflects register addresses; I damped it. (5) Weak links: the resident share of the mirror (L2) rests on a hint and an assumed value per fishing hour; L3 and L4 are proportions of the resident amount, not measured; L5 has no direct evidence and is near zero. These are why true-export ranges are wide and skewed upward. (6) No layer uses licence or access payments, vessel names or company names.

Checked each layer against P1-P8. L1 follows P1; L2, L3 and L4 are FOB, so no second valuation step. Fixes made: (1) L3 was first drafted in proportion to the Nauru and Tuvalu series, but P4 gives no evidence that their operators are resident in Kiribati, so I cut it to about 1.7% with a floor near zero. (2) The 2025 resident share was first tied to hours (about 50% or more); P3 and P8 say hours are a hint with no denominator and the mirror did not move, so I damped it to 36% and widened the range. (3) The 2025 timing term rests on thin early-2026 months, so I halved it and widened the range. (4) L5 stays at zero because nothing in the pack sizes it. L2 and L4 share the resident share, so true-export ranges come from a joint simulation with that common driver, not a sum of widths, and are skewed upward. The official figures were used only as coverage evidence (P5), not as a target. The largest unresolved uncertainty is the resident share of the Kiribati-flag mirror.

Checks and fixes. (1) Order: L2 is applied to FOB fish after L1, and L3, L4 and L6 scale with the same resident share, so no layer double-counts; an early draft cut non-resident fish from the CIF value and was corrected. (2) L4: the annual-only partner gap was first taken at full CIF value; it is now FOB and resident share only. (3) L3 and L4 do not overlap: off-flag resident fish sent by non-reporting routes is not added separately (small, inside the ranges). (4) The 2025 resident share leans on a tripling of address-hint hours that the mirror and customs only partly echo; I held the share down and widened its range. (5) L6 uses provisional early-2026 Thai arrivals, which may reflect rerouting; its range allows for that. (6) L5 rests on a small share of customs tuna and on unsized processing and merchanting cases, so it stays near zero with a wide range. No layer treats an official total as the target. The resident share in L2 drives most of the width of the true-export ranges, which are correlated across layers and so are wide.

principle_themes.statement: A goods export is a change of economic ownership from a resident to a non-resident, valued free on board at the point of sale; direct sales at sea or abroad by resident operators count.

Operator residence follows incorporation and base of operations, not flag or registry: a Kiribati-flagged vessel run or chartered from abroad is non-resident, while a Kiribati-based operator is resident whatever the flag.

Importers record the origin of sea-caught fish by the catching vessel's flag, so the partner-reported series includes Kiribati-flagged fish run by non-residents and omits fish of resident operators under other flags.
Importers value fish including freight and insurance (CIF), so a deduction to free-on-board value is needed; analysts put it at a few percent to about ten percent of value, varying by route.

Analysts sized the resident-operated share of Kiribati-flagged fishing from register address hints and resident-pattern fishing hours, mostly finding a minority share, wide uncertainty and a higher share in 2025.

The monthly partner-reported series misses some resident sales: partners reporting annually only, buyers that do not report, third-country landings, and fresh or other products outside the listed customs codes.
Official goods and customs figures show what compilers recorded; customs cannot see fish sold at sea or landed abroad, so analysts used them for coverage and direction, not the level of true exports.

Ownership often passes in sales at sea to carriers, with about two-thirds of tracked transfers followed by a Thai port call roughly six weeks later; importers record arrival, so year-end timing shifts slightly.

Treatment rules narrow what counts: goods processed abroad without change of ownership, merchanting and fish kept at home are not ordinary exports; analysts judged these effects small, with little direct evidence on size.
Kiribati-resident operators may run vessels under other flags, notably Nauru and Tuvalu, whose coded imports are large; no data identify those operators, so analysts add a small, uncertain amount.
Resident-pattern fishing hours and official tuna and goods exports rose in 2025 while the partner-reported series did not, which analysts read as a possible sign of higher resident activity.
The Thai share of the partner-reported series (87%, 70%, 71%) and monthly reporter counts vary by year; the high 2023 Thai share and few reporters may signal thin coverage of non-Thai flows.
